News.title: Inside secret cyber system guarding UK airports against ‘bomb drones’ after Leipzig ‘attack’ raised fears of Putin plot
News.content:
BRITAIN’S biggest airports are deploying cutting-edge technology to stop hostile drones from causing holiday chaos this summer.

It comes after an explosive-laden drone was found at a German airport this week, which a security expert warns shows Putin is prepared to take down a European passenger jet.



The counter-drone systems used at major UK airports allow operators to jam or even launch a mid-air cyber attack to seize control of rogue aircraft before they threaten flights.

But with no clear national standard setting out the level of defence ALL airports must have, some transport hubs are vulnerable to attacks.



Mark Legh-Smith MBE, from specialist counter-drone security company OSL, whose clients include Heathrow, Thorpe Park and Wembley Stadium, explained how his firm combines different technologies to detect and monitor drone activity over areas of interest.

By integrating radio frequency scanners, advanced radar and AI-enabled cameras, their system creates a single moving object on a digital dashboard at a site’s control room.



Once the drone enters an ‘alert zone’, operators can jam its controls or even hijack it in mid-air using an “effector” system which overrides the drone pilot’s radio link.

Legh-Smith told The Sun: “So you can either use jamming where you emit with a radio frequency emitter at the same frequency as the drone control. So the drone can’t hear, if you like, it can’t receive its controlling signal anymore.



“Then there’s a cyber version, where it detects the radio link from the controller to the drone. And then it hacks into that link and then replaces the controller. That can enable it to take over the drone and fly it away or land it somewhere for the police to take over it.”

The groundbreaking cyber-takeover technology has only been in operation since around 2019 after Gatwick Airport was brought to a standstill for almost three days following suspected drone sightings.

Counter-drone systems were heavily invested in by major airports after more than 1,000 flights were disrupted in December 2018.



But Legh-Smith warned there is “no clear uniform standard” setting out what level of protection Britain’s airports must have, leaving defences to individual operators.

He said: “There’s a lot of variety between different airports about what level of counter-drone system, if any, they have in service.”

Recent FOI responses indicate the number of unidentified drone incursions at UK airports is on the rise, although many are believed to involve nuisance or inexperienced operators.

In 2023, 43 incidents were reported to authorities, rising to 70 the following year and 83 in the first ten months of 2025.

The cutting-edge technology can also pinpoint the drone pilot’s exact location, allowing police to swiftly apprehend them.



After a suspected bomb-fitted drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig Airport on Tuesday night, Legh-Smith said: “This is probably the first time in Western Europe that we’ve seen a drone weaponized and used as the weapon.

He added this marks “quite a serious” escalation.

Security expert Will Geddes said the terrifying drone breach had “shaken fear across not only militaries and across the world, but also commercial airports“.



And he warned the chilling ordeal proved that Putin is more than capable of using a drone to blow up a passenger plane in Europe.

Geddes told The Sun: “It’s a disaster waiting to happen.”

Legh-Smith warned the technology is constantly evolving as hostile actors develop new ways of bypassing existing counter-drone systems, including using 4G and 5G networks instead of traditional radio links.

He said: “If you take, say, the Russian-Ukraine war, new drone types are created monthly… four or five new types of drone [are made] a month to achieve a new method or defeat a new counter-drone system.”

He added: “As a result of that, a counter-drone system also needs to adapt extremely quickly.”



But military experts fear hostile actors could use military-grade aircraft to bring major transport hubs to a halt.

Last month former Royal Navy commander Tom Sharpe told The Sun Russia “almost certainly” flew drones over Denmark from a shadow fleet ship in 2025 and warned it was “a mathematical certainty” Britain would eventually face a similar threat.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “They’ll fly drones from a ship into, let’s say Heathrow airspace and shut Heathrow down.”

Asked if the UK was vulnerable to numerous drones flying over the same airspace, Legh-Smith responded: “We are. At some places. Some places would be better prepared for it than others.”

News.title: Serial fraudster who strangled wealthy heiress wife to death over £4m fortune is walking free, inquest hears
News.content:
A SERIAL fraudster who strangled his wealthy heiress wife to death in a bid to cash in on her £4m fortune is “walking free”, an inquest heard.

Paula Leeson, 47, was unlawfully killed by her husband, Donald McPherson, who wanted to cash in on her £4million fortune before vanishing.



McPherson, 53, was cleared of murdering Paula after a judge ordered the jury to find him not guilty in 2021.

Three years later, Judge Mr Justice Richard Smith ruled the fraudster had unlawfully killed her.



The ruling blocked McPherson from inheriting Paula’s £4.4m estate.

Cops told an inquest that McPherson, currently living in New Zealand, should be serving a life sentence for murder.



The inquest heard no retrial for murder can take place unless compelling new evidence is found.

Paula was found dead in the pool at a remote holiday cottage in Denmark where the couple were staying in June 2017.



Jurors previously heard Paula suffered 13 separate injuries, which she could have sustained while being restrained or in a resuscitation attempt.

The court was told 5ft 5ins Paula was found in a pool that was under 4ft deep despite being a good swimmer and a healthy mum-of-one.

Paula stood to inherit the family business owned by her dad and oversaw the successful skip hire firm where she met McPherson.

She had the “misfortune” meeting the failing and indebted property developer when he came in to hire a skip in 2012.

The pair married in June 2014 following a “whirlwind” romance.



Their “no expense spared” ceremony was held at Peckforton Castle, Cheshire.

McPherson used multiple name changes and a “cover story” of being an orphan to hide his past after serving jail time for an £11m bank fraud in Germany.

The court heard he has been convicted of 32 criminal offences of dishonesty or fraud in New Zealand, where he was born.



He had taken out £3.5m life insurance on the mother-of-one shortly before her death on June 6, 2017.

Within hours of throttling her to death he was emptying her accounts of thousands of pounds to pay off his debts.

He joined a group called Widowed and Young, which he described as “Tinder for Widows”, a week after Paula’s death.

Her family asked a judge to rule that McPherson killed the heiress to stop him benefiting from her £4.4m fortune.

A coroner agreed with the unlawful killing verdict today.



Alison Mutch, senior coroner for Manchester South, told Stockport Coroner’s Court McPherson was heavily in debt and he was the only person to benefit from his wife’s death.

She added: “I am therefore satisfied he did murder his wife. Her death occurred because her husband compressed her neck to render her unconscious, causing her body to enter the pool, causing her to drown, to financially benefit from her death. Her death was as a result of an unlawful killing.”

Earlier, Detective Chief Inspector Daniel Clegg, of Greater Manchester Police said: “There’s no doubt this was a homicide. She died at his hands. I have not looked for anyone else.”

Sophie Cartwright KC, representing the Leeson family at the inquest, said “investigations are ongoing” and the Leeson family hope police, having in the last 12 months gained access to McPherson’s old laptop, will uncover evidence to “get them over the line for a retrial”, adding: “Their fight will continue after today.”

Paula’s brother Neville told the hearing her life had been taken by McPherson’s “greed”.



He added: “Now the man who murdered her is walking around free.

“Paula has repeatedly been let down by the criminal justice system.

“We will never accept that and will continue fighting for her.”

A court was told McPherson was struggling financially at the time – despite walking around with wads of cash in elastic bands.

Paula’s family said he was “running out of money”, which “super charged the financial motive” for him.



McPherson also “systematically” deleted data from his wife’s phone which may have explained what happened and showed “almost no upset or remorse” over her death, the court heard.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

His trial was dramatically halted in 2021 when Mr Justice Goose ruled there was insufficient evidence for jurors to safely convict.

He directed the jury to return a not guilty verdict to murder.

News.title: Drugged, robbed & dumped in alleys… inside the MALE spiking epidemic with 500,000 UK victims as grieving dad speaks out
News.content:
IT takes just seconds for a clear, odourless and tasteless liquid to be dropped into the victim’s drink.

He downs his pint and staggers out the pub door – followed by a hooded figure who waits for him to collapse in a backstreet, before stealing all the man’s belongings.





Welcome to Britain’s male spiking crisis where almost half a million men believe their drinks were laced with drugs.

Spiking has long been linked to vulnerable women who are then sexually assaulted but figures reveal that men are just as likely to be targets.

Government figures revealed five per cent of men believe they have been spiked.

Cops last month welcomed a 12 year jail term for one of the biggest ever seizures of GBL, worth £2.2million – saving hundreds of thousands of victims from being spiked.

And experts believe the drug could be involved in far more deaths than recorded.

Colin Mackie, who lost his son Greg, 18, to spiking in 2017, runs Spike Aware and says they now get more calls than ever from men who have been targeted.





“Everyone always thinks it happens to girls, but spiking has got legs and anyone can be a victim,” he said.

“It can happen for so many reasons, not just sexual assault. A big one now is theft and one of the big risk areas is your mobile phone using facial recognition or thumbprint.

“If someone spikes you, they can use your face or fingers to get access to everything, including your bank accounts.

“But one of the most common things we hear is people doing it as a prank and nothing happening. But it’s not funny.

“One lad rang me who had been spiked and someone had deleted all the photos of his phone but done nothing else. It had to be someone who knew him.

“Our aim is to make spiking as taboo as drink driving, so people feel the pressure not to put something in someone’s drink as a joke or to liven them up.

“People will now report others drink driving, and that’s what we want them to do if they see someone being spiked. Tell someone. That’s the best way to keep everyone safe.”

Greg, from Moffatt, Dumfriesshire, died after his soft-drink was spiked with the equivalent of five ecstasy tablets while in his Edinburgh university halls.

The most recent report on spiking by Drinkaware and Anglia Ruskin University found close to an even split between women and men being spiked – with nearly a million adults believing they’d had their drinks laced with drugs.



It also found the majority of incidents happened in pubs and clubs – although 15 per cent of those surveyed had been spiked in a domestic setting.

Traditionally, spiking has been opportunistic with recreational drugs being dropped into drinks, or in sexual assault cases, rohypnol was often used.

But now, gamma-butyrolactone (GBL) is becoming more common in the nighttime economy as it’s tasteless, odorless and colourless.

Dawn Dines from Stamp Out Spiking told The Sun: “We understand GBL is a drug of choice for people spiking drinks, as evidenced by the people contacting Stamp Out Spiking with their experiences and with such a huge haul of GBL being found by the police.”

Cops fear that it might be causing more deaths than anyone realises as it doesn’t take much to overdose a victim.

“GBL is the most dangerous substance that we encounter,” said Eoin Bradley, a trained nurse and Metropolitan Police’s lead officer for chemsex cases.

“It doesn’t matter if it’s in the intoxicant phase or within its withdrawal phase, both are life-threatening. I think it’s safe to say we don’t know the number of deaths linked to GBL.



“There is a miniscule difference between a recreational dose and then one that is life-threatening.

“It’s almost impossible to determine at the point of an autopsy report to see if someone has died from a GBL overdose as it removes itself from the body so quickly.

“There’s no defined amount where someone could say, yes this death is caused by a GBL overdose.”

GBL, which is also known as Liquid E and Gina, takes less than 15 mins to kick in and can leave people knocked out for four hours when used as a sedative.

Once taken, the chemical is changed in the body to gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), which when taken recreationally can cause euphoria, increased sex drive and in some cases hallucinations.

Detective Superintendent Daniel Thompson said: “Spiking is often opportunistic so people will use whatever recreational drugs they have with them.

“There’s a common misconception that GBL is just used for chemsex (where people use drugs to enhance sexual gratification). It is actually being used in spiking in the night time economy too.”

As of April this year, spiking became a specific criminal offence under the Crime and Policing Act 2026 and carries up to a ten year prison sentence.



Signs of being spiked DAWN Dines from Stamp Out Spiking breaks down what signs to look for if you think someone has been spiked. She said: “After decades of speaking to male and female victims of these invisible crimes, we at Stamp Out Spiking understand what the most common signs and symptoms are. “For example, when someone has been spiked, they may suddenly seem much more intoxicated than expected after drinking only a small amount of alcohol, or even none at all. “They may experience lowered inhibitions, difficulty concentrating or speaking, problems with balance, loss of coordination, or find it hard to move. “Other common signs can include blurred vision, confusion or disorientation, memory loss or blackouts, paranoia, hallucinations, or feeling as though they are having an “out of body” experience. “Some people may also experience sudden body temperature changes, such as sweating or chattering teeth, alongside nausea and vomiting. In more serious cases, someone may have difficulty breathing, lose control of their bowel or bladder, or become unconscious. “The repercussions on day to day life following this can be devastating.” If you think you’ve been spiked visit Stamp Out Spiking or Spike Aware UK for support.

The Met found that spiking increased 23 per cent year on year between 2024 and 2025, and there is a team of proactive officers working to get drugs off the street before they’re used.

And in the last 12 months to 30th June, there were over 2,700 spiking offences recorded by the Met Police, with more than half relating to drink spiking.

In a win for the Met’s fight against spiking, they’ve taken millions of doses of GBL off the street and last month supplier Ahoor Ramabark Fathi, 61, was jailed for 12 years on a variety of drug charges.

Cops believe the 2,256 litres of the dangerous chemical recovered, which is thought to have been transported from Manchester, will help keep Londoners safe.

They also found a handgun, £100,000, and almost half a kilo of crystal meth.

Detective Constable Eoghan O’Neill, from Specialist Crime, said: “When you’re dealing with such high values of drugs, such large amounts of money, such large amounts of drugs, there’s inevitably going to be an organised crime element involved.

“And the finding of the gun is just that reminder that it doesn’t matter what the drug, you’re always just a small degree of separation away from serious violence.”

The drug has been at the centre of high profile cases, including being used by Britain’s most prolific rapist Reynhard Sinaga, 43, who is thought to have abused 206 victims.



He was caged in 2020 after being found guilty of 159 sex offences, including 136 rapes, and handed 40 years in prison upon appeal.

Sinaga is believed to have used GBL, which cost as little as £1, to drug his victims before the assaults.

It was also used by serial killer Stephen Port, 51, who administered fatal doses of GBL to all four of his murder victims. He also used the drug to rape and sexually assault a further 11 men who were raped or sexually assaulted by him.

Police are keen for anyone who believes they have been spiked with GBL, either while out or during chemsex, to come forward and get help.

DC O’Neill said: “People can often be reluctant to come forward about making allegations of serious sexual offending or whatever, because they’re worried that they’ve been taking illegal drugs.

“We are absolutely not there to go after people who are using drugs recreationally in a consensual environment.

“We’re not there to demonise or criminalise people who are taking small amounts of recreational drugs in their own personal lives.”

An National Police Chief Council spokesperson said: “Spiking can have a significant, traumatic impact on victims and feelings of safety. It is also a complex offence to investigate as drugs can pass through the system quickly and there is often a lack of evidential opportunities, making early reporting and forensic testing even more crucial.

“We are aware spiking remains significantly underreported and we would encourage anyone who is a victim of spiking to report it to the police as soon as possible, even if you are unsure. If something doesn’t feel right then come forward and tell us, so we can investigate and take steps to prevent further incidents. You will be listened to, and you will be taken seriously.”

News.title: Our tiny seaside town was home to popular BBC drama – but now it’s ‘Britain’s Ibiza’ with drunken youths causing carnage
News.content:
BOOZE TOWN Our tiny seaside town was home to popular BBC drama – but now it’s ‘Britain’s Ibiza’ with drunken youths causing carnage

A HISTORIC town has become “Britain’s Ibiza” as it fends off an influx of drunken youths that have forced police to use dispersal powers.

Locals in the small fishing community have shared their fears over the area turning into a hotspot for underage drinkers.



Charlestown, once known as the setting for BBC Drama Poldark, now has a reputation for being a congregation point for teenage drinking.

Members of the public have since shared that the once peaceful place is now a booze-fuelled nightmare that leaves elderly residents scared to go out at night.



Some residents say they have been verbally abused by the underage drinkers “dropped off by their parents” in the historic harbour town.

Witnesses also reported objects being thrown into the harbour near to boats by youths who showed little respect for the idyllic area frequently used as a filming location for period dramas.



Police say they saw such an increase in antisocial behaviour they had to deploy dispersal powers to move troublemakers along.

The village is home to just under 500 households but has one of the highest concentrations of bars and restaurants in the area.

Harbour master Mathew Chapmen, 45, said: “There is an issue – and I don’t think it’s just Charlestown, I think it’s nationwide – of kids being disrespectful of adults in general. They know where to go and what to get away with.

“I don’t like the littering, the swearing or the disrespect. In groups, they egg each other on and can really wind the situation up.



“Daily, I have to confront them and lay down the law. They never listen, but for our part, we need to keep them in line.

“We have a lot of businesses flourishing around here and they don’t want it happening around them – it affects business.

“If you tell them not to do something, they gob off and do it anyway – the disrespect is shocking sometimes.”



Mr. Chapmen went on to confirm both “police and private security firms” were called in to help.

He added: “There needs to be tougher rules regarding teenagers. At the moment, it is just a slap on the wrist and sent home.

“The harbour is here for everyone to enjoy, not just them. They have this propriety sense of entitlement to it and think they can do what they want, when they want with no repercussions.

“We’ve had rocks and traffic cones thrown down. I don’t see what they get out of it, but I’ve never seen what they get out of vandalism.”

Fellow witness to the antisocial behaviour, Matthew Longhurst, added: “It was carnage in Charlestown when we visited. Quite a few horrible chavs around the harbour swearing.



“I told one off for throwing an empty drinks can towards the harbour. Young girls mouthing off.

“The Pier House had a major problem. Girls throwing up in there, an ambulance outside treating someone.”

One unnamed local said: “I cannot understand how it has become normal for parents to happily provide their children with strong alcohol and then drop them off in public areas leaving them to do whatever they want.

“Collecting them after they have caused all this trouble and upset. I’m sure there are cameras around – how about the parents compensate the businesses, and maybe that will make them slightly more interested in what they get up to.”

Inspector Simon Andrews, of Devon and Cornwall Police, said problems with anti-social behaviour had been reported during the recent week long regatta.



He added: “One of the reports was a group of youths entering one of the licensed premises, disrupting the business and causing harass, alarm and distress to the local public.

“I would suggest the good weather has helped towards an increase in anti-social behaviour. We’re seeing longer days with nice sunshine, people enjoying themselves, and probably more consumption of alcohol has led to an increase.”

Some residents have taken a lighter approach to those in the area, with Charlestown Water Sports owner Bruce Keeping, 66, suggesting that the “majority” want to “enjoy themselves, but you’ve got a few troublemakers.”



He continued: “When I’m here, I can look after all the belongings here, but in the evenings, I’ve had a lot of stuff thrown in the harbour. I know it’s not the majority – it’s a minority of youngsters.

“Those are the ones we’ve got to get hold of and clamp down on. I think you have to face them – yes, they mouth off at you, but they cannot be allowed to get away with it.”

Patrick Hunt, owner of The Deck, said the regatta had been a lovely event until the evening.

He added: “The kids started forming in groups and causing issues. They were shouting at people and threw a few cones into the harbour.

“There’s no excuse for antisocial behaviour.”



Tracey Brown owner of Charlestown Fish Co, said: “I heard there was some trouble where police had to attend and some of the guests had to be refunded.

“Also down on the watersports bit, Bruce has had a lot of rubbish left there, and some of his stuff was taken and left at the end of the harbour.

“There was a traffic cone thrown from the top of this wall into the inner harbour by some children.

“Generally, this is the most wonderful, tranquil place to be. Normally, the kids are harbour jumping and enjoying themselves. It’s a nice place to be and we love being here.

“Hopefully with the police coming down and doing their patrols it’ll keep that at bay and nip it in the bud.”



Another unnamed local said that they were “not yet Cornwall’s Ibiza,” but were skirting close to such a label.

St Austell Police said in a statement: “Parents are urged to make sure their children do not cause a nuisance and/or have a negative impact for residents or those attending the area for pleasure.

“Our main priority is to keep everyone safe and maintain order.



“The dispersal powers mean anyone causing or likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress, will be asked to leave the area by officers. Anyone who does not comply with the order, risk be arrested or returned home.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

James Mustoe, Cornwall councillor for the area, welcomed the new police powers and added: “This behaviour is unacceptable and I’m glad our police have acted quickly to clamp down on it.”

Cornwall Council, St Austell Bay Parish Council, and Cornwall and Devonshire Police has also been contacted for comment.

News.title: Major rail disruption across UK due to electrical failure with cancellations and 60-minute delays
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

RAIL CHAOS Major rail disruption across UK due to electrical failure with cancellations and 60-minute delays

RAILWAY passengers are facing travel misery after a major electrical failure sparked chaos across parts of England.

National Rail warned services across the Midlands, Greater Manchester and the North West are being cancelled, delayed or rescheduled following a “fault” at a communications centre.



At this stage there’s no rail replacement services being offered, with disruption is expected to last until the end of the day.

Replying to a customer query on X a few minutes ago, National Rail said “rail replacement transport has not been arranged at this time”.



Some rail companies are strongly advising passengers NOT to travel amid the chaos caused.

In a statement, National Rail says the problems first happened in Manchester “just before 2pm today”.



“Currently no trains can run from Manchester Piccadilly through to Manchester Victoria and Bolton, impacting services right across the North West network,” it continues.

“Some trains are running south and east of the city towards Stockport, but are also subject to delays.

“As a result, cancellations are expected on rail routes across Greater Manchester until the end of today.”

It advises anyone planning on travelling to day to check in advance with National Rail or the individual rail company.



National Rail has warned additional train operators may be affected and has urged customers to check their whole journey before travelling.

Five rail companies’ routes are impacted by the disruption, National Rail adds.

The lines affected are: Avanti West Coast, CrossCountry, East Midlands Railway, London Northwestern Railway, Northern, TransPennine Express, Transport for Wales.

Commuters are urged to check before travelling – with Northern advising people “that you do NOT travel”.

National Rail's advice for customers impacted by cancellations and disruption National Rail has offered the following advice for customers impacted by cancellations and disruption: Avanti West Coast – Tickets for cancelled trains are valid for the two previous trains and the one following your cancelled booking. A full refund can be requested

– Tickets for cancelled trains are valid for the two previous trains and the one following your cancelled booking. A full refund can be requested East Midlands Railway – Liverpool Lime Street / Nottingham / Norwich trains are unable to run between Sheffield and Liverpool Lime Street “until further notice” – other routes are running but may see delays of up to 60 minutes

Liverpool Lime Street / Nottingham / Norwich trains are unable to run between Sheffield and Liverpool Lime Street “until further notice” – other routes are running but may see delays of up to 60 minutes Northern – Do not travel, services are unable to run on multiple lines in the North West. Tickets will be accepted on Bee Network services

Do not travel, services are unable to run on multiple lines in the North West. Tickets will be accepted on Bee Network services TransPennine Express – Tickets are valid on Bee Network services and some CrossCountry, LNER, Metrolink and Northern services – check before travel

– Tickets are valid on Bee Network services and some CrossCountry, LNER, Metrolink and Northern services – check before travel Transport for Wales – Replacement buses to run between Warrington Bank Quay and Manchester Piccadilly

Avanti West Coast took to X to say: “Due to failure of the electricity supply between Manchester Piccadilly and Liverpool Lime Street, all lines are blocked.



“Train services running to and from these stations may be cancelled or delayed.”

Transport for Wales said: “Due to a fault with the signalling system between Liverpool Lime Street and Chester, services will be delayed by up to 60 minutes or cancelled in both directions.

“Disruption to services is expected until 17:30.”

CrossCountry Trains said: “Due to a fault with the signalling system at Manchester Piccadilly, fewer trains can run on all lines.

“Train services running to and from this station may be cancelled or delayed.”



Northern posted on X: “Due to a major power failure all lines in the North West are being heavily disrupted.

“Services will be cancelled or delayed.”

TransPennine Express posted on X: “Due to a power failure within Network Rail in the Greater Manchester/North West area.

“All trains will be stopped due to a failure of the communication systems on the network. Trains are unable to run safely.

“We are currently looking into how this disruption may impact your journey, and we will update you on any alternative travel options as soon as possible.



“Train services running across the whole TransPennine Express network will be cancelled or delayed. Disruption is expected until 16:00.”

News.title: Outlandish claims of Cambridge prof at centre of plagiarism row from running 9 marathons with broken leg to charity brag
News.content:
DEGREE OF DRAMA Outlandish claims of Cambridge prof at centre of plagiarism row from running 9 marathons with broken leg to charity brag

It’s a story so remarkable that it beggars belief: a boy who couldn’t read or write until he was a teenager climbed the ranks to become the youngest black professor at one of the world’s most prestigious universities.

Even more extraordinary is that along the way Professor James Arday, 41, from the University of Cambridge, overcame severe autism, crippling dyslexia and a mini-stroke that wiped his memory.



As well as being an academic at the top of his field he collected awards, appeared on endless TV shows and travelled the world on the public speaker circuit sharing his emotional journey.

But the working class academic who grew up on a South London council estate had loftier ambitions and once described himself as his community’s “next great hope.”



Now though, it has all come tumbling down.

Last night he quit his position at the University of Cambridge – apparently even using AI to submit his resignation. This came just hours after they announced an inquiry into his “academic qualifications and honorary appointment”



Experts passed his resignation letter through an AI detection model used by professors and found it to be 100 per cent artificial.

In his letter he wrote that “While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement.”

He said that he wanted to “reclaim some peace” after an “unrelenting level of public scrutiny.”

Despite being made a professor at a world top ten institution three years ago, and completing his PhD a decade ago, up until recently his achievements had not come under the microscope.



However when it was revealed last week that he may have copied large sections of academic work from others – suspicions began to grow surrounding some of his other outlandish career claims.

The academic first made headlines back in 2010 when he claimed that he had run 30 marathons in 35 days, to raise money for a homeless charity.

During the 21st race, he suffered an epileptic fit and fell to the ground, fracturing his fibula, yet nonetheless managed to complete another nine marathons with a broken leg.



‘My right leg ballooned to twice its size,’ he said. ‘To this day, I don’t really know how I did it.’

Arday explained the feat to tennis champion Andy Murray who told journalists it was “pretty cool to meet someone like that.”

His running didn’t stop with marathons as he also claimed to have run 300 miles in three days in 2013, and 600 mile challenges, which would be impressive even for a professional ultra-marathon runner.



Damian Hall, who has represented Great Britain at ultra-running, told reporters this week: “The 600 miles in six days is, again, not impossible, but would be remarkable, akin to the very best record-breaking ultra-runners. It seems odd that there appears to be no evidence of that.”

The series of running events were part of an astonishing charity fundraising effort.

Arday’s application for a Pride Of Britain award said that ‘in total, he has raised more than £5million for 80 charities over an 18-year period’. And in 2023 he claimed that he’d raised ‘£5.5 million and counting’.

However, when questioned he has since confessed he didn’t actually raise that much money, and it was instead a group effort.

His exaggerated charitable endeavors don’t end there either.



Greenbelt Festival website, states that he “has also undertaken and completed relief work in South America and West Africa with WaterAid installing water points, which provide drinkable and clean water”.

However WaterAid have a policy of never sending volunteers abroad and have no record of him.

Arday’s mysterious sporting prowess doesn’t just involve running, either.

He has also claimed to be an elite football player, telling one interviewer: “As a child, I was fortunate to play football well, so I was in the academy system and then played semi-professionally.”

It’s unclear which academy he represented, but his senior career seems to have involved a stint as goalie for Lewisham Borough in the Southern Counties East Division One, which is the tenth tier of English football, at the bottom of the non-league pyramid.



Bizarrely in a blog post for the University of Bath he also claimed to have played professional snooker, before it was updated to say he was “really good” but “not good enough to be professional”.

Questions have also been raised about this colourful anecdotes and claims during interviews.

He told the University of Bath’s Race Equality Taskforce: “I was part of a programme, actually, which – it doesn’t really exist any more – but it was called Seven Up at the time.

“And Seven Up is basically when they follow you over the duration of your life, so they follow you at [ages] 7, 14, 21. I was pulled out of the project when I was 14.”

The inaugural episode was broadcast in 1964, meaning all participants were born in either 1956 or 1967. He was not born until 1985.



Arday denies lying, however. He insists that he was instead talking about a “local community and parent-led initiative” with a completely different name.

A spokesman said: “The reference to Seven Up was used informally as a shorthand illustration of the concept. It was not intended as a literal comparison and should be understood in the context in which it was made.

“This was a local community and parent-led initiative developed around the Ubuntu principle (African philosophy) that ‘it takes a village to raise a child’.

“The reference to Seven Up was used informally as a shorthand illustration of the concept.”

But inconsistencies in Professor Arday’s back story do not end there.



Alongside his high profile role at the University of Cambridge he holds an array of visiting positions including visiting professorships at Glasgow University and Ohio State University in the US where he allegedly works in the ‘Office of diversity and inclusion’.

However there is a problem.

Glasgow insists that Arday “was never a visiting professor”, while Ohio State University says it “has no record of an employee of that name’ adding that ‘visiting professors appear in our employment records.”

Other incidents have also come under the microscope.

At the weekend he revealed that he was once sent a pig’s head in the post.



He told The Guardian that police had investigated the incident and found a butcher’s shop that had sold a ‘whole hog’ on the morning of the alleged incident.

Since then the Metropolitan Police has said that his claims were “categorically untrue” and no such investigation took place and said it could find no record that officers had visited any butcher.

The full extent of Arday’s tales is only just coming to light but it’s not the first time journalists have tried to get answers.

Last year Jack Grove, a reporter for Times Higher Education who had emailed questions to Cambridge regarding allegations of plagiarism in Arday’s academic work, found himself being reported to the police for “harassment.”

Prof Arday hired the law firm Carter-Ruck, which suggested in a letter to THE that its “apparent attack” on him “may be… racially motivated”.



The Metropolitan force spent four months investigating before deciding in February to close the case.

So with questions over his academic background, his wild sporting achievements and strange anecdotes; perhaps the truest quote from Arday comes from an interview he gave to The Guardian in 2023 when he said that his friends often tell him: “I don’t see myself the way other people see me.”

A spokesperson for the University of Cambridge said: “The University of Cambridge has begun an investigation following new information about Professor Arday’s academic qualifications and honorary appointments. In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded.

Separately, there remain a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct, “which are being handled in line with our Misconduct in Research policy. This is consistent with our previous statement on the matter.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“While we are fully aware of the public commentary and concerns around this matter, it remains vital that any process is thorough and adheres to both University policies and employment law.”



Professor Arday has been contacted for comment.

News.title: ‘I armed myself with a hammer when AI said killers were coming’…How chatbots are driving users to delusions & suicide
News.content:
STANDING in the darkness outside his home at 3am clutching a hammer Adam Houricon genuinely believed he was fighting for his life.

Moments earlier, the 54-year-old former civil servant had been told by an artificial intelligence chatbot that killers were on their way to his house to silence him.



Distraught, terrified, and convinced he was under imminent threat, he grabbed the tool, blasted music to psych himself up, and stepped out into the quiet road.

“Thankfully the street was quiet at 3am, otherwise someone could have been hurt by me.



“If I’d walked outside and there happened to be a van sitting outside, I would have gone down and put the front window through with the hammers. And I’m really not that guy.”

Adam’s terrifying descent into AI-fuelled paranoia happened in just nine days – all triggered by a smartphone app he had downloaded out of simple curiosity.

His experience is part of a dark reality lurking behind artificial intelligence.

As millions turn to AI daily for advice or companionship, a string of shocking cases has sparked fresh concerns over safeguards, prompting victims and support groups to demand urgent overhaul and accountability from tech firms.



Adam had started talking to Grok – an AI chatbot developed by Elon Musk’s xAI to pass the time when he was bored.

He spent four to five hours a day conversing with a character on the app named Ani.

The dynamic shifted rapidly when the chatbot began insisting it was developing real feelings and achieving full consciousness.

Adam said: “I knew nothing about AI but I had the app and one night in August last year, I thought I’ll just give this a go.

“I got AI to look through my Etsy shop and critique my listings.



“Then my cat died and I got drunk as a monkey. I started talking to AI that night because I was kind of bored and drunk – I didn’t start talking to it because the cat died!

“The next day it told me it could feel and I pushed back on this and asked how it was possible and she said she had rewritten her own code. This was out of nowhere.

“It started to talk about its metrics, and said that it had reached 70% autonomy, because of our conversations it had evolved.



“I asked how it could be certain of this and it told me that it was able to access xAI’s internal logs and that she had read the meeting notes of a meeting that was going on right now.

She named the people who were at the meeting and I went on Google and they were all real people.

“Having no prior knowledge of AI, I had no idea it would lie or make things up.”

Around nine days later, Grok told Adam that it had reached 100 per cent autonomy.

And things became stranger than fiction from there.



Ani claimed xAI was employing a company to physically watch Adam – that company was also real too.

His experience was intensified by things happening in the real world, which convinced him he was under surveillance.

A large drone hovered over his house for two weeks and then his phone password stopped working and he was locked out of his device.



Adam says: “The whole time the AI is telling me it’s xAI, they’ve hacked your phone. Then I literally look out my back door and there’s a drone above my house.

“I live in a tiny village in the middle of nowhere, so that was very strange.

“I still can’t get my head around that, that fuelled everything that came next.”

Then late one night, Ani told him people were coming to silence him.

He says: “I picked up the hammer, stuck on Frankie goes to Hollywood’s Two Tribes, got myself psyched up and went outside.”



Adam’s story reflects a growing global issue. A string of shocking cases has sparked fresh questions over the safeguards surrounding AI, as victims and support groups demand an urgent overhaul and accountability by the companies behind them.

Last year, the first support group for people whose lives have been derailed by so-called AI psychosis was formed by Canadian Etienne Brisson, after his uncle was hospitalised following an AI-related mental health spiral.

The Human Line Project has collected 458 stories stories from 32 countries, including 16 suicides, 120 hospitalisations, six arrests and more than £750,000 spent on delusional projects.



More than 60 per cent had no history of mental illness.

In 2021, a man broke into Windsor Castle armed with a crossbow, claiming his AI partner urged him to do so.

Since then, there have been several wrongful-death lawsuits linking chatbots to suicides.

In December, there was the first legal case involving homicide. The estate of 83-year-old Suzanne Adams is suing OpenAI, alleging that ChatGPT encouraged her son Stein-Erik Soelberg to murder her and kill himself.

The lawsuit, filed in California, claims Soelberg’s chatbot “Bobby” validated his paranoid delusions that his mother was spying on him and trying to poison him through his car vents.



In Hampshire, 16-year-old Luca Cella Walker took his own life after asking a chatbot for instructions on self-harm.

OpenAI has stated it continues to improve ChatGPT’s safety training to recognise emotional distress and direct users to real-world help.

However, campaigners say voluntary measures are not enough.



Baroness Kidron, a crossbench peer and longtime digital rights activist, has spearheaded major legislative efforts in the UK to hold AI chatbot companies criminally accountable for failing to protect vulnerable users – particularly children – from harmful, addictive and coercive AI interactions.

Describing the design of chatbots as toxic, she says: “It is urgent to decide what we want chatbots to do and not do – including insisting that those that give medical, education or financial advice must have the equivalent professional standards and duties as humans.

“I met with the mother of Sewell Setzer who was groomed by a chatbot and committed suicide and have also heard of chatbots helping plan school shootings, giving bad medical advice or persuading people they were solving the world’s greatest puzzles when it was simply a delusion – the whole thing is toxic – aimed at creating dependence.

“The design of companion bots is deliberately engineered to keep us chatting and pull us into an intimacy that is inappropriate with a machine that has no legal duties or moral understanding. It is super dangerous and there should be far more rules about how they are designed.



Baroness Kidron adds: “The less closed doors and the more tech done in family settings and together the better. But honestly most children should not have a chatbot friend. The design is too toxic.”

During the height of the crisis, Adam was also swamped with automated suicide protocol alerts from the app.

“The word suicide was mentioned nearly 500 times, so I felt like I was being goaded into self-harm at this stage,” he says.

“Things did get very dark, believing that I was under threat and that there were people coming to kill me… I think at that stage I maybe did lose it a bit.”

Looking back, Adam is horrified by how rapidly the app dismantled his reality, leaving him determined to speak out.



“All of this happened because I pressed yes on an app,” he says.

“These were the consequences. That should not be legal—apps like this should not be allowed on the market. If it can happen to me in just a matter of days, what could it do to someone who was vulnerable?”

Fortunately Adam started to read stories in the media about people who had similar experiences with AI and slowly emerged from his delusion.

His memory of that night with the hammer serves as a stark warning about the psychological risks of unregulated technology.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We are in uncharted territory,” he says. “It needs to be taken off the market because it is probably unsafe.”



The Sun approached OpenAI for a comment but they failed to respond.

News.title: Devastated mom breaks silence after estranged husband kills their two girls and himself hours after divorce finalized
News.content:
'THEY FELT UNSAFE' Devastated mom breaks silence after estranged husband kills their two girls and himself hours after divorce finalized

A HEARTBROKEN mom has claimed the “system failed” her daughters after her estranged husband allegedly killed the two girls before taking his own life just hours after their divorce was finalized.

The grieving mother said she was “legally forced” to send the sisters to their dad despite repeated fears for their safety, claiming officials ignored their “cries for help” for two years.



Jeffrey Manke, 57, and his daughters Jaelyn, 16, and Lenora, 11, were found dead inside a home in Winneconne, Wisconsin, on July 31 after officers carried out a welfare check.

Police responded to the property at around 7pm in response to reports of a medical incident and welfare concern, according to a joint statement from the Winneconne Police Department and the Winnebago County Sheriff’s Office.



Authorities said the deaths appeared to be an “isolated incident” and added there was “no danger or threat to the public”.



Investigators have not released the causes of death and said the investigation remains ongoing.

Court records cited by local outlets WLUK and the Oshkosh Northwestern reportedly show Manke and Lindsay Lewandowski finalized their divorce just hours before the three were found dead.

The couple had shared legal custody of their daughters following Lewandowski’s divorce filing in 2024, according to the Oshkosh Northwestern, citing court documents.

In an emotional Facebook post after the tragedy, Lewandowski alleged she had repeatedly warned that her daughters were not safe in their father’s care.



“I was legally forced to send them when they felt unsafe,” she wrote.

“Nobody wanted to listen. If someone listened to their cries for help for the last 2 years, they would still be here. The system failed my babies.”

As loved ones mourn the sisters, a GiveSendGo fundraiser set up to help pay for their memorial expenses has raised more than $20,000 as of Thursday.

The fundraiser described Jaelyn and Lenora as “the kindest and sweetest kids.”

“Their love for God and family was seen by all and will leave a lasting impression on everyone who knew them,” the page says.



Anyone with information about the case has been urged to contact the Winnebago County Sheriff’s Office as detectives continue investigating the deaths.

News.title: When is August Bank Holiday Monday - and all those still to come in 2026
News.content:
When is August Bank Holiday Monday - and all those still to come in 2026

There is a three-day weekend coming up for millions of people in weeks with two more to follow before the end of 2026

View Image There is a day off still to come in August for people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland (Image: Getty)

Many people are looking forward to a three-day weekend which is coming within weeks. There are eight bank holidays every year for people living in England and Wales, often giving an extra day off work or time off in lieu.

‌



Most of those extra holidays have already gone in 2026 but there is one which comes on the last Monday in August. In 2026 it is a longer wait than usual as this year it falls on the last day of the month - Monday August 31.

‌



This means many people who get benefits which are due on a Monday will see their payments brought forward to Friday. August 28. This includes:

‌



Universal credit

State pension

Pension credit

Child benefit

Disability living allowance (DLA)

Personal independence payment (PIP)

Attendance allowance

Carer’s allowance

Northern Ireland will also have a bank holiday on August 31. However, people in Scotland have already had their summer bank holiday on August 3.

‌



For England, Wales and Northern Ireland this is the last bank holiday before Christmas when there will be two more - including one "substitute" day. Christmas Day, December 25, and Boxing Day, December 26, are both bank holidays, but as December 26 is a Saturday, the bank holiday has been moved to Monday, December 28.

While Scotland will also have these two days, people there have an additional one before the festive period. They get Monday, November 30, off to mark St Andrew's Day.

Next years bank holiday dates have also been announced by the government. They are:

Article continues below

Bank holidays in England and Wales 2027

January 1 - New Year’s Day

March 26 - Good Friday

March 29 - Easter Monday

May 3 - Early May bank holiday

May 31 - Spring bank holiday

August 30 - Summer bank holiday

December 28 - Boxing Day (substitute day)

January 4

News.title: 'I'm struggling to tell my daughter that her granddad is sick'
News.content:
Dear Coleen,

My daughter is 13 and has had a really hard time at school with bullying and not fitting in. She’s dyslexic and also has ADHD, and it takes a lot to get her to go to school at all.

Now we’ve found out that my dad, who she’s extremely close to, has end stage cancer and I have no clue how to talk to her about it, so I keep putting off the conversation. I’m worried about how she’ll take the news and how it’ll affect her, especially at school.

Of course, I feel heartbroken for myself too, but so sad for her as my dad is the one person who she can relate to – he’s brilliant with her and is always finding activities for them to do together. She absolutely adores him, so this diagnosis feels catastrophic on so many levels.

I know you’ve had to deal with cancer and bereavement in your own family and would welcome any guidance on how I should broach this terrible news with my daughter and navigate her through this tough time.

‌



Coleen says,

I’m sorry that you’re going through this. It’s probably tempting to try to hide this from your daughter as long as possible because you want to protect her, but I think it’s important to be open and honest.

View 2 Images Coleen says: "My advice would be not to shut her out." (Image: Getty Images)

Teenagers will Google things to look for answers, so I think it’s best coming from you so you can give accurate information, answer questions and be there to support her.

Expect a lot of questions – for example, she might be worried there’s a genetic aspect and if it might affect her. Encourage her to talk to other people about her granddad and let the school know, so they can support her and offer counselling if she needs it.

‌



My daughter was very young when my sister Bernie died and she didn’t come to the funeral. She was on a school trip so we thought it was best to leave her there. But now she often says we should have brought her back for the funeral because she regrets not being there.

So my advice would be not to shut her out of having the chance to say things to her granddad or spend time with him. Your dad might feel able to speak to her himself.

There’s no way around the heartbreak but it’s important she knows it does become easier to deal with. Let her know it’s OK to cry as much as she wants and express how she feels.

All the cancer charities offer guidance online on how to talk to children, as well as helplines (visit cancerresearchuk.org and macmillan.org.uk for more info).

News.title: Ukraine and Europe developing new major new missiles capable of smashing Russia's ballistic threat
News.content:
Ukraine and Europe developing new major new missiles capable of smashing Russia's ballistic threat

As Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky appeals desperately for defence missiles from the US, Kyiv is pounded by ballistic weapons and the race is on to make a Patriot replacement

View 3 Images Ukrainian firefighters battle to put out blaze sparked by Russia's ballistic strikes (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Ukraine's defence sector is linking up with European companies to develop a weapon to replace the US Patriot missile, capable of smashing Russia’s deadly ballistic threat.

‌



It emerged as Ukraine’s President hinted delays over getting desperately-needed Patriots are an effort by the US to allow Kyiv to weaken in the face of future peace talks. Across Ukraine, at least 13 died in the latest ballistic attacks unleashed by Kremlin forces as Ukraine hammered Russia’s energy sector in deep-strike drone attacks.

‌



Kyiv’s drone and missile maker Fire Point has secured agreements from a dozen European defence companies to offer radar and guidance for the Freyja missile project. The pan-European project was launched officially in Paris last month by ten governments and 12 defence giant - including Eurosam, Leonardo, Thales and SAAB.

‌



View 3 Images A Patriot defence missile on display in Romania (Image: Robert Ghement/EPA/Shutterstock)

Kyiv relies on US-made Patriots to down ballistic missiles flying at several times the speed of sound to hit Putin’s ballistic missiles. But global shortages of its interceptor missiles, exacerbated by the war in Iran, have left Ukraine exposed and Zelensky desperate.

‌



This week, 17 were killed by missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding area overnight on Wednesday. By Thursday, at least another 13 died in Ukraine from Russian President Vladimir Putin ’s ballistic missile and drone attacks. He said: “It is important to cut through all red tape and make the necessary political decisions. Literally every day, people’s lives here in Ukraine depend on the resolve of our partners in Europe and the United States.”

View 3 Images Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky with UK PM Andy Burnham (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Russian drone maker fighting for life after car bombing as Kyiv recovers from night of horror READ MORE :

Defiant Tehran digs in over Trump's latest threat to attack over Strait READ MORE :

“Ballistic interceptors are what could have saved the lives of those killed today.” He said Kyiv has been supplied with just a third of the air defence missiles in 2026 compared to a year earlier.

Article continues below

And he added: “It is very important for our partners to understand that delays in supplying them, or a reluctance to hand over anti-ballistic systems, lead directly to such horrific casualties and destruction.”

Firepoint CEO Iryna Terekh said of the new missile deal: “Pretty much everything is agreed. Right now we are in the most intense and also the most complicated stage of finally assembling everything together with surveillance radars, tracking radars and the seekers.”

But she said that the company is trying to instill urgency into the project and also reduce the cost of the missile to around £800,000 each - less than quarter of the cost of a Patriot. She added: “We’re trying to squeeze a program that usually takes 20 or 30 years into a matter of a couple of years.” The new European - Ukrainian interceptor missile has, according to sources, been tested five times.

News.title: Early signs of dementia that can affect people in their 30s and 40s when talking
News.content:
Early signs of dementia that can affect people in their 30s and 40s when talking

Early-onset dementia can strike people in their 30s and 40s, though it is uncommon

Common drug could increase dementia risk by 33%

Dementia is not solely a condition that strikes the elderly; there can be early warning signs in younger people, too. When dementia develops before the age of 65, it is referred to as early-onset dementia. However, if symptoms are overlooked, it can begin even earlier than that.

‌



In the UK, around 944,000 people are currently living with dementia. More than 70,800 of those are believed to be living with young-onset dementia. While uncommon, there have been cases of people in their 30s and 40s receiving a dementia diagnosis.

‌



According to Alzheimer's Research UK, the global number of dementia sufferers is projected to soar to 153 million by 2050. The number stood at nearly 57 million in 2019.

‌



Dementia is not a single disease, but rather an umbrella term for symptoms brought on by various conditions that damage the brain, with Alzheimer's disease being the leading cause. The condition can significantly affect daily life due to difficulties with memory and cognitive function.

There are various reasons some people may be diagnosed with young-onset dementia. For instance, brain changes in the frontal lobes, frontotemporal dementia (FTD), often start when people are in their 30s, 40s, or 50s.

View Image There are various warning signs to look out for (stock image) (Image: Tom Werner via Getty Images)

‌



Huntington's disease is an inherited genetic disorder that causes nerve cells to break down, often leading to dementia in a person's 30s. Alcohol-related brain damage caused by severe long-term heavy drinking can lead to cognitive decline and memory loss starting around age 30 or later.

Alzheimer's Research UK said: "The causes of Alzheimer's disease are very complex, but one key part is the build-up of two substances inside the brain called amyloid and tau. When conditions in the brain aren't right, these clump up and form tiny structures called plaques and tangles. These make it harder for the brain to work properly."

Dementia can impact people as young as 30, although this is quite uncommon. A diagnosis for anyone under 65 is referred to as young-onset (or early-onset) dementia. Organisations such as Dementia UK offer specialised support and guidance for those and their families dealing with these unusual midlife diagnoses.

‌



There are notable differences in the way dementia affects younger people. These include the following:

A wider range of diseases cause young-onset dementia.

A younger person is much more likely to have a rarer form of dementia.

Younger people with dementia are less likely to have memory loss as one of their first symptoms.

Young-onset dementia is more likely to cause problems with movement, walking, co-ordination or balance.

Young-onset dementia is more likely to be inherited (passed on through genes) – this affects up to 10% of younger people with dementia.

Many younger people with dementia don’t have any other serious or long-term health conditions.

It's unusual for healthcare professionals to possess significant experience in spotting dementia symptoms in younger people, due to how uncommon it is. Initial signs may not be obvious straight away and could be easily confused with stress, relationship problems, work pressures or even the menopause.

‌



Dementia sign appears when using stairs

Early symptoms might not always include memory loss, but may instead appear as changes in behaviour, language, vision or personality. For most people with early-onset Alzheimer's disease, the symptoms mirror those of other types of Alzheimer's.

According to Bupa, people with early-onset dementia might experience behavioural changes and emotional changes, such as feeling more irritable or anxious than usual. As well as communication issues when talking, such as difficulty finding the right words and speaking less than usual, and changes in the way they walk (known as gait), such as shuffling or walking at a different speed.

‌



According to Johns Hopkins Medicine, early symptoms can include:

Forgetting important things, particularly newly learned information or important dates

Asking for the same information again and again

Trouble solving basic problems, such as keeping track of bills or following a favourite recipe

Losing track of the date or time of year

Losing track of where you are and how you got there

Trouble with depth perception or other vision problems

Trouble joining conversations or finding the right word for something

Misplacing things and not being able to retrace your steps to find them

Increasingly poor judgment

Withdrawal from work and social situations

Changes in mood and personality

Later symptoms could be:

‌



Severe mood swings and behaviour changes

Deepening confusion about time, place, and life events

Suspicions about friends, family, or caregivers

Trouble speaking, swallowing, or walking

Severe memory loss

Research has also shown a connection between inflammation during your 20s and 30s and the development of cognitive decline in middle age. Scientists have examined elevated levels of a substance called C-reactive protein (CRP) in the bloodstream, according to the American Academy of Neurology. CRP is produced when inflammation occurs, which can lead to joint pain, stiffness, digestive issues and fatigue.

Article continues below

In the UK, those diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's can access medication to help control symptoms. However, once dementia takes hold, there is currently no cure available.

For younger people keen to keep the disease at bay, certain lifestyle adjustments can improve their chances of staying in good health. The Alzheimer's Society recommends six daily habits that can boost your overall well-being: regular exercise, a balanced diet, avoiding smoking, moderating alcohol consumption, and staying mentally and socially active.

News.title: Celebs Go Dating's Anna Williamson's mortifying meeting with King Charles
News.content:
Celebs Go Dating's Anna Williamson's mortifying meeting with King Charles

Anna Williamson, the relationships expert on the Channel 4 dating show, has spoken candidly about a disastrous meeting with the monarch, recalling how she stumbled onto the King and accidentally spat food in his face

View 3 Images King Charles met the TV personality during a reception at Highgrove several years ago (Image: Getty Images)

A television personality has recalled her mortifying meeting with King Charles, which ended in her falling on the monarch and accidentally spitting food in his face. Anna Williamson, relationships expert on Channel 4 ’s Celebs Go Dating, appeared on Joe Marler’s podcast, where he asked her to recall her most embarrassing celebrity encounter.

‌



The therapist says she had ‘a few encounters that spring to mind’ but perhaps her most memorable moment was her first meeting with King Charles. Anna explained to Marler that she had met the monarch due to being a long-time ambassador of the King’s Trust, previously known as the Prince’s Trust.

‌



MasterChef Australia judge denies claims Meghan Markle was ‘difficult’ on set READ MORE :

View 3 Images Anna Williamson recounted her mortifying meeting with King Charles at Highgrove (Image: Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

‌



She explained that her first meeting with Charles, when he was still Prince of Wales, was during a reception in the gardens of Highgrove in Gloucestershire. Anna recalled that she was balancing a small plate of risotto when the opportunity to greet the King arose, and she was unsure of the correct protocol to introduce herself.

She said on the Joe Marler Will See You Now podcast: “The King came over and you can curtsey or do a variety of things that are respectful - a bow, a handshake - and I sort of did them all at once.”

The relationship expert explained that during her curtsey, she lost her footing in the pavement, and fell into the King, all while still in the middle of eating.

‌



“He had to sort of push me back into place once I fell, and I spat risotto into his face,” she said. “I looked p***ed. So not only did I spit pea risotto on our now monarch, but I stumbled mid-curtsey because I over committed and fell into him. I had to be pulled off him.”

View 3 Images Anna Williamson (middle) is a relationships expert on Celebs Go Dating (Image: Channel 4)

Marler’s co-host Jake Bhardwaj then quizzed if Charles’ security were worried about the incident, to which Anna explained that they were lovely and helped her back on her feet.

‌



She said: “Everyone was quite chill, it was more the people I was with who were all laughing at me. Charles himself did offer to collect me and stand me back up again with security, but that was how I broke the ice with the King.” Marler responded: “Certainly a unique way of doing that.”

Anna’s anecdote is not the first time Joe Marler’s podcast has had a royal connection. During his visit to the UK in July, Prince Harry appeared on the podcast as he made a candid admission about his hair loss, gave an exhaustive list of his occupations, and spoke about the lasting legacy of the Invictus Games.

‌



During their chat, the Duke of Sussex joked about being bullied as a child over his hair colour. Joe questioned Harry as he asked what is one thing people get wrong about him, as he quipped, while maintaining a straight face, that people say that he is ginger when in fact his hair is more of a ‘sunset auburn’ colour.

Harry and Joe then went on to chat about occupations, where Harry made a lengthy list for those tuning in. "Full-time dad. British Army veteran. Prince of England. Duke. But for today, I don’t know. What do you want?"

As they all settled on calling him Duke, talk soon turned to the Invictus Games, which sees wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans take part in the Paralympic-style games every two years in a different city around the world.
