News.title: Catwalk model, 26, dies of rare cancer weeks after making runway debut
News.content:
Catwalk model, 26, dies of rare cancer weeks after making runway debut

Sydney Towle documented her stage four disease for more than one million followers on TikTok

View 3 Images Sydney Towle had just made her catwalk debut (Image: sydneytowle/Instagram)

A model and social media influencer has died from a rare form of cancer just a couple of months after making her runway debut.

‌



Sydney Towle was aged 26 when she died yesterday, with the news announced by her family on social media today. In a post on Sydney's social media accounts, they said: "We will always love you so much Sydney.

‌



"I am so proud of how hard you fought. I love you." The post included a picture of Sydney smiling on a mountain, accompanied by a "rest in peace" message and another one reading "An endless ray of sunshine. A daughter, sister and friend to so many."

‌



The model suffered from stage four cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer that affects the bile ducts. She was diagnosed in 2022, when she was 23 years old.

View 3 Images Sydney pictured in hospital (Image: sydneytowle/Instagram)

‌



The disease usually affects older adults, making Sydney's diagnosis exceptionally uncommon. The model appeared at Miami Swim Week at the end of May, marking her first time strutting down a catwalk.

Only on Tuesday, her brother, Austin Towle, revealed in a TikTok that his sister had been moved into hospice care. Alongside a picture of Sydney's family and friends surrounding her hospice bed, Austin wrote: "Sydney has been moved into hospice and is surrounded by her friends and family. Thank you for all your love and support."

Sydney was very open about her diagnosis on social media, where she was followed by 1.1million accounts. She documented everything, from gruelling chemotherapy sessions to quiet walks in New York City.

Article continues below

View 3 Images Sydney described walking at Miami Swim Week as one of the proudest and most empowering moments of her life (Image: sydneytowle/Instagram)

She also shared how she explored new pathways and clinical trials that might heal her condition, including preparing for tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy when her cancer spread to her lungs and stomach.

Her appearance at Miami Swim Week included wearing adaptive designs tailored for post-cancer bodies and surgical scars. She described her catwalk debut as one of the proudest and most empowering moments of her life.

News.title: Pregnant mum said ‘I’m off’ and plunged 10 storeys to her death – but baby lives
News.content:
Pregnant mum said ‘I’m off’ and plunged 10 storeys to her death – but baby lives

Emma Atkinson, 38, was more than seven months pregnant when she plunged 10 storeys to her death from a window - but her baby survived

View 4 Images Emma Atkinson fell 10 storeys to her death

A pregnant woman who died after a 10-storey drop from a tower block said "I'm off" before the fall, which her baby miraculously survived.

‌



Mother-of-five Emma Atkinson “deliberately propelled herself” out of the window but may not have intended to kill herself, a coroner has found.

‌



Her daughter was successfully delivered within half an hour of the fall at Shakespeare Towers, in the Burmantofts area of Leeds, on October 22 2024.

‌



An inquest heard Ms Atkinson, 38, who was more than seven months pregnant, had gone to visit her father David Atkinson, who lived on the ninth floor.

View 4 Images Emma's baby was delivered after she had died (Image: Facebook)

Mr Atkinson told police that his daughter went into the living room of the flat, sat on the back of a chair and started smoking a cigarette in front of the window.

‌



In a statement summarised at the inquest, he said she removed the safety catches on the window and opened it fully, so it was horizontal.

The inquest heard Mr Atkinson asked what she was doing and told her to shut the window because it was cold, but she told him “not to worry (as) she was just getting some fresh air”.

Shortly afterwards he heard Ms Atkinson say: “I’m off,” and saw her feet going out of the window. The inquest heard he ran over and saw his daughter on the pavement below.

‌



Detective Constable Emily Parnham said Ms Atkinson’s fall from the window at 10.20am was captured on CCTV, and she “did not appear to be distressed”.

View 4 Images Tributes left outside Shakespeare Towers in Burmantofts Leeds (Image: Lee McLean/SWNS)

The coroner heard how paramedics who arrived at the scene found that Ms Atkinson had not survived the fall, and all further treatment done was in the hope of saving the baby.

‌



The child was delivered by an emergency Caesarean section after Ms Atkinson arrived at Leeds General Infirmary. The inquest heard Mr Atkinson “believes Emma went to the flat with the intention of jumping out of the window to take her own life”.

Ms Parnham said West Yorkshire Police ’s investigation concluded there was no third party involvement in her death, and no suspicious circumstances.

Coroner Naomi McLoughlin said Ms Atkinson had struggled with her mental health in the past and was worried about possibly being sent to prison after missing a court appearance days before her death, over an allegation of shoplifting.

‌



Her family, who attended the inquest, said she was “so excited” about the impending births of her daughter and grandson and “would never have left her kids”, adding that her “life revolved around her children”.

View 4 Images Shakespeare Towers, in the Burmantofts area of Leeds (Image: Google Maps )

Ms McLoughlin said there was not enough evidence to say whether Ms Atkinson’s death was suicide or an accident, and recorded a narrative conclusion that said: “Emma Atkinson died from a self-inflicted act but her probable intent cannot be ascertained either way.”

‌



She said she was satisfied that Ms Atkinson had deliberately propelled herself out of the window, but added: “I have to consider the issue of her intent.

“I note the deliberate act of removing the safety catches from the window … and the manner of her falling, captured by the CCTV.”

The coroner said she balanced that with the fact that there were no concerns raised about her mental health in the weeks leading up to her death, and that she had been making plans to see family.

Article continues below

Ms McLoughlin said Ms Atkinson was “a much loved woman by all who knew her”.

For mental health support, contact the Samaritans on 116 123, email them at jo@samaritans.org or visit samaritans.org to find your nearest branch.

News.title: Burnham orders review of grooming gang early releases
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has ordered an "urgent" review to identify any grooming gang members who may be eligible to be freed from jail under the government's early release scheme.

The announcement comes after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch raised concerns that child sex offenders could leave jail well before the end of their sentences.

She pointed out that indecent assault was not included in the list of offences that the government said would be excluded, external from the early release scheme.

Five men convicted of indecent assault as part of a historical grooming-gang case in Bradford are among the prisoners whose offences were not included in the list of exclusions.

The prime minister's spokesperson said Burnham had asked the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) to "conduct an in-depth review of cases to ensure that grooming cases were identified".

"This work is happening urgently," Burnham's spokesperson said.

"This is extremely important to the PM and he has personally intervened to ensure everything possible is being done so that vile groomers are dealt with in the way their victims deserve."

It is understood that at this stage the review will only seek to identify offenders who might be released early.

The government has not confirmed whether the review will lead to the prevention of any early releases of offenders convicted of grooming-related crimes.

Badenoch described the intervention as "another U-turn secured" and "another review from Burnham following my letter".

The government is planning to release about 5,000 offenders in England and Wales early in an effort to make space in overcrowded jails.

Burnham launched a review of the scheme after he became prime minister and this week he announced that some prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sex and other grooming offences would barred from early release.

But in a letter, external, Badenoch said many more types of offenders - including those convicted of sexually assaulting children - could be freed early.

"On Tuesday, you told the country that those convicted of grooming offences would be excluded," she wrote. "Your own government has now put in writing that some of these men will be released early anyway."

Highlighting that indecent assault was not excluded from the early release scheme, Badenoch said "many cases of child sex abuse committed before 2004 were charged this way, including Rotherham and Rochdale".

Badenoch branded this a "betrayal of victims", and urged Burnham to publish the full list of offences that remain eligible for early release.

Under changes made by Burnham, external, people sentenced for rape, serious child sex and grooming offences will now not be eligible for early release from October.

But some prisoners who are not excluded could be freed after serving a third of their total custodial sentence rather than after 40% or 50% of their term.

Burnham said he had wanted to exclude more offenders, but prison overcrowding prevented this.

The prime minister said making more prisoners exempt was not possible without the prison system collapsing and putting the public "at much greater risk".

The prison population in England and Wales on 3 August was 86,495, which was 97% of useable capacity.

The number of places in jails in England and Wales has not kept pace with the significant rise in the prison population in recent decades under successive governments.

There are cases of offenders who were convicted of indecent assault under section 14 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1956.

These sections of the 1956 Act were not included in the government's list of exclusions, suggesting prisoners convicted of these crimes could qualify for the early release scheme.

Five men who were jailed in October 2005, external, after being convicted of indecent assault for abusing a teenage girl in Bradford in the early 2000s, could be eligible for early release under the scheme.

In December 2024, Ajaz Karim was jailed for 21 months after he was convicted of indecent assault for sexually abusing a 13-year-old girl at the school where he was a sports coach.

In another case, Shahid Hussain was jailed for eight years in September 2024, after he was convicted of indecently assaulting a 14-year-old girl in Rotherham in 2003.

The government has not yet confirmed exactly which offenders will be released.

The mother of PC Andrew Harper also said she was "devastated" to learn two men jailed after her son was killed will still be eligible for early release.

PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

His family previously said they had received a letter from the Ministry of Justice confirming that two of the offenders could be included in the early release scheme.

Earlier this week, Justice Secretary Alex Norris apologised to families affected by the early release scheme, saying they were "carrying the can from previous failures".

The justice secretary said about 5,000 extra releases will take place in 10 batches from October - down from about 6,000 before the revision.

The changes are due to be phased in, beginning with prisoners serving sentences of fewer than 575 days, going up to inmates jailed for 12 years or more being eligible for early release in June 2027.

The number of individuals released each time will depend on the prison population, which the government says will evolve between now and implementation.

News.title: Calls for inquiry into Army training college for teenagers after reports of rape and abuse
News.content:
The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was rapedâ¦ by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.

Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".

Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of AFC staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.

She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."

The Army told the BBC a visit to AFC by the Children's Commissioner and safeguarding authorities in January 2026 had recognised "the culture of care and the confidence junior soldiers have in raising concerns".

It added that the college's "robust discipline system" has been graded "outstanding" by the schools' inspectorate, Ofsted, which visits the college every three years.

Ashleigh Percival-Borley, a veteran who served for 13 years in the British Army as a sergeant and multi-disciplinary instructor, said "incidents like this have "really taken my confidence out of the institution and that makes me really sad".

She told Radio 4's Today programme there was a "level of frustration" from women who wanted to serve in the army.

She said hearing the allegations "sickened" her as a female veteran as well as a former instructor who knew "the embodiment of the army's values and standards" needed for the role.

News.title: Stephen Bear jailed for harassing ex-partner Georgia Harrison
News.content:
After serving half his original sentence, Bear was released from prison, but between 1 March 2025 and 21 July 2025 began posting on Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube and Facebook about the case and Miss Harrison.

The court heard these were "consistently posted messages of the most abhorrent and harmful type".

Addressing Bear, Judge Morgan said: "What you did in that three to four month period is simply victim blaming."

Georgia Harrison did not attend court, but the prosecution read out a statement where she described feeling isolated, exposed and unsafe, and asked for the restraining order to be extended.

She said the significant stress made her worry about her unborn child and said it "caused her to spiral" on some occasions.

"I shut him out of my mind for a long time and it's not fair that he's managed to crawl his way back in," the statement read.

Bear arrived for Thursday's sentencing with his wife, who is eight months' pregnant.

As he walked in to court, he refused to answer questions but gave a thumbs up and said: "Wish me luck guys. See you soon, hopefully."

As his barrister spoke about why Bear should be given a reduced sentence, he appeared to briefly cry.

He shook his head as he was taken away to begin another prison term.

News.title: Majority of England's rivers and lakes fail new environmental review
News.content:
The government is already on course to miss its legally binding target of restoring 77% of England's waters to good ecological status by 2027 - a goal the environmental watchdog, the Office for Environmental Protection, has warned will be missed by a "considerable margin".

It's now investigating both the government and the Environment Agency over possible rule breaches.

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle said the figures "underline the need for wholesale change across the water sector".

She pointed to new laws the government has introduced to hold water companies to account and record investment. "We will drive forward a system that puts the public interest first," she said.

Much of the debate about the state of England's waters has centred on water companies and the sewage they release into rivers.

But campaigners and scientists also point to agriculture as an equally large source of pollution - one that attracts far less public attention.

Erica Popplewell, of the campaign group River Action, said some farming, particularly intensive poultry units - vast sheds housing hundreds of thousands of birds - were a growing threat to rivers such as the Wye and Severn.

"There's a lot of poo that comes out of the chickens," she said. "If it goes straight into a river, it causes eutrophication. The whole ecology of the river is damaged, and the river is dying." She called on the government to tackle sewage and farming "with the same urgency".

The National Farmers' Union of England and Wales has been approached for comment.

Other types of pollution affecting England's bodies of water, the Environment Agency pointed to, include petrol, garden pesticides and contaminated water running off roads picking up microplastics.

News.title: Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns
News.content:
A University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row has resigned "with immediate effect".

On Wednesday the university said it had launched an investigation into Professor Jason Arday "following new information" about his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".

Arday - who became the university's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - has admitted errors in his work, but said he had faced "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack" and was not a "liar".

It came after a series of media reports questioning some of his achievements and allegations of plagiarism in his PhD thesis.

Arday said he had "concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".

In the statement posted by the Good Law Project on Wednesday, Arday said that being appointed professor had been "without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life".

But he added: "There comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great."

He said his resignation should not "be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge.

"Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

Thanking his students and colleagues, he said that "for my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".

Arday said "this is not the end of my work" and that he needed "time to heal".

"When that time comes, I will return," he added.

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher and self-defined "race realist", whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He claimed on Substack that he had put Arday's work through a plagiarism detection software, which found that "many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source".

Cambridge had initially described allegations made against Arday as a "vile campaign to undermine his credibility".

Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated allegations of plagiarism in his thesis that were made last year, but did not uphold the charges.

The BBC has contacted the university for further comment.

News.title: Why is Amanda Knox's upcoming Edinburgh Fringe comedy show causing controversy?
News.content:
Amanda Knox, a woman involved in one of the world's most famous murder cases, is set to perform a comedy show at The Edinburgh Festival Fringe.

Knox was convicted and later acquitted of murdering her British roommate, Meredith Kercher, in Italy in 2007.

Knox's show, Cartwheel, is about motherhood and how she will explain her experiences to her daughter, according to the festival's website.

"I don't joke about Meredith's death. I joke a lot about how I was vilified, but I don't joke about her murder," she had told the Telegraph newspaper, external.

Kercher's sister, Stephanie told BBC Breakfast her sibling "wouldn't find these topics of any comedy value".

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by just over 2,400 people, and says the show disrespects her memory and also risks normalising violence against women.

A spokesperson for Knox said the show, set to run over 11 days from Friday, honours Kercher's memory.

Find out more about what Stephanie Kercher told the BBC.

News.title: Man charged with killing Scottish aid worker in Greece
News.content:
An Afghan boxer has been charged with killing Scottish aid worker Elisabeth Ross in Greece.

Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, has been charged with homicide with intent, alongside robbery and weapons offences.

The body of Ross, who was 38, was discovered in a suitcase by a homeless man in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of the Greek capital on 18 July.

Ahmadzai was remanded in custody until his trial, which could take up to 18 months. During the hearing he asked for an English translator but did not respond to the charges.

Ahmadzai arrived in court in Athens on Thursday morning in an unmarked Grey car. He was escorted out with masked officers holding his head down.

On Wednesday, he was assigned a court-appointed lawyer and given time to prepare his defence.

Ahmadzai was initially detained on illegal weapons possession charges and is facing a charge of homicide with intent, as well as allegations that he stole more than â¬10,000 (Â£8,500) from the victim's bank accounts using her bank cards.

Homicide with intent is equivalent to a murder charge in Scots law.

A statement from the police's organised crime directorate said Ahmadzai was brought to a police station on 30 July.

"In particular, it emerged that the 26-year-old placed the body in a suitcase and transported it to the abandoned site," the statement said.

The BBC understands he denies the charge of murder but admits moving the body, claiming that he did so because he feared he would be blamed for her death.

News.title: All schools in England to get pupil attendance targets, government says
News.content:
Every mainstream state school in England will be given their own target to improve pupil attendance, the government has confirmed.

Schools will also be encouraged to offer more clubs and activities on Fridays, to improve attendance at the end of the week.

It comes as official attendance data, published on Thursday, suggested school absence rates in England remained above pre-pandemic levels, with nearly one in five pupils missing at least 10% of school in the 2025/26 academic year.

Education minister Paul Waugh said the new attendance targets would take each school's local challenges into account, but that "every school has a role to play to improve attendance".

Before the Covid pandemic, when many schools closed to pupils for significant periods of time, attendance rates at English mainstream state schools regularly stayed above 95%, but schools have struggled to get back to those rates in the years since.

Thursday's figures, external suggested an overall attendance rate of 93% for 2025/26, a slight decrease on the previous year. That includes both authorised absences, such as illness, and unauthorised absences, which is when pupils miss school without permission or a valid reason.

The rates of persistent absence have doubled since the pandemic. A pupil is described as persistently absent if they miss at least 10% of school sessions.

In 2018/19, persistent absence rates for England state schools were around 10%, while the most recent data showed it was at 19% in 2025/26.

Pupils on free school meals and those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) were also still more likely to be absent from school than their peers.

News.title: Meredith Kercher's sister criticises Amanda Knox's Edinburgh comedy show
News.content:
The sister of Meredith Kercher has criticised a solo comedy show by Amanda Knox, who was convicted and later acquitted of murdering the British student in Italy in 2007.

The Edinburgh Festival Fringe website says Knox's show, Cartwheel, is about motherhood and how she will explain what happened in Perugia to her daughter.

Stephanie Kercher, addressing Knox directly on BBC Breakfast, said: "What I would say [to Knox] is to think about the family here, think about her friends and to turn the tables if it was your sister that this had happened to, because I know you have a sister as well."

Knox said the show, set to run over 11 days from Friday, honours Kercher's memory.

Her comedy show's title Cartwheel references a story that once claimed she did cartwheels in the police station after her friend's death.

Knox told the Telegraph newspaper, external last week: "I don't joke about Meredith's death. I joke a lot about how I was vilified, but I don't joke about her murder."

Asked if Meredith Kercher would have found her comedy funny, she added: "Yeah, I think so. I mean, it is funny!".

Responding to that suggestion, Stephanie Kercher told the BBC: "Meredith absolutely wouldn't find these topics of any comedy value."

She said: "Our family's pain is immense. I can't explain to you how much pain our family have been through, and also we're talking two decades later now, this pain."

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by just over 2,400 people, and says the show disrespects her memory and also risks normalising violence against women by making light of such a harrowing event.

News.title: Woman charged after four stabbed near Covent Garden
News.content:
A 47-year-old woman has been charged after four men were stabbed near Covent Garden in central London.

Stella Gollovena, of no fixed address, was charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and one count of possession of an offensive weapon in a public place.

Police were called to Endell Street at about 12:30 BST on Wednesday after four men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 56, were found with stab wounds. They were taken to hospital with injuries that were not life-threatening or life-changing. All have now been discharged.

Gollovena was arrested at the scene and taken into custody. She will appear at Highbury Magistrates' Court later.

The incident took place in the capital's busy tourist area filled with bars, theatres and restaurants.

London's Air Ambulance landed at nearby Trafalgar Square following the incident, but the four men were taken to hospital by paramedics via road.

News.title: Arrests and injuries amid anti-immigration disorder
News.content:
Two police officers have been injured after a second night of disorder in a market town which has seen anti-immigration protests.

Norfolk Police said "significant police resources" were deployed to Thetford on Wednesday to maintain public safety, after a large group gathered on Clover Way.

The force said members of the group "became physically aggressive towards officers â a male officer was struck with a rock and a female officer was seriously bitten, breaking the skin."

Assistant chief constable Julie Dean said: "We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties."

The scenes followed unrest on Tuesday in St John's Way, Bracken Road and Elm Road, when properties were damaged with windows smashed and fences broken, and people attempted to break into a residential property, police said.

The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, said the "ugly scenes in Thetford over the past few days have been difficult to watch and are deeply concerning".

News.title: Families' anger at jailed funeral boss's apology letter
News.content:
Natalie Smith's grandfather Norman Bridger was one of the bodies found at Legacy.

He had been there for 11 months and was 95 when he died, with a funeral held for him before they found out his body was still at the site.

Smith said Bush's letter was a "tick box exercise to try and make himself look like he'd approached the families".

She said she reacted with "disbelief" when she received the letter, which contained "no real substance, no emotion, nothing".

"They're just words and there was nothing behind them," she said, adding she would never forgive Bush for what he had done.

Robert Bush's letter in full:

To everyone who has been affected by my actions.

"I have spent a great deal of time thinking about the events that [sic] wish to say something directly to you.

"I know that many of you entrusted me and my business with the care of someone you loved during one of the most difficult times in your lives.

"I recognise that what happened has caused distress, upset and uncertainty for many families. I am deeply sorry.

"There are no words that can undo what has happened or take away the pain that many of you have experienced. I understand that this has affected not only your confidence in me, but also memories surrounding the loss of those closest to you.

"I accept responsibility for my failures. Looking back, I know that I should have acted differently and much sooner. I regret that I did not do so.

"I do not expect forgiveness, nor do I write this letter in the hope of reducing the seriousness of what has happened.

"I simply wanted you to know that I genuinely regret the consequences of my actions, and the impact they have had on so many people.

"I appreciate that every family's experience has been different, and I respect that some people may never wish to accept my apology. That is entirely understandable.

"I hope that, in time, each of you can find some peace and remember your loved one for who they were rather than for the circumstances that have followed. I am truly sorry."

If you have been affected by issues surrounding bereavement, information is available via BBC Action Line, including contact details of organisations that can help.

News.title: Farmer jailed for lodger's 'body in barrel' murder
News.content:
A farmer who shot his lodger and dismembered his body has been jailed for 35 years.

Richard Dyson, 55, disappeared in November 2019, but his remains, kept inside a concrete-filled barrel in a trailer on a farm near Barnsley, were not discovered for nearly six years.

A trial at Sheffield Crown Court heard how Christopher Wright killed Dyson when he tried to steal a gun from him before disposing of the body with the help of his childhood friend Karl Schwalbe.

Last month, Wright, 73, was convicted of murder and Schwalbe, 72, was found guilty of perverting the course of justice.

Wright, a former butcher, was also found guilty of conspiracy to pervert the justice, preventing a lawful burial and six firearms offences.

Jailing him, Mr Justice Cotter said: "You had worked as a butcher and were skilled enough to do such a terrible thing, something few ordinary people would have the stomach for."

Schwalbe was given a three-year sentence for perverting the course of justice.

Bethany Dainty, Dyson's daughter, said her life had become a "living nightmare".

She had issued numerous appeals for help tracing her father in the years he was missing.

In a victim impact statement read to the court, she said: "Someone watched me suffering for years and said nothing. That level of cruelty is impossible for me to understand."

News.title: Car washes and vape shops can still sponsor skilled foreign workers despite visa changes
News.content:
More than 1,900 small high street businesses including mini-marts, vape shops and car washes are licensed to sponsor foreign workers under a specialist scheme intended for high-earning individuals despite visa rules being tightened, BBC Verify has found.

The Home Office scheme allows registered employers to recruit workers from overseas who meet a certain skill level. The rules were tightened in July 2025 to restrict the scheme mostly to graduate-level employees who would be earning at least Â£41,700.

But a year on from the rule change, BBC Verify has found more than 1,500 grocery and convenience stores, 150 taxi operators, 100 barber shops, and dozens of car washes and vape shops are still on the register and able to sponsor people to apply for visas.

More than 100 of those businesses were added to the skilled worker sponsorship list after the rules were tightened. Being on the register does not mean applications for individual visas would be approved.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said on Thursday the government will "make sure that the rules are being properly enforced because we cannot have employers getting round the rules or finding different ways to deviate".

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered an urgent review into the presence of vape shops, barbers and car washes on the skilled worker sponsor register two months ago, following concerns over the "potential misuse of the system". The Home Office said at the time that any businesses seeking to abuse the system would have their licences revoked.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "We have raised the skilled worker threshold and over 100 occupations are now ineligible for new skilled worker visas."

It is understood some of the companies that joined the register after the rules changed may have applied before they took effect. Some companies may have also remained on the register because they were approved before July 2025 or are sponsoring workers who were already in the UK.

There are more than 120,000 businesses with licences to sponsor skilled workers. The skilled worker scheme was introduced after Brexit for employers to recruit workers after EU free movement ended. Smaller firms must pay a Â£611 fee to apply to join the register while larger businesses, such as those with more than 50 staff, pay a fee of Â£1,682. Anyone can be visited by the UK Visas and Immigration service during the application process.

Until July last year, someone being hired from abroad could qualify for sponsorship if their qualifications met an A-Level or equivalent standard, as long as they were paid at least Â£38,700 in most cases. Since the rule change, non-graduate professions, such as shop managers, are no longer eligible to apply. There are also higher English-language skill requirements that were introduced in January this year.

The Home Office said there were 68,067 skilled worker visas granted in the 12 months to March this year - 29,745 to main applicants and 38,322 to their dependants - which is 30% lower than the year before. IT professionals were the most common type of people to be granted the visas, followed by those people working in finance, while the fall in approvals was mostly attributed to those in food preparation and hospitality trades no longer qualifying for the scheme.

News.title: Emmerdale actor Lawrence Robb joins Strictly line-up
News.content:
Emmerdale actor Lawrence Robb is the latest star to join the line-up for this year's Strictly Come Dancing.

Robb has played Mackenzie 'Mack' Boyd in the ITV soap since 2020, and has also appeared opposite Billie Piper in I Hate Suzie and in stage productions such as Legally Blonde The Musical.

In a statement, the actor joked: "I don't know who's more excited about this, me or my mother.

"I can't quite believe that I am going to be getting my dancing shoes on this September on one of my favourite shows of all time."

He added: "It's a dream come true, and I can't wait to bring my all to ballroom. Wish me luck, and any advice is very welcome - trust me I'll need it!"

Robb is the 12th celebrity to be confirmed for this year's series, joining stars including Delta Goodrem, Lacey Turner, Dani Dyer, Will Best, Jaime Winstone and Dame Sarah Storey.

News.title: Mark Hughes' son died of sudden adult death syndrome
News.content:
The son of former Manchester United footballer Mark Hughes died from sudden adult death syndrome, a coroner has found.

Alex Hughes was found collapsed at his home in Macclesfield, Cheshire, on 19 June by his two sons.

The 38-year-old, who followed his ex-Wales international father into football and held roles in recruitment at Grimsby Town, Manchester City and other clubs, could not be revived by paramedics, his inquest heard.

Following his death, Mark Hughes and his wife Jill said they were "totally heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected loss of our beloved son".

Sudden adult death syndrome (SADS) - also known as sudden arrhythmic syndrome - is diagnosed when the cause of death cannot be explained in a post-mortem examination because the structure of the heart appears normal.

It affects about 500 people in the UK every year.

The British Heart Foundation said SADS "usually happens when a dangerously abnormal heart rhythm goes untreated and leads to a cardiac arrest".

The foundation added that inherited heart conditions are "often the cause of SADS if the person who has it doesn't know they do".

News.title: Witnesses in Nolan Wells case plagued by menacing phone calls including ‘clock is ticking’ threat
News.content:

Three people have been charged with threatening a judge, a witness and local officials involved in the investigation into the death of Nolan Xavier Wells, an 18-year-old who was found dead after a July Fourth boat trip with friends to an island off Mississippi’s Gulf Coast.

The three individuals do not appear to have any connection to Wells, his family, the group he was with or the investigation itself. The threats emerged amid widespread speculation and heightened scrutiny surrounding the case, fueled by unanswered questions about Wells’ final hours, mistrust of law enforcement and Mississippi’s history of racial violence.

Wells, who was Black, had traveled to the uninhabited island with several white classmates from his high school. He did not return to the mainland with the group that night, and his body was discovered two days later in waters near the island.

Authorities have not announced any arrests or identified suspects in Wells’ death. An independent autopsy requested by his family determined his cause of death was “undetermined” pending further investigation.

open image in gallery An independent autopsy commissioned by Wells’ family found the 18-year-old’s cause of death to be ‘undetermined’ pending further investigation ( AP Photo/John Amis )

Attempts to reach the defendants for comment were unsuccessful. Phone numbers listed for some of the defendants in affidavits weren't active and a call to another number went unanswered. Emails sent to addresses listed in an affidavit for one of the defendants went unanswered. It is unclear if they have attorneys yet.

One of the defendants, Edward James Porter of Illinois, allegedly called an unnamed witness on July 31 and threatened to kill them and their family, according to an affidavit. Porter also allegedly told another person in Mississippi in a phone call that he would cut them up and put them “into a suitcase.” Porter was charged on July 31 in federal court for the Southern District of Mississippi for the threat.

Porter threatened two members of the family of Bart Edminston Jr., a 21-year-old who knew Wells and provided aid to the boat the group used on July Fourth, said family attorney Russell Latino. Latino said that one of the family members who Porter threatened is a witness in the investigation into Wells’ death.

An Ohio woman was also charged with allegedly placing bomb threats at the George County Chancery Clerk's Office and the Jackson County Sheriff’s Office on July 23. The woman, Michelle Francine Edwards, allegedly called the clerk's office 21 times and said, “the clock is ticking,” according to an affidavit.

open image in gallery Nolan Wells’ heartbroken parents listen to remarks at a news conference about the investigation into his death ( Getty )

A California man, Joseph Alfredo Vasquez Dumarce, was charged on July 14 for allegedly sending a threatening Facebook message to a Jackson County Chancery Court judge with ties to the Wells investigation. According to an affidavit, a Facebook user believed to be Dumarce sent a message to the judge's account that constituted a “threat that a bomb would be mailed to the judge's office."

Judge Ashlee Cole posted a screenshot of Dumarce's threatening message on Facebook on July 9. Cole wrote in an earlier Facebook post that her son last saw Wells on July Fourth around 3 p.m. and decided to “stay on the island and return inland later with another group of friends.” Cole wrote that she deactivated her Facebook and that she fears for the safety of her children.

“No one in our family is trying in any way to impede with the investigation by law enforcement or to otherwise hamper the family and law enforcement’s quest for answers,” Cole wrote, adding that her son “cooperated fully” with the sheriff's investigation.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor says he was chased by an alleged stalker wearing a balaclava in a face-to-face confrontation close to his Sandringham home, a court has heard.

Alex Jenkinson, 39, is charged with using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour towards the former Duke of York in Norfolk on May 6.

Suffolk Police are also applying for a civil Stalking Protection Order against Jenkinson, relying on evidence from Andrew and searches on Jenkinson’s phone.

At Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Thursday, Deputy Chief Magistrate Tan Ikram read out parts of Andrew’s witness statement which is due to form the centrepiece of both legal proceedings.

The royal said that when he was out for a walk with his dogs on the estate, he spotted a car which he assumed to belong to press photographers, and then he and his security detail “drove past the car”.

He said a man “turned and faced me – he was wearing a balaclava face covering”.

open image in gallery Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor ( AFP/Getty )

Andrew provided a description of the “out-of-place” man, and added in his statement: “I then saw a loose dog running towards him.

“Then he realised who I was and began to sprint after my vehicle.”

Thursday’s court hearing took place in Jenkinson’s absence after he arrived with his dog, Indie, and was blocked from entering the building by court officials.

As Jenkinson stood on the pavement outside, his lawyer, Claire Howell, told Judge Ikram: “He has had to bring his dog with him, so he wasn’t allowed inside the court.

“He is homeless and currently in accommodation in a Travelodge.

“He is not allowed to leave the dog there. It provides him with support, he suffers from ADHD.”

She conceded that she has no documents to prove Jenkinson’s medical condition, or his need for a support animal, and the judge told her: “I’m not prepared to have a dog in the courtroom simply because he is homeless and he happens to keep a dog.

“I’m not saying he is not telling the truth but there’s nothing to corroborate it.”

He added: “We accommodate people who have ADHD and have support animals.

“I would want something more than he is homeless and happens to have a dog.”

The judge heard and agreed an application for the police bid for a Stalking Protection Order to be adjourned, and decided the hearing could take place in Jenkinson’s absence.

open image in gallery Andrew now lives in Marsh Farm on the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk (Joe Giddens/PA) ( PA Wire )

Ms Howell told the court Jenkinson has now been found temporary accommodation where he can leave the dog for future hearings, and she added: “I don’t want to give character evidence on behalf of the dog, but having spent the last hour and a half with him, I can say he is a very well-behaved animal.”

Jenkinson is accused of causing the former Duke of York to “fear unlawful violence” during the confrontation in Wolferton, close to his Marsh Farm property.

Jenkinson was detained under the Mental Health Act for around a month afterwards. He has pleaded guilty to failing to provide a specimen of blood while in custody on May 6.

But he denies the public order offence against Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and has also pleaded not guilty to a further charge of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause fear or provoke unlawful violence against another man, Stephen Terry, in King’s Lynn, on May 5.

Andrew is due to give evidence by videolink at the criminal trial, which has been set for December 21.

Jenkinson, who comes from Stowmarket, Suffolk, is also fighting the making of the Stalking Protection Order.

Judge Ikram ruled on Thursday that the former duke, as well as Mr Terry and an eyewitness to the Norfolk incident, must give evidence for a second time at the hearing to determine the Stalking Protection Order application.

“I am persuaded that fairness demands the respondent to these proceedings (Jenkinson) be allowed to call and cross-examine these witnesses”, he said.

At a hearing at the end of July, the court heard that evidence from Jenkinson’s phone – including alleged searches on Andrew, Sandringham and “weapons” – is due to feature in the trial.

In the criminal proceedings, Jenkinson is on bail with conditions not to go near a number of sites linked to the royal family – Sandringham, Buckingham Palace, Balmoral, Windsor and Highgrove.

He must also not try to contact Andrew directly or indirectly, or approach him or enter Norfolk.

As the hearing concluded, Judge Ikram extended the interim Stalking Protection Order against Jenkinson, he set a pre-trial hearing at Loughborough Magistrates’ Court for January 22, and said the final hearing would take place at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on February 16.

Dr. Anthony Fauci’s cell phone is now in the hands of Republicans who want him held in contempt of Congress after he refused to answer questions about his actions during the COVID-19 pandemic at a hearing last week.

Fauci repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right during testimony last week, declining to answer more than 100 times, with Republican Senator Rand Paul leading the charge against the infectious disease expert.

The Senate Homeland Security Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations has obtained a copy of the doctor’s iPhone, The Wall Street Journal first reported, which Republicans hope could shed more light on the matter. The Republican-led committee already has copies of Fauci’s private journals, publicly released last week. On Thursday, the committee voted to hold in contempt.

Fauci used the iPhone while he was director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases during the Trump administration, his spokesperson told the WSJ. The revelation of the cell phone comes as the committee voted to refer Fauci to the Department of Justice for contempt of Congress.

The doctor helped lead the nation’s response to the pandemic and is accused by Paul of not being forthcoming about the potential origins of the virus, in addition to guidance he gave on vaccine mandates and social distancing. He has vigorously denied the allegations.

Dr. Anthony Fauci’s cell phone is now in the hands of Republicans pushing to charge him with contempt of Congress after he refused to answer questions about his actions during the COVID-19 pandemic at a hearing last week ( Reuters )

He stayed in government during the first year of the Biden administration and was pardoned by former president Joe Biden as one of the Democrat’s final acts in office.

Concerned that the doctor could become a future target of Republicans, Biden issued a preemptive pardon for Fauci that effectively blocked federal criminal prosecutions for any official conduct between 2014 and 2025, a period covering his response to the pandemic.

Fauci noted the pardon does not protect him from possible state prosecutions or from any allegations of false testimony before Congress.

Paul threatened that Fauci would face “consequences” for asserting his Fifth Amendment right after the infectious disease expert blasted the Republican lawmaker for his “unhinged obsession” with him.

Fauci “didn’t need to hide behind the Fifth Amendment, and maybe the Fifth Amendment doesn’t attach when you have a pardon in place,” Paul told reporters after the hearing.

Before the hearing, Fauci said he still faced potential legal risks despite the pardon. In a statement, he accused Paul of trying to force him into saying “something, anything” that could fulfill the senator's repeated pledge to see him “behind bars.”

Paul said Wednesday he does not plan to immediately seek a full Senate contempt vote, acknowledging such resolutions often fail to secure the required 60 votes. Instead, he said the committee will first vote on sending a recommendation to federal prosecutors, with the possibility of a Senate vote later if necessary.

The Associated Press contributed to this article

News.content:

Sitting in her car one morning before work, Sabrina Javellana was frantically scrolling through photos of herself online that someone anonymously sent her a link to, with an ominous warning of their explicit content.

As she sifted through the dozens of images, posted on 4chan, she came across one that made her freeze.

“I recognized one from when I was 17 in high school, just taking a cute picture in a mirror of my outfit, about to go hang out with my friends…except my clothes were totally removed,” she recalled.

“It was the same exact photo, except they used this AI-generated technology to remove my clothes, and it looked hyper-realistic. But I knew this wasn't real. From that day on, my world turned upside down.”

Javellana was 23, working in local politics in Florida, when she fell victim to AI deepfake pornography in 2021, which she describes as an act of sexual violence.

open image in gallery Sabrina Javellana was 23 and working in local politics when she fell victim to AI deepfake pornography in 2021. She said it turned her life ‘upside down’ ( Sabrina Javellana/Getty )

With the unstoppable rise of AI technology, it has never been easier for perpetrators to create and share nonconsensual sexually explicit deepfakes. The estimated number of deepfakes rose from approximately 500,000 in 2023 to 8 million in 2025, according to analysis. And 99 percent of deepfakes target women.

Still, it remains unclear how serious tech bosses are about tackling the problem. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appeared unaware of the latest deepfake bill being pushed by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle when The Independent quizzed him on it in Washington, D.C. recently, while Elon Musk’s xAI is suing Minnesota over its attempts to ban so-called “nudification” apps in the state.

Momentum to tackle nonconsensual sexually explicit deepfakes by the U.S. government had been picking up steam after Congress passed the TAKE IT DOWN Act last year. It prohibits the publication of authentic and AI-generated sexual images published without a person’s consent, and requires online platforms to remove them within 48 hours of a complaint.

The DEFIANCE Act would allow victims to file civil lawsuits against people who produce, distribute, and solicit nonconsensual deepfake AI pornography, as well as those who intend to distribute such images.

It was cleared the Senate by unanimous consent in January but is languishing in the House, with time running out. The bipartisan bill, introduced by New York Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and co-sponsored by Republican Rep. Laurel Lee of Florida.

But some Republicans, it seems, do not want to hand Ocasio-Cortez a win so close to the midterms in November, when she is up for election.

When The Independent recently asked Ocasio-Cortez about the GOP lawmakers reportedly blocking the bill because her name is attached to it, her response was blunt. “I don't think that we should be emboldening child pornographers and helping abusers just because of some personal beef that they may have,” she said.

open image in gallery Paris Hilton told The Independent: ‘Every day the DEFIANCE Act isn’t put on the calendar in the House, more women and girls become victims without a meaningful path to justice’ ( Getty Images )

Ocasio-Cortez said that she would welcome the assistance of first lady Melania Trump, who supported the TAKE IT DOWN Act.

“I think that this is a really great opportunity, just as we have in the House, to be able to champion and for women to uplift one another across party lines,” she told The Independent.

Javellana said the issue transcends party politics and described the blockage as “petty.”

“It feels like a slap in the face to the women and girls who have spoken so bravely to tell their stories,” Javellana, 28, told The Independent. “This is not about making AOC's star even brighter.”

At a January press conference, Ocasio-Cortez teamed up with Paris Hilton, where the pair spoke of what it feels like to be a victim of deepfake AI pornography. Hilton said that more than 100,000 deepfake images of her exist online and has urged lawmakers to pass the DEFIANCE Act.

“Every day the DEFIANCE Act isn’t put on the calendar in the House, more women and girls become victims without a meaningful path to justice,” Hilton exclusively told The Independent in an emailed statement.

I felt fear for my family, my home; I purchased a firearm. It impacted my stress, my health, everything. It crushed me to step away, but I had to for my sanity, for my survival, for my health, for my safety Sabrina Javellana

Hilton added that there is “no legitimate policy reason” for the bill to be stalled and hit out at Rep. Jim Jordan, Chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. “Representative Jim Jordan and House leadership have an opportunity to protect millions and send a clear message that people who knowingly create or distribute nonconsensual explicit deepfakes to cause harm will be held accountable,” Hilton said.

Jordan’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

As AI technology advances at pace, the law is yet to catch up on holding perpetrators and Big Tech accountable for sexually explicit deepfakes and other online harms. And while the DEFIANCE Act “isn’t perfect,” Javellana said, introducing civil penalties provides victims with “more tools in the toolbox.”

In 2018, then aged 21, Javellana became one of the youngest elected officials in Florida when she won a seat on the Hallandale Beach city commission in Broward County, located between Miami and Fort Lauderdale. The young politician threw herself into issues she cares about deeply, which her critics deemed progressive.

“I'm speaking about climate change, I'm speaking about police reform, I'm speaking about government corruption,” she said.

open image in gallery Javellana suffered in silence for a year, not wanting to tell her family or friends about the images. After speaking out, she has joined advocates like Paris Hilton to call for legislation to stop AI deepfake pornography ( Getty Images for The Ford Founda )

The online abuse soon followed. “Because I was outspoken, because I was a young woman and an easy target,” Javellana said.

Everything changed on the day she received the first AI deepfake, depicting her nude. More popped up, and still do to this day, she said. “It’s not just the photos, but the comments from all these anonymous users. I would do her, I would rape her... just disgusting, vulgar comments.”

She served her four years in office but decided not to run for re-election following the ordeal.

“I felt fear for my family, my home; I purchased a firearm,” she said. “It impacted my stress, my health, everything. It crushed me to step away, but I had to for my sanity, for my survival, for my health, for my safety.”

She had limited options for recourse but reached out to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and consulted with a New York-based attorney. Due to a lack of state and federal legislation about AI deepfakes at the time, neither resulted in any morsel of justice. It was baffling to Javellana that what happened to her did not constitute a crime.

“It wasn't illegal to do this to people, to take their own likeness and make it into a new nude image and put their face on it and destroy their life, their career,” she said. “I totally lost my sense of self. I felt like I had no agency over my own body…I felt like this was a new form of sexual violence.”

open image in gallery Hilton has hit out at Republican leadership for stalling on the bill. ‘Representative Jim Jordan and House leadership have an opportunity to protect millions and send a clear message that people who knowingly create or distribute nonconsensual explicit deepfakes to cause harm will be held accountable,’ she said ( Getty Images )

Javellana suffered in silence for a year, not wanting to tell her family or friends about the images.

“It felt like a losing battle,” she said. “I decided maybe no one will ever see these. I'll never talk about it to anyone. I'll just, you know, compartmentalize it and try to move on with my life.”

Then, in January 2022, then-Florida Democratic state senator Lauren Book introduced a bill making it a felony to create sexually explicit deepfakes without consent. Book went public with her own experience where she was blackmailed with sexually explicit deepfake AI images.

Javellana reached out to Book to share her story and testified about her ordeal in the Florida Senate, marking the beginning of her public fight for women and girls. “I reached out to [Book’s] office and I told her, ‘Hey, this happened to me, and I want to help support your bill and make sure it gets passed.’”

With Javellana’s help, the Florida bill was swiftly signed into law by Governor Ron DeSantis. She hopes the DEFIANCE Act will follow suit, stressing that federal lawmakers can’t afford to delay.

open image in gallery First lady Melania Trump supported the TAKE IT DOWN Act last year, which prohibits the publication of authentic and AI-generated sexual images published without a person’s consent, and requires online platforms to remove them within 48 hours of a complaint ( Getty Images )

Prince Harry and Meghan are the latest high-profile names to back the bill. The couple criticized House lawmakers given the bill has been passed by the Senate.

“This begs the question: why the delay?” a release last week from the Duke and Duchess of Sussex asked. “The answer may lie in the deepest offense to families and children: the tech industry’s commitment to pushback on these bills to protect their bottom line.”

It isn’t only high-profile women and girls who are being targeted, as instances of deepfakes are cropping up more and more in schools, an issue Hilton has also raised.

“Around 99 percent of nonconsensual explicit deepfakes target women. But anyone can become a victim,” she told The Independent. “These AI tools and nudification apps are becoming cheaper, faster, and easier to use. All it takes is a single photo, and within seconds a coworker, stranger, classmate, or ex-partner can create realistic explicit images that can devastate someone’s reputation, career, relationships, and mental health.”

Javellana added: “Big tech has started this revolution where it's growing so fast, our laws are not catching up to it. It's going to continue to grow, impacting women and girls in all different aspects of life, not just public figures, politicians, celebrities. It's impacting more and more every single day, [including] girls in school.”

The bill is flailing even though it enjoys the support of House Speaker Mike Johnson as well as right-wing firebrands like GOP Reps. Nancy Mace of South Carolina and Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, in addition to progressive Democrats like Reps. Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Ro Khanna of California.

It has not so much as come up for a vote in the Judiciary Committee - which handles legislation relating to legal affairs and votes on whether to put a bill on the House floor - which is galling to many survivors.

open image in gallery The DEFIANCE Act is flailing in the House and time is running out to pass it. Javellana is calling on lawmakers to get it done ( AFP via Getty Images )

“AOC is a very powerful force, but it's so much bigger than her,” Javellana said. “And I know that these [Republican] leaders see that. It would be a win for them just as much as for her, as for President Trump.”

“This is common sense and to survivors, to victims...it's upsetting.”

But Javellana and other advocates remain confident that the DEFIANCE Act will become law. She is already looking ahead to the next fight.

“We're still not going to be done because this is still very reactive and not preventative,” she said of the bill. “And the preventative is once we start talking big tech, once we start talking about holding the platforms liable.”

“They are not good at all about responding to inquiries and reports of people asking to take this [content] down or regulating their users,” she added.

Indeed, when The Independent asked OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for his take on the DEFIANCE Act last week, he said he was “unfamiliar” with it. This was the same week the entrepreneur was in Washington, D.C., to talk with lawmakers about AI policy.

Javellana doesn’t believe she will ever discover the identities of the people who created the deepfake pornographic images of her, but whatever happens, she won’t be silent anymore.

“I wanted to hide for a while, but you know what? I can't do that,” she said. “That's letting them win.”

If you need support, call the Rainn National Sexual Assault Hotline at 800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit rainn.org

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Rodri makes decision, Bruno Guimaraes nears Arsenal move and Liverpool target PSG duo
News.content:
Why Arsenal Want Bruno Guimaraes So Badly

Bruno Guimaraes has received permission to travel to Arsenal and complete his £75m move from Newcastle United. The 28-year-old midfielder will undergo a medical at the Premier League champions within the coming days after both clubs agreed a fee with an announcement of his signing expected shortly afterwards.

The deal represents a key piece of business of Mikel Arteta ahead of Arsenal’s title defence - while Newcastle will be left to wave goodbye to another key player following the departures of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali this summer.

Arsenal will now turn to continuing their pursuit of Guimaraes’ international team-mate Vinicius Jr, although the Gunners believe it is increasingly likely that he stays at Real Madrid, who have significantly upped their new contract offer to the Brazilian star.

Liverpool, meanwhile, want to sign Bradley Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain and have also lined up his teammate Ibrahim Mbaye in what could be a double swoop for Andoni Iraola’s side. The European champions may be willing to let them go with Maghnes Akliouche is set to join from Monaco.

Elsewhere, Manchester United want to sign a left-back with Lewis Hall reportedly now set on a move to Old Trafford, but Newcastle are determined to stop the exodus and insist he is not for sale.

News.title: Air India flight plummets 300ft during severe turbulence
News.content:
An Air India flight suddenly plummeted 300ft during severe turbulence, with more than a dozen people hurt.

Footage from inside the aircraft, which was flying from Phuket to Delhi, shows passengers panicking as an air stewardess frantically tells them to fasten their seatbelts.

The pilots then managed to regain control and safely landed at its destination in India at 11am local time on Tuesday (4 August).

According to the tracking platform Flightradar24, the plane lost altitude sometime before landing in the Indian capital.

A total of 13 passengers and four crew members “sustained injuries and were taken to hospital for medical evaluation,” the airline said. On Wednesday (5 August), all had been discharged.

An investigation into the incident is underway,.

News.title: Best beauty advent calendars for 2026, reviewed as they drop
News.content:
I audibly gasped with excitement when I saw the selection for John Lewis's beauty advent calendar for 2026, and as someone who's going into her third year reviewing these coveted collections – I don't say that lightly. The selection for this year is seriously enticing, with six more products than last year, £160 more value (minus the extra £15 cost) and a mix of brands that appeal to a broad audience. There's Sisley, Trinny London and Dermalogica for more mature beauty buffs, K-beauty from Dr. Jart+ for the younger generation, plus heaps of big-name brands – from Clinique to Estee Lauder – for everyone else.

Admittedly, some of the sizes (those around the 5-10ml range) feel a little stingy, but when you look at the price of Sisley full-size items, you soon understand why John Lewis' hands were tied.

I appreciated the inclusion of the Foreo ufo 3 to mix things up a bit, and I spotted new launches (from the past 12 months) from Dr. Jart+ and Benefit, which can't be said of all the advents in this guide. Watch this space for an IndyBest tried and tested review but, on paper, I'm pretty impressed. Join MyJL Beauty now to be the first to secure the calendar when it launches next week for pre-orders.

John Lewis is also entering new territory with its first-ever fragrance advent calendar. Rather than relying on familiar designer perfumes, it's curated an impressive edit of luxury and niche scents, with names including Frédéric Malle, Maison Crivelli, BDK Parfums, Kilian Paris and Jo Loves. At £99 (worth £305), it looks like a great way to discover premium fragrances before committing to a full-size bottle, particularly if you're keen to venture beyond the usual department store favourites.

Robert Pattinson’s very big year is continuing with Primetime, a highly anticipated new thriller in which he plays famous paedophile hunter Chris Hansen, who spent years confronting child predators on the ethically and morally dubious US entertainment show To Catch a Predator.

Ahead of the film’s premiere at the Venice Film Festival in September, A24 has unveiled the first proper look of the movie, which marks the feature debut of documentarian Lance Oppenheim.

Pattinson plays Hansen as a crazy-eyed martyr with what seems to be a bit of a God complex, while he’s supported by Emmy winner Merritt Wever as his producer and Righteous Gemstones star Skyler Gisondo as an actor hired to play a 13-year-old boy in a paedophile sting. Musician Phoebe Bridgers also makes her acting debut in the film, while Scary Movie star Anna Faris plays Hansen’s wife.

The movie is inspired by the enormous success of To Catch a Predator, which began in 2004 first as a single segment on the US magazine show Dateline NBC, before being spun off into its own series. The show saw alleged child predators lured into the homes of children they’d been communicating with online, unaware that the children in question were actually adult crew members of the series pretending to be underage.

open image in gallery Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen in 'Primetime' ( A24 )

Hansen would famously emerge from the shadows in each home to confront the men who’d been targeted by the show. Men were found with help from the now-defunct watchdog group Perverted-Justice, which was known to scour internet forums to find instances of adults engaging in sexually explicit conversation with children, or arranging meets with them.

To Catch a Predator proved a controversial sensation, with Hansen becoming an overnight star. But the show was swiftly cancelled in 2008 when a 56-year-old assistant district attorney killed himself in his home shortly after a sting involving a fake child had taken place, with crew members from To Catch a Predator capturing the suicide on camera.

The show previously served as inspiration for the acclaimed documentary Predators, which was released last year.

Hansen has spoken little of Primetime, beyond a cryptic exchange with newscaster Jesse Weber on the magazine show News Nation in May.

“[Pattinson’s] an actor, right? Young, talented guy?” Hansen asked before being shown a clip of the film.

“I mean, he sounds a lot like you,” argued Weber. “Did you have any idea about this? Did you have any working relationship with this?”

“We had heard that there was something like this in the works,” Hansen replied. “They reached out to me this week, and I’ve been asked not to talk about it a great deal at this point.”

When Weber suggested Pattinson’s impression of Hansen was fairly accurate, Hansen somewhat agreed. “Little bit,” he said. “Very dramatic.”

open image in gallery Chris Hansen (left) is played by Robert Pattinson (right) in the new film ( Getty )

Primetime marks yet another sharp turn in a sensational run of projects for Pattinson, following his appearance in this year’s The Drama as a terrified Englishman convinced his fiancée may be insane, and his role last month as Anne Hathaway’s sneakiest of suitors in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.

He’s also due to star as another villain in Dune: Part Three in December, and has a Denzel Washington thriller called Here Comes the Flood in post-production, too. He’s currently filming the long-awaited sequel to 2022’s The Batman, which will finally hit cinemas in early 2028.

Primetime will be released in the US on 25 September, with a UK and Ireland release this autumn.

News.title: El Nino could cause explosion of rabid seals, animal health experts warn
News.content:
This year’s El Nino weather event risks propelling an outbreak of rabid seals around the world, the world’s animal health body has warned.

Countries in South America and Australasia are being urged to look for signs the deadly infectious disease has reached their waters, only two years after it was first confirmed in South Africa.

The 2024 discovery of rabies in South Africa’s Cape fur seals was the first significant outbreak ever found in marine mammals and has been described as a “significant shift in rabies ecology”.

More than 100 cases have been confirmed in South Africa and Namibia since then, raising fears that aggressive rabid seals could infect humans, pets and other wildlife.

Changing patterns in fish stocks caused by the El Nino phenomenon now potentially risk widening the spread, as uninfected seal populations migrate for food and come into contact with rabid colleagues.

Scientists believe warming sea temperatures off Antarctica could send seal populations northwards into Southern African waters, where they could be exposed to rabies.

They could then return to their home waters, taking the virus with them and infecting other seal populations.

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”
