The Buenos Aires stock exchange had a clear case of post-rally fatigue on Wednesday. The S&P Merval, which tracks Argentina’s largest listed companies, fell 1.02% to settle at 3,156,332 points.

This was a day for counting winnings rather than chasing new highs. The heaviest selling fell on the stocks most closely tied to President Javier Milei’s ambitious reform agenda—a sign that investors were hitting pause to see if real-world improvements in the economy can catch up with the blazing rallies in their brokerage accounts.

The Argentine peso, trading at 1,496 to the dollar on the official market, remained barely changed. It now sits dangerously close to its 52-week low of 1,500, a line in the sand that keeps both local savers and foreign funds watching every tick.

Unlike a panic, the session was orderly. Volume concentrated in the biggest names, and while nearly every sector shaded lower, the exits were measured. It was the kind of trading day that asks the question every rally eventually faces: how much good news is already in the price?

Assessment — A Pause, Not a Panic MEDIUM Wednesday’s decline looks like a textbook cool-down, not the start of something more worrying. The stocks hit hardest—YPF and Grupo Galicia—are exactly the names that have led the Milei-reform rally, suggesting the selling came from investors banking recent gains rather than fleeing new risk. Turnover was solid but not panicked, and the peso held steady at the very edge of its 52-week range. The key variable to watch now is whether the 3.1-million-point area on the Merval can act as a floor, or if another wave of selling pushes the index into a deeper technical retreat.

Wednesday’s dip was about gravity, not a change in the weather. The stocks that fell hardest—YPF, Grupo Galicia, Banco Macro, and Pampa Energía—are the very names that have become synonymous with the ‘Milei trade’, the bet that Argentina’s president can successfully deregulate the economy, slash the fiscal deficit, and eventually stabilise the peso.

When a narrative stock like YPF, Argentina’s state-controlled oil and gas company, falls 2.0% on the heaviest volume of any local name, it suggests institutional investors were trimming positions rather than retail investors bolting for the exits. The $12 million turnover tells you big money was moving, calmly.

Banking stocks softened in sympathy. Grupo Galicia, one of Argentina’s largest private financial conglomerates, lost 1.3%. The logic is straightforward: financial shares are a leveraged bet on the economy, and they had run up sharply on hopes that Milei’s reforms would end the era of capital controls and forced government lending.

Country risk, the extra yield investors demand to hold Argentine debt over US Treasuries, is the invisible hand shaping these moves. Any hint that the reform process is stalling sends this risk gauge higher, and the whole equity market wobbles in response. Wednesday’s measured selling suggests the market is waiting rather than worrying.

Among the brighter spots, some cross-listed CEDEARs—local certificates representing foreign shares—offered pockets of green. A small clutch of domestic names edged higher, with DISN surging 28.4% on thin volume, a move typical of a lightly-traded stock catching a sudden bid rather than a sector-wide shift. The real story remained the orderly retreat of the market’s biggest reform-sensitive names.

06 The technical picture

The Merval’s drop back to 3,156,332 points leaves it testing the strength of its recent breakout. The index is still in the upper reaches of its multi-year range, but technical traders will be watching the 3,100,000 area as a key near-term floor. 01 The session in one read

The S&P IPSA — the benchmark that tracks the 29 most liquid stocks listed on the Santiago Stock Exchange — notched a clean 1.47% gain on Wednesday, closing at 11,158 points. That left the index just 4% below its 52-week peak of 11,628, a threshold traders increasingly treat as the next bullseye.

Liquidity gathered around lithium giant SQM and the country’s two largest retailers, Falabella and Cencosud. SQM-B, the most accessible local listing of the world’s No 2 lithium producer, rose 2.4% with $16 million in turnover, extending a run that has made it one of the IPSA’s most consequential names.

Retail reflected a broader consumer optimism. Falabella, a department-store group with regional reach, added 1.4% on $30 million of volume. Rival Cencosud rose 1.7% on $14 million. Shopping-centre operator Mallplaza outperformed both, gaining 2.6% on $27 million.

The Chilean peso did not share the equity market’s cheer. The dollar bought 913.57 pesos at the session close, a 0.28% increase that nudged the exchange rate a little further from the 851.67 low of the past 52 weeks. Global dollar weakness, visible in the DXY index slipping 0.18%, failed to pull the peso along for the ride.

Assessment — Domestic strength, peso softness MEDIUM The session’s pattern — equities rising while the peso edged lower — suggests local real-money buyers were active in retail and lithium shares, while offshore investors may have trimmed modest peso exposure. With the IPSA at 11,158 it remains 4% shy of its 52-week high of 11,628, leaving clear air if the incoming inflation data prints benignly. The variable to watch is Thursday’s CPI: a reading below the 3.7% estimate could ignite a run at that record ceiling by convincing traders that rate cuts are nearer.

03 Why it moved — lithium optimism meets consumer strength

SQM-B’s 2.4% gain with $16 million in turnover was the session’s most telling datapoint. As one of the world’s largest lithium producers, supplying battery-grade chemicals to the electric-vehicle supply chain, SQM acts as Chile’s proxy for the global energy transition trade. Wednesday’s buying suggests investors see near-term value even as the stock has been volatile alongside lithium spot prices.

The retail bloc — Falabella, Cencosud and Mallplaza — posted gains on heavy volume, a pattern that often signals local institutional conviction. Falabella traded $30 million, the second-heaviest print of the day, while rising 1.4%. Mallplaza, the shopping-centre operator, surged 2.6% on $27 million. Together they paint a picture of a market betting on domestic consumption holding up.

The peso’s 0.28% slip to 913.57 is the puzzle piece that does not quite fit the equity narrative. With the US dollar index down 0.18% and copper — Chile’s export lifeblood — firm in global trade, a stronger peso might have been expected. The mild depreciation suggests that some corporate dollar demand or portfolio outflows created a counterweight to what should have been a supportive external setup.

The small-cap and mid-cap fringes delivered the most dramatic swings. Cencomalls, the real-estate arm of Cencosud that operates neighbourhood shopping centres, surged 7%. Construction and engineering names followed: Las Condes added 5.4%, Salfacorp rose 4%, and Besalco gained 3.6%. Losers were sparse, with CMPC easing 1% and Enel Americas slipping 0.7%.

Colombia’s COLCAP fared worst among the major benchmarks, losing 1.26%. Peru’s BVL, not shown in the curated table, bucked the trend with a 0.81% rise, making Lima and Santiago the only markets to record positive sessions on the day.

06 The technical picture

The IPSA’s close at 11,158 places it cleanly above the 11,000 round-number zone that had been a congestion point in recent sessions. That level now switches roles to act as near-term support. The next obvious target is the 52-week high of 11,628, roughly 4.2% above Wednesday’s finish.

On the downside, the index has established a pattern of higher lows since bouncing from the 8,161 trough. The 200-day moving average, a widely followed trend gauge, sits below current levels and provides a medium-term cushion. For dollar-based investors, the currency layer matters: the peso at 913.57 means a US dollar buys roughly 8.2% more Chilean equity than it did at the strong-peso extreme of 851.67.

01 The session in one read

Mexico’s S&P/BMV IPC — the country’s benchmark equities index that tracks its most liquid and representative stocks — lost its footing on Wednesday, closing at 66,537 points for a decline of 0.47%. The move lower was carved out not by a wave of selling across the board, but by painful single-day plunges in a few of the nation’s most widely held consumer and telecom names.

While the index fell, the currency market told a different story. The Mexican peso actually strengthened, pushing the USD/MXN exchange rate — the number of pesos needed to buy one US dollar — down 0.19% to settle at 17.23 pesos, helped by a softer US dollar that retreated against most major currencies.

The sharpest pain was felt by shareholders of Walmart de México (Walmex), the country’s dominant supermarket and discount-store chain, which slumped 3.2%, while billionaire Carlos Slim’s América Móvil, the telecoms colossus, fared even worse with a 3.5% drop.

These deep losses were partially offset by a fierce rally in precious-metals miners, led by a 5.4% surge in Peñoles and a 2.2% gain in Grupo México. The buying was fuelled by a sharp upward move in gold, which jumped 5.03% to $4,277.69 an ounce, and silver, which shot 4.65% higher, as the US Dollar Index slipped 0.18%.

Assessment — Selective selling, not a broad rout HIGH The session’s damage was highly concentrated in specific large-cap consumer and telecom stocks, which fell significantly harder than the broader index, while the peso actually strengthened and global precious metals rallied. This pattern points to a thematic or flow-driven rotation out of select high-weight defensive names rather than a systemic negative shock to the Mexican market. The key variable to monitor tomorrow will be whether Walmex and América Móvil find buyers at these lower levels or whether the selling pressure indicates the start of a broader repositioning.

World.title: Man helps police find his stash, then gets arrested
World.content:
Man helps police find his stash, then gets arrested

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A San Pedro Town man who candidly directed police to his own stash of suspected cannabis has been formally charged with possession with intent to supply, after the find weighed in at 232.9 grams, nearly a quarter kilogram.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Tuesday, August 4, 2026, at about 9:30 a.m., a police inspector and a detective went to conduct an apartment search in the Boca Del Rio Area of San Pedro Town. At the third floor apartment of a three-storey building, officers identified themselves to the occupant and informed him that a search would be conducted for firearms, drugs, and ammunition.

The occupant was identified through his driver’s licence as Devan Tristan Paulino, a 25-year-old self-employed resident of the Boca Del Rio Area.

Before the search began, the detective asked Paulino whether he had anything illegal to declare, and his answer was direct: he stated he had some weed in a transparent plastic bag underneath a table beside his bed. Checks under the table produced exactly that, a transparent plastic bag containing wrapped green leafy substance suspected to be cannabis.

Paulino was informed of the offence of possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply to another, cautioned, remaining silent, and informed of his constitutional rights. A further search of the apartment found nothing else incriminating, and he was escorted to the San Pedro Police Station with the suspected drugs in his view at all times.

At the station, the process ran by the book. His rights were explained and acknowledged in writing, the scale’s working procedure was explained before the weighing, which registered 232.9 grams in his presence, and the suspected cannabis was sealed in a labelled envelope with evidence tape, signed by Paulino as witness to the sealing and by the inspector.

That same day, police formally arrested and charged Paulino with possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply to another. Cautioned again, he chose to remain silent.

World.title: Farmer wakes to police warning and ends the night behind bars
World.content:
Farmer wakes to police warning and ends the night behind bars

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 62-year-old San Pedro Columbia Village farmer who was found lying on the stairs near a village bar, and who twice refused to leave the area, has been formally charged with loitering in a public place and is due before the Punta Gorda Magistrate Court on Friday.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Monday, August 3, 2026, at about 10:00 p.m., an officer conducting motorcycle patrol within San Pedro Columbia Village made checks at a village bar and observed a man lying face up on stairs about ten feet from the establishment.

The officer woke the man and asked him to leave the area, noting a strong aroma of alcohol as he spoke, and warned him for loitering. After making further checks at the bar, the officer returned about ten minutes later to find the same man in the same location.

Asked to leave a second time, the man refused, declaring that he was not going anywhere, that he was doing nothing, and that he was not afraid of any police. He was informed he was under arrest for the offence of loitering, cautioned, informed of his rights, and escorted with the assistance of other officers to the Punta Gorda Police Station. Due to his level of intoxication, his name could not be obtained that night, nor could he be issued an acknowledgement form.

The formalities waited for sobriety. On Tuesday, August 4, the officer found the man in a sober state of mind at the station’s detention center, where he was identified through his voter identification card as George Domingo Maquin, a 62-year-old farmer of San Pedro Columbia Village. His rights in custody were then read, explained, and issued in an acknowledgement form, which he signed.

That same date, police formally arrested and charged Maquin with loitering in a public place. The charge was read to him, he confirmed he understood, and upon being cautioned once more, he chose to remain silent.

Maquin was granted police bail and is to appear at the Punta Gorda Magistrate Court on Friday, August 7, 2026.

World.title: Son tries to punch father after he refuses to give him money
World.content:
Son tries to punch father after he refuses to give him money

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): An Orange Walk Town father washing dishes at his own sink ended the night defending himself from his son’s raised fists, and the young man has now been formally charged with common assault.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 57-year-old pharmacist of Orange Walk Town reported that at about 9:50 p.m., while he was washing dishes at his residence, his son arrived home appearing to be under the influence of alcohol or drugs and demanded money from him.

The father refused, and his reason traced back to that same morning. At about 6:00 a.m., he had discovered that BZ$300 was missing from his wallet, and he confronted his son about it, believing, he told police, that only his son could have taken it, since the only other person living in the house is the young man’s mother, who is chronically ill. The son denied taking the money.

The denial, according to the report, turned to aggression. The son raised his fist twice to hit his father, but the older man grabbed his son’s hand to prevent the blows from landing, and asked a neighbour to call the police for assistance.

Police recorded a statement from the father, and the son was detained. He was identified as Rojer Ismael Duran, a 26-year-old unemployed man of Orange Walk Town.

The custody process moved at the pace his condition allowed. On August 4, he was read and issued his suspect’s rights in custody acknowledgement form, which he signed and received a copy of, the step having awaited a state in which he could properly receive it, as he had appeared highly intoxicated and was behaving aggressively. On August 5, police obtained a warrant in the first instance and formally arrested and charged Duran with the crime of common assault. Cautioned once more, he chose to remain silent.

Behind the charge sheet sits a household’s quiet sorrow: a father forced to hold off his own son’s fists, and a family whose troubles have now crossed from the kitchen to the courtroom. For families struggling with a loved one’s substance use, support through health services and community organizations can reach the problem before the police must.

World.title: Woman survives choking and knife attack at her Punta Gorda home
World.content:
Woman survives choking and knife attack at her Punta Gorda home

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Punta Gorda Town woman survived a terrifying attack at her own home, reporting that her former common-law partner choked her with one hand while trying to cut or stab her throat with a sheetrock knife in the other, leaving her with stab wounds to the arm, hands, and armpit sustained as she fought to shield her neck.

According to the Belize Police Department, the 41-year-old labourer of the Indianville Extension area visited the Punta Gorda Police Station on Friday, July 31, 2026, to report the attack, which she said occurred on Tuesday, July 28, at approximately 6:30 p.m.

She told police she was at her residence when she first saw the man approaching her yard accompanied by her 5-year-old son. She instructed him to return the child to where he found him, which he did. About ten minutes later, he returned while she sat underneath her house.

She instructed him to keep his distance and sit on a nearby chair, according to her report. He refused, made threatening remarks that included a claim of violence against another person, and accused her of breaking up his home, saying he would not leave the matter so. She responded that she owed him nothing, had not broken up his home, and wanted no further contact with him.

The man then advanced on her. When she attempted to use her cell phone to call a relative for assistance, he demanded the phone, and upon her refusal, produced an orange-handled sheetrock knife about five inches long from his pocket. According to her report, he came at her with a stabbing motion and uttered the threat, “I wa kill you, and I wa kill miself, I nuh gwen da jail,” before grabbing and choking her with his left hand while raising the knife in his right, attempting to cut or stab her throat and declaring that she was dead.

She fought for her life, punching, kicking, and using her left arm to shield her neck from fatal injury. In the struggle she sustained a stab wound to the left armpit, the right palm, the left forearm, and the left hand, as well as a cut to the left ring finger. The man then released his grip and stomped on the left side of her face. Bleeding and in pain, she screamed for help, causing him to step back briefly, and when he attempted to approach again, she picked up a glass pint bottle to defend herself, at which point he fled the scene. She ran to her room and called a relative for assistance.

She told police conditions were clear, that she clearly identified the man, that she fears for her life, and that she requests formal court action.

The police report does not indicate that the man has been detained at this time, and as he has not been charged, no names are being published. The matter is under investigation.

World.title: Man returns home to find pickup windows smashed with stone
World.content:
Man returns home to find pickup windows smashed with stone

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Silver Creek Village man’s pickup truck had two of its windows completely shattered as it sat parked in his own yard, and an 18-year-old relative by marriage has been formally charged, in a case where the village Alcalde carried out the detention in a display of Belize’s traditional and formal justice systems working side by side.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 42-year-old retired soldier of the Toledo District village reported that on Monday, August 3, 2026, at about 10:30 a.m., he received a phone call from a relative informing him that a young man known to the family had broken the back glass and front passenger side window of his white 2014 Ford Ranger pickup.

On arriving home, the man found the truck still parked in his yard facing his house, exactly where he had left it undamaged, but with the back glass and front passenger door window completely shattered. Checking inside, he found a large stone on the front passenger seat, which he believes was used to shatter the windows. He produced an estimate placing the total cost of the damage and repair at $825.

Police recorded statements from the complainant and the witness, and the scene was processed by a scenes of crime technician.

The detention took a distinctly Toledo path. Police contacted the Alcalde of Silver Creek Village about the report, and it was the traditional village authority who detained the young man, who was subsequently identified through documentation provided by his family as Nigel Butz, an 18-year-old unemployed resident of the village.

On Wednesday, August 4, police visited the Punta Gorda Police Station cell block, informed Butz of the report against him and the crime of damage to property, and cautioned him. His rights in custody were read, explained, and issued in an acknowledgement form, which he signed. Police then obtained a warrant in the first instance and formally arrested and charged Butz with damage to property. Asked if he understood the charge, he answered yes, and upon being cautioned once more, he remained silent.

World.title: Sunshine returns as the wave clears and heat climbs to 95
World.content:
Sunshine returns as the wave clears and heat climbs to 95

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The midweek tropical wave has moved on, and Belize returns to its August baseline: warm and relatively dry conditions, sunshine overhead, and the inland heat climbing back to 95 degrees.

According to the National Meteorological Service, skies will be sunny with a few cloudy spells today and partly cloudy tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, with only a low chance of a few more over southern Toledo tonight, the last echo of the wave that crossed the country on Wednesday.

Temperatures along the coast will reach a high of 88 degrees Fahrenheit (31 Celsius) and a low of 82 (28 Celsius). Inland areas will return to the top of the charts, climbing to 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 Celsius) before dropping to 74 (23 Celsius). In the hills, expect a high of 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius) and a low of 68 (20 Celsius). With the mercury back at 95, hydration and shade breaks stay on the daily checklist.

At sea, some bounce remains behind the wave, with easterly winds of 10 to 20 knots, choppy conditions, and waves of 3 to 5 feet, so smaller vessels should keep exercising the usual care even with no caution currently in effect.

On the tropical front, the calm holds. Tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the region over the next 48 hours.

Looking ahead to Friday and Friday night, similar weather conditions are expected, carrying the sunshine toward the weekend.

The forecast was issued by forecaster Derrick Rudon.

World.title: Sanitation worker killed after falling into path of school bus on Lord’s Bank Road
World.content:
Sanitation worker killed after falling into path of school bus on Lord’s Bank Road

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained a school bus driver following a fatal traffic accident that claimed the life of a sanitation worker on Lord’s Bank Road in the Belize District.

The accident occurred at approximately 1:15 p.m. on Wednesday, August 5, 2026. Police say Andrew Smith was standing near the left rear of a garbage truck that had been parked along the roadside when he allegedly fell into the traffic lane.

Smith was subsequently struck by an approaching school bus and died from his injuries. Public reports have identified the victim as 39-year-old Andrew Alexander Smith. (Facebook)

The bus driver was detained, and urine samples were obtained as part of the standard investigative process. Police have not indicated whether impairment is suspected.

Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the fatal accident are continuing.

The cause remains framed as preliminary, since police are still investigating how Smith fell into the roadway.

World.title: F**k Around & Find Out: Delivery truck man shoots two robbers who held him up
World.content:
F**k Around & Find Out: Delivery truck man shoots two robbers who held him up

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two men are receiving medical treatment under police guard after they were shot during an armed robbery on Mahogany Street in Belize City on Wednesday afternoon.

According to police, the incident occurred at approximately 1:00 p.m. while a salesperson was seated inside a parked delivery truck. Two armed men reportedly approached the vehicle and demanded the sales proceeds in the salesperson’s possession.

The salesperson complied with the demand initially then subsequently fired upon the alleged robbers, shooting and injuring both men. Earlier reports confirmed that police had responded to a robbery and shooting involving a delivery truck in the area.

The injured men were transported for treatment and remain under police guard. Their identities, medical conditions and the amount of money stolen have not yet been disclosed.

Police investigations into the incident are continuing.

World.title: Wayne Wonder, Busy Signal to be named Reggae Icons at Grand Gala
World.content:
Among the features at this year’s Grand Gala will be a 1,000-drone show. (Photo: Rochelle Clayton)

Both Wayne Wonder and Busy Signal are the latest dancehall artistes to be recognised at the annual Independence Day Grand Gala.

This year’s event, in celebration of the nation’s 64th anniversary, will be hosted under the theme ‘United in Celebrating Resilience’.

Dancehall music has never been short of colourful characters, especially in the 1980 and 1990s when Wayne Wonder was making his name. Still, the singer says being outrageous has never been his style.

In an interview with the Jamaica Observer, Wayne Wonder, born Von wayne Charles, said: “This is special because being recognised by your country, the Government, is a blessing. It’s an honour to receive this.”

From East Kingston, he got his start on sound systems in areas like his hometown of McIntyre Villa (popularly known as Dunkirk). Wayne Wonder’s career flourished during the 1990s at Penthouse Records and Mad House Records, where he worked with producers Donovan Germain and Dave Kelly, respectively.

That era was noted for risque and violent songs by acts like Shabba Ranks and Ninja Man. There were also infamous artiste clashes at the annual Sting concert and the Bounty Killer/Beenie Man feud.

Wayne Wonder — whose hit songs include Saddest Day of My Life, Joy Ride, and No Letting Go — says avoiding confrontation has never been a problem.

“Over di years, dat’s jus’ my personality, jus’ conduct myself with principle an’ respect. A jus’ me dat bro, mi jus’ want to be a good yute an’ guh through.”

Artiste Busy Signal hails from St Ann and has been a leading figure in contemporary dancehall since 2003. His first hit single, Step Out was followed buy successful releases such as Nah Go A Jail Again, Smoke Some High Grade, Tic Toc, and Unknown Number.

In 2012, Busy Signal released his first authentic reggae album, Reggae Music Again. He is known for his energetic dancehall style and versatility, blending reggae and dancehall influences.

Busy Signal remains an influential figure in entertainment, particularly his contributions to the global music scene.

Veterans Beres Hammond, Sizzla, and Sanchez have been named Reggae Icons, as well as ska legend Derrick Morgan and reggae band Third World.

Jamaica’s 65th anniversary celebrations next year will mark the final staging of the country’s flagship national celebrations at the National Stadium in Kingston before the facility undergoes major redevelopment.

Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange made the announcement during a post-Cabinet press briefing held at Jamaica House last week.

“Next year, we have a milestone year, Jamaica 65, and it will be the last year that our celebrations will be held at the National Stadium. After that, we will prepare for our expansion and redevelopment. But I’m just putting everyone on alert, Jamaica 65 will be a special year,” she said.

Turning to this year’s celebrations, Minister Grange said members of the public who are unable to secure tickets for the Grand Gala at the National Stadium, will still be able to enjoy the event through a special watch party at Independence Village.

She explained that the arrangement was made in response to an overwhelming demand for tickets.

“I am making a special appeal that if… we’re unable to provide you with tickets for the stadium, that you will accept the tickets we have available for Independence Village where you can be a part of the watch party,” she said.

The Gala will conclude with its customary fireworks display, alongside an expanded drone show featuring 1,000 drones, as well as a motorcycle display by the Jamaica Constabulary Force.

— Howard Campbell

World.title: ‘No court decision can erase the pain of losing a loved one’
World.content:
The entrance to The University Hospital of the West Indies in St Andrew.

THE University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), in acknowledging that last Friday’s judgement by the Supreme Court, which ordered it to pay millions following a medical negligence suit, “may cause concern among patients, families and the wider public”, has reaffirmed its commitment “to transparency, transformation, accountability and continuous improvement, ensuring that every opportunity to strengthen [its] systems contributes to safer, higher quality care”.

In a statement issued to the media following the publication of the judgement in the Jamaica Observer Wednesday, the UHWI said “our thoughts remain with the family, whose loss is deeply tragic”.

“We recognise that no court decision can erase the pain of losing a loved one, and we extend our sincere condolences,” the hospital said.

In the meantime, the entity said it has “in recent years taken significant steps to strengthen its clinical governance, patient safety and quality assurance systems, while investing in modern technology, digital transformation, staff development and enhanced multidisciplinary care and improved governance”.

“These improvements reflect the hospital’s ongoing commitment to continuously strengthening the quality, safety and experience of care for every patient,” the UHWI said in the statement.

At the same time, the UHWI’s legal officer Kimani Brydson said, “As is standard practice following a judgement of this nature, [the entity’s] attorneys are reviewing the court’s comprehensive written judgement”.

“As part of UHWI’s ongoing transformation and commitment to responsive, patient-centred care, we recently launched dedicated customer care channels, providing patients and their families with a direct way to ask questions, share feedback, raise concerns or make complaints. The customer care team can be reached via

WhatsApp at 658-220-2907 or by e-mail at wecare@uhwi.gov.jm,” Brydson said.

“Every day, UHWI’s physicians, nurses, allied health professionals and support teams care for thousands of Jamaicans, performing complex surgical and medical procedures, treating critically ill patients and helping many recover. That responsibility is one we carry with humility and a steadfast commitment to continuously transforming and strengthening the quality and safety of the care we provide,” the UHWI said further.

Supreme Court Justice Anne-Marie Nembhard, in handing down the judgement, said the facility “fell below the standard of care” expected of it and also “breached the duty of care” provided to a 16-year-old girl, who died six days after being admitted to the hospital in March 2018.

The teen’s parents had sued the hospital’s board of management for failing to “use all proper professional skill, care, competence, and diligence during their investigation, diagnosis, management, and treatment” of their only child.

The court on Friday awarded approximately $1.7 million “for pain and suffering” endured by the child prior to her death. For loss of life/loss of expectation of life, the court awarded just over $344,000 with interest at three per cent per annum from April 15, 2021 to July 31 this year. In assessing how much the child, who was described as “a perennial high achiever”, would have lost in terms of earnings from before the trial to the last hearing date, the court awarded $6 million. In satisfying the parents’ claims for special damages, the court awarded just over $975,000 plus interest of three per cent per annum, from the date she died to the date the judgement was handed down. It also awarded US$8,000 in respect of the report prepared by the expert witness relied on in the case.

According to the civil negligence and estate lawsuit filed by the parents, on admission to UHWI, the parents informed the medical team that they suspected that their daughter was suffering from another bout of meningitis, an illness she had been previously diagnosed with. They were told that their daughter was suffering from hemiplegic migraine. After some 18 seizures and two heart attacks, the teen, who had also been placed on life support, was pronounced dead on April 5, 2018.

According to court documents, two medical professionals who gave evidence on behalf of the hospital maintained that the UHWI and its medical teams acted in accordance with standard practices and that there were no actions of negligence in the diagnosis, treatment and/or management of the teen.

However, the court, in choosing to rely on the evidence of an expert witness called by the parents, said there were “aspects of negligence on the part of the UHWI, which were of great concern”.

World.title: DREAM OVER
World.content:
Reggae Boyz Under-20 and Mount Pleasant Academy midfielder Jabarie Howell (foreground) is a key figure in Jamaica’s team to the Concacaf Under-20 Championship in Mexico, a qualifier for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup. The top four teams from the championship will qualify for the World Cup. (Photo: Concacaf)

JAMAICA’S campaign at the Concacaf Under-20 Championship ended in defeat on Wednesday night as a 1-3 extra-time loss to Canada at Estadio Cuauhtémoc ended their chances of qualifying for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup and the Los Angeles Olympic Games.

Rodolph Austin’s team fought back to force extra time after an unbeaten group stage, but two goals in that period sent Jesse Marsch’s Canada through to the semi-finals.

Canada controlled the early stages with a high press that made it difficult for Jamaica to keep the ball in midfield. Richard Chukwu broke through in the second minute to set up Lucas Lima, who shot wide, before Owen Graham-Roache missed a similar chance five minutes later.

Jamaica struggled to build attacks under Canadian pressure. Their best chance of the first half came in the 26th minute when Raequan Campbell-Dennis crossed to Jahmarie Nolan at the back post, but the forward’s header missed the target. Canada held 62 per cent of possession in the first half and kept Jamaica without a shot on target.

The second half was more open. Jahmani Bell nearly caught Canada goalkeeper Nathaniel Abraham off his line in the 54th minute with a shot from 60 yards that went just wide. However, Canada took the lead three minutes later. Liam Mackenzie ran through the Jamaican midfield, beat several defenders, and shot past Joshua Grant.

Canada continued to create chances, but Grant made key saves to keep Jamaica in the match, while Marius Aiyenero had a goal ruled out for offside by VAR in the 73rd minute.

Jamaica found an equaliser late in regulation time.

In the 86th minute, substitute Giovanni Taylor was fouled in the box by Dylan Jonelson. Captain Nolan scored the 87th-minute penalty, marking his fourth goal of the tournament and the fourth-straight game Jamaica scored in the final five minutes of regular time.

However, Canada retook the lead early in extra time. In the 93rd minute, Campbell-Dennis brought down Aiyenero in the box, and Mackenzie scored the penalty for his second goal of the match.

“I think it’s just a mindset thing,” Nolan said after the match regarding the extra-time collapse. “One slip-up in the back and we gave away a penalty. Other than that, I think we fought to the end. We just have to regroup and come again.”

Jamaica pushed for another equaliser, but Orel Miller missed the target from a lobbed pass in the 105th minute. By the end of the match, Canada held a 10-2 advantage in shots on target.

Canada secured the win in the 116th minute. Grant cleared a cross from Marsel Bibishkov into the path of Max Vogele, who volleyed the ball into the net from the edge of the box.

“It’s just unfortunate that we tried our best but lost, so we just have to come again in the next qualifiers,” Nolan said. When asked about Jamaica’s future his focus was on, “Preparation, trying to finish off the games better, and just try again to qualify for the World Cup.”

The result ends Jamaica’s tournament despite an encouraging group phase during which they went unbeaten, scored in three straight games for the first time since 2018, and picked up points against two Central American teams for the first time in competition history. Canada advances to the semi-finals and earns qualification for both the Under-20 World Cup and the Los Angeles Olympics.

World.title: Shan’s Crispy Fried Chicken Tacos
World.content:
(Photo: Alan Smith)

Next take my crispy fried chicken and turn it into a fun, flavour-packed taco! These tacos combine crunchy fried chicken with fresh homemade salsa, creamy guacamole, crisp purple cabbage, Mexican cheese, sour cream, and a simple creamy sauce, all tucked into crunchy taco hard shells.



Ingredients

For the Tacos

• Crispy fried chicken, prepared using my fried chicken recipe

• Hard taco shells

• Purple cabbage, thinly shredded

• Mexican cheese, shredded

• Sour cream

• Fresh lime wedges, for serving

Simple Salsa

• 2 ripe tomatoes, finely diced

• ¼ small red onion, finely diced

• 1 small Scotch bonnet pepper, finely chopped, or to taste

• Fresh cilantro, finely chopped

• Juice of ½ lime

• Salt, to taste

Simple Guacamole

• 2 ripe avocados

• Juice of ½ lime

• 1 little red onion, finely diced

• 1 little Scotch bonnet pepper, finely chopped, optional

• Salt, to taste

Creamy Sauce

• Mayonnaise

• Fresh lime juice

• Hot sauce, to taste

Method

1) Prepare the salsa: In a bowl, combine the tomatoes, red onion, Scotch bonnet pepper and cilantro. Add the lime juice, season with salt and mix well. Set aside.

2) Prepare the guacamole: Scoop the avocado into a bowl and mash until creamy but still slightly chunky. Add the lime juice, red onion and Scotch bonnet pepper, then season with salt to taste.

3) Make the creamy sauce: Mix the mayonnaise with a squeeze of fresh lime juice and hot sauce to taste. Stir until smooth and creamy.

4) Prepare the chicken: Prepare the crispy fried chicken according to my fried chicken recipe. Once cooked, cut or break the chicken into bite-sized pieces.

5) Assemble the tacos: Prepare the hard taco shells according to the package instructions. Fill each shell with crispy fried chicken, then add shredded purple cabbage and Mexican cheese.

6) Add a spoonful of the home-made salsa and guacamole, followed by a dollop of sour cream. Drizzle with the creamy sauce and finish with a squeeze of fresh lime juice.

Serve immediately while the chicken and taco shells are crisp.

Kitchen Note: The crispy chicken, crunchy purple cabbage, creamy guacamole, fresh salsa, Mexican cheese, cool sour cream, and tangy sauce come together for the perfect balance of textures and flavours.

World.title: Jamaica plants 100 Kenyan Wambugu apple trees in import substitution drive – Green
World.content:
Designed for resilience, the Wambugu apple tree flourishes in both hot and cold conditions, making it ideally suited for tropical environments.

One hundred Wambugu apple trees were recently imported to Jamaica from Kenya and planted across agro parks at Amity Hall, Ebony Park and Parnassu, as the Caribbean island steps up its programme to support import substitution of apples and to diversify the earning potential of farmers.

Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining, Floyd Green made the announcement at the 72nd staging of the annual Denbigh Agricultural Industrial and Food Show in Clarendon last weekend.

“These demonstration plots will allow us to evaluate performance while encouraging wider adoption among farmers,” Green said of the development.

“A single acre can accommodate as many as 500 trees,” he continued, adding that “Within approximately five years, each tree can produce up to 500 apples and, with proper care and management, yields can reach between 30 and 40 tonnes per acre annually.”

The Wambugu apple is a crisp, juicy red variety similar to American apples. It was developed by Kenyan farmer Peter Wambugu to grow in warmer, tropical climates, which makes it suitable for Jamaica.

In the project spearheaded by the Agro-Investment Corporation (AIC), Jamaica aims for the crop to become a viable addition to local fruit production, contributing to agricultural diversification and farmer profitability.

Peter Wambugu’s daughter, Catherine conducted training sessions in Jamaica last year and distributed seedlings to agro park farmers as part of the programme.

Emphasising the potential of the initiative, Green noted that last year alone, Jamaica imported more than 1.4 million kilogrammes of apples at a cost of more than J$260 million.

“Just imagine what could happen if even a portion of that market could be supplied by Jamaican farmers,” he said.

“The Wambugu apple gives us an opportunity to do precisely that,” he added, noting that the fruit has demonstrated tremendous potential as a commercial crop.

The agriculture minister stressed that the introduction of a new crop “requires more than simply putting trees into the ground”.

“It requires research, training, monitoring and strong partnerships. That is why the Agro-Invest Corporation will continue to work closely with farmers as we assess the long-term potential of this crop under local conditions,” he said.

Green urged farmers who are interested in participating to contact the Agro-Invest Corporation to learn more about the programme and the opportunities that it presents.

World.title: UHWI at fault
World.content:
A view of the University Hospital of the West Indies

The University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) has been ordered to pay millions in damages after the Supreme Court found that the facility “fell below the standard of care” expected of it and also “breached the duty of care” provided to a 16-year-old girl, who died six days after being admitted to the hospital in March 2018.

The girl’s parents later sued the hospital’s board of management for failing to “use all proper professional skill, care, competence, and diligence during their investigation, diagnosis, management, and treatment of their only child”.

The court on Friday awarded $1,687,380.19 “for pain and suffering” endured by the child prior to her death. For loss of life/loss of expectation of life, the court awarded $344,127.70 with interest at three per cent per annum from April 15, 2021 to July 31 this year. In assessing how much the child, who was described as “a perennial high achiever” and a “polyglot” (a person who knows, speaks, or writes several different languages) would have lost in terms of earnings from before the trial to the last hearing date the court awarded $6 million. In satisfying the parent’s claims for special damages, the court awarded $975,573.41 plus interest of three per cent per annum, from the date she died to the date the judgement was handed down. It also awarded US$8,000 in respect of the report prepared by the expert witness relied on in the case.

The teenager who was described as “an accomplished and promising fifth-form student at Campion College, St Andrew” was preparing to sit the May/June sitting of the Caribbean Secondary Examination Council (CSEC) examinations at the time of her passing. She was said to have “entrepreneurial dreams and aspirations to become a scientist or a medical researcher”.

According to the civil negligence and estate lawsuit filed by her parents in the civil division of the Supreme Court in 2021, the young girl, on or around March 30, 2018 was admitted by the UHWI for treatment at its medical facility. Her mother said the ordeal began on March 27, 2018 when her daughter complained of what had become a persistent headache. She said after being examined by the family doctor, her daughter — who had also been warm to the touch — was prescribed medication. When that headache persisted three days later, along with weakness the parents — who said they began to “suspect that their daughter was suffering from another bout of meningitis, an illness with which she had been diagnosed at the age of eight years” — decided to take her to the UHWI.

Once there, they said they informed medical staff of her symptoms and history of meningitis as well as their suspicions. The parents said on March 31 after blood samples, a CT scan and an unsuccessful lumbar puncture procedure (which was to be done over), they were informed that their daughter was suffering from hemiplegic migraine. After some 18 seizures and two heart attacks, the teen who had also been placed on life support was pronounced dead on April 5, 2018.

Unmoored and set adrift by the loss of their child, the parents asserted that they suffered emotional and psychiatric distress. The father alleged that he became unable to focus, depressed and angry, making it difficult for him to hold onto a job. His wife maintained that, as a sales manager, the mental distress caused by, and the toll of, her daughter’s death affected her so drastically that she could not do her job as well as she did before.

According to court documents two medical professionals who gave evidence on behalf of the hospital maintained that the UHWI and its medical teams acted in accordance with standard practices and that there were no actions of negligence in the diagnosis, treatment and/or management of the teen.

However the court, in choosing to rely on the evidence of an expert witness called by the parents, said there were “aspects of negligence on the part of the UHWI, which are of great concern”.

“The documentary evidence discloses that, during the course of [her] admission to the UHWI, it was noted on three separate occasions that a diagnosis of meningitis was to be ruled out… in fact, it is readily apparent from the medical docket that no further attempt was made to rule out or to exclude the differential diagnosis of meningitis. This court is of the view that there is an absolute need for a physician to ensure that sufficient tests and detailed investigations are conducted before ruling out one disease over another. Negligence must be ascribed to the UHWI, by its servants and/or agents, for its failure to properly employ all usual diagnostic aids in ruling out the possibility of meningitis, including a lumbar puncture test,” the court said.

“The court finds that the UHWI was negligent in the failure on the part of its servants and/or agents to recognise that [name withheld] was brain-dead on 1 April 2018 at 11:00 pm. The evidence of the rapid deterioration in [the child’s] condition in the five days following her admission to the UHWI is concerning,” said the ruling handed down by Supreme Court Justice Anne-Marie Nembhard.

“The court finds that there was no clear plan of treatment, on the part of the servants and/or agents of the UHWI, to treat [her] in the face of her rapid deterioration, whilst being admitted as a patient to the UHWI. Nor does there seem to have been a corresponding, commensurate escalation in the UHWI’s plan of treatment or course of treatment in the face of her rapid deterioration,” the justice added.

In additional findings, the court said based on the evidence of the expert witness, an accurate diagnosis could have been arrived at, had a lumbar puncture been performed.

World.title: Power in unity
World.content:
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama (left) shakes hands with Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness after addressing a joint sitting of the Houses of Parliament at Gordon House on Tuesday. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama is urging Africa and the Caribbean to speak with one voice on the global stage, saying stronger cooperation is essential to reform the United Nations (UN) and international financial institutions to secure fairer treatment for developing countries.

Addressing a joint sitting of Jamaica’s Parliament, Tuesday during his State visit, Mahama argued that the historic relationship between Africa and the Caribbean must now evolve into a strategic partnership capable of influencing international decision-making, reducing global inequality and creating greater economic opportunities for developing nations.

Rather than allowing the relationship to remain rooted solely in a shared history of slavery and colonialism, the Ghanaian leader said the two regions should work together to influence policies on climate change, global finance, trade, food security and public health, areas in which he believes developing countries have long struggled to make their voices heard.

“We must strengthen cooperation between the African Union and Caricom. We must deepen our collaboration within the United Nations and other multilateral institutions, and we must coordinate our positions on issues that will define the future of humanity. Whether the challenge is climate change, reform of the international financial architecture, food security, public health, or digital transformation, our voices will carry greater weight if we speak together,” he declared.

Caricom and the African Union have steadily expanded cooperation in recent years, driven by shared positions on reparatory justice, climate finance, sustainable development and reform of the international financial system.

In 2021, the two regional organisations signed a memorandum of understanding aimed at strengthening political and economic cooperation, while regular Africa-Caricom summits have sought to deepen collaboration on trade, investment, education and technology.

Mahama said that cooperation must now extend beyond diplomacy and deliver meaningful change for citizens across both regions.

“The partnership between Africa and the Caribbean should therefore no longer be defined only by our shared past, but also by our shared future. It should be recognised for the future we are determined to build together. It is this conviction that inspired me to call the Accra Reset Conference recently,” he said.

He used his address to criticise what he described as persistent inequalities within the international system, arguing that many of the institutions governing global finance and politics were created in a different era and no longer adequately reflect the realities of today’s developing world.

The Accra Reset, launched by Ghana earlier this year, calls for reforms to international governance and development financing, with greater emphasis on productive investment, industrialisation and fairer representation for developing countries.

“The Accra Reset reflects our belief that institutions governing the world must evolve to reflect the realities and aspirations of the 21st century. Too many developing countries continue to confront structural barriers to financing, unequal trading arrangements, and inadequate representation in global decision-making bodies. These inequities cannot define our future,” Mahama argued.

He said Africa and the Caribbean should work together to change those conditions rather than continue operating within a system that limits their economic potential.

“The Accra Reset calls for a new development paradigm founded on mutual respect, productive investment, and genuine partnership. It seeks to accelerate industrialisation, promote value addition, encourage innovation, exercise national sovereignty over our resources, and equip our young people with the knowledge and skills to compete successfully in the global economy. But above all, it calls for a more balanced international order in which developing countries participate as equal partners in shaping global solutions,” he added.

Among the reforms he proposed was a renewed push to restructure the United Nations Security Council, which has remained largely unchanged since its creation after the Second World War. Africa, despite representing 54 sovereign states, does not hold a permanent seat on the council, a long-standing concern raised by African leaders.

Mahama also called for changes to international financial institutions, arguing that developing countries should have greater influence over decisions that affect access to financing and economic development.

Although much of Mahama’s address reflected on the historical ties between Africa and Jamaica, he repeatedly stressed that history alone would not improve the lives of future generations.

Instead, he said both regions should use their shared experiences to build stronger economic partnerships, coordinate their positions on major international issues and pursue reforms that give developing countries a more equal role in shaping global policies.

“When we work together, our partnership becomes more than just a historical connection. It becomes a powerful force for global progress, for shared prosperity, and for lasting justice,” he added.

World.title: Daydreams shows up white-hot before YUSH nostalgia
World.content:
Dexta Daps holds a vibe onstage at Daydreams on Saturday at the Montego Bay Convention Centre.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Dream Wknd transformed the Montego Bay Convention Centre into two completely different worlds on Saturday. From the elegance and romance of Daydreams to the nostalgic throwback energy of YUSH, patrons experienced a seamless journey through two distinct eras of music and celebration.

The afternoon belonged to Daydreams, where thousands dressed in all white filled the venue for one of the festival’s most-anticipated events. Against a backdrop of premium décor, unlimited drinks, and an atmosphere that balanced sophistication with celebration, patrons eagerly awaited dancehall’s leading man, Dexta Daps. And the singer delivered exactly what fans had come for.

Opening to deafening screams, Dexta Daps commanded the stage with a performance that blended passion, charisma, and crowd interaction. Couples embraced, friends sang ‘at the top of their lungs’, and phones lit up the venue as fans captured every moment.

His catalogue of hits, including WIFI, Owner, Call Me If, and Breaking News, had the ladies in the audience swooning and singing every word.

For nearly an hour the space became less of a concert venue and more of a shared celebration of music, romance, and dancehall culture, led by Dexta Daps.

For Sophia Khan, who flew in from Birmingham, Daydreams stood out as one of the highlights of Dream Wknd.

“This is my first-ever Dream Wknd, and Daydreams has definitely lived up to the hype. The vibe was amazing, the all-white theme looked so good, and Dexta Daps gave us everything we wanted. It’s one of those events you don’t want to leave,” she said.

As the sun went down, the atmosphere shifted from polished and elegant to playful and nostalgic as YUSH took over.

Presented by Casamigos, the throwback event invited patrons to relive their school days with a uniform dress code that saw party-goers arriving in creative takes on the classic classroom looks. This set the tone for an evening dedicated to celebrating the unforgettable sounds, style, and spirit of the late 1990s and early 2000s.

The nostalgia only intensified once the music started. Dancehall star Tifa took to the stage first, delivering a high-energy performance from the opening song. She set the tone for the night with a string of crowd-favourites before passing the baton to dancehall veteran Elephant Man, who raised the energy even further with his trademark infectious hits and signature dance moves. Together, the performances perfectly complemented the event’s retro concept, transporting the audience back to one of dancehall’s most celebrated eras.

The seamless transition highlighted the festival’s ability to deliver distinctly different experiences, each with its own unique personality while maintaining the premium standard patrons have come to expect.

Scott Dunn, group managing director of Dream Entertainment, expressed that, “Saturday really showcased what Dream Wknd is all about, offering completely different experiences within the same festival while maintaining the same level of quality. Daydreams delivered the premium, feel-good atmosphere we envisioned, and then YUSH allowed patrons to relive the music and culture that defined an era. Watching thousands of people fully embrace both concepts is incredibly rewarding and reinforces why Dream continues to evolve year after year.”

World.title: Leipzig drone incident fuels fears of Russian election meddling
World.content:
“We do of course see that Russia attempts every day, in one way or another — through hybrid means and various measures — to exert influence here in Germany in a manner that seeks to undermine our democracy and erode trust in politics and politicians,” said Martin Giese, a foreign ministry spokesperson.

Russian disinformation campaigns have portrayed German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his government as warmongers. They aim to undermine the already unpopular chancellor and boost Russia-friendly forces such as the AfD and the far-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) — both of which are strong in eastern Germany.

“The state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and in eastern Germany are, of course, a major target of Russian influence, because these are pivotal elections in the heart of Europe,” said Stefan Meister, a Russia expert at the German Council on Foreign Relations.

He said that it is too early to attribute the explosive-laden drone to Russia as investigations are still ongoing. But he added that Moscow is clearly waging a broad hybrid campaign targeting the region ahead of next month’s votes.

“This could be the first time right-wing populists come to power,” Meister said. “And with that, the chancellor might even fall — or at the very least, the coalition would be severely weakened — and a pro-Russian party would come to power in one of the federal states.”

“There is a major campaign underway on the Russian side to influence these elections in favor of the AfD and the BSW,” he added.

World.title: Hormuz deal with Oman in final stage, says Iran
World.content:
Ships sail near the Strait of Hormuz on July 13, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images

The countries are finalizing an agreed route for shipping in case the strait reopens.

Negotiations between Iran and Oman on delineating a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz have reached the final stage, the Iranian Foreign Ministry confirmed on Wednesday.

The shipping lane would primarily lie within Iranian territorial waters, with parts extending into Omani waters.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists that “the geographical coordinates of the proposed maritime route have been agreed upon by both sides,” adding that the bilateral process was “professional” and “forward-moving.”

World.title: German interior minister suggests state actor behind drone attack
World.content:
"Of course, we all want to know which foreign powers are involved. But it would be reckless to give credence to any kind of speculation at this point," he added.

Leipzig Airport serves as a strategic hub for NATO, including for military transports to Ukraine. The airport is also international courier service DHL’s largest European air hub and serves as a temporary home for some Ukrainian Antonov aircraft, protecting them from Russian attacks. The armed drone was found just meters away from such a plane, said officials Wednesday.

Armin Schuster, minister of the interior for Saxony — where Leipzig is located — told ZDF that the incident represented a new threat level.

"Without wanting to preempt the investigation, I would describe this as a suspected attack scenario because this is the first time we’ve had a drone that was also loaded with explosives," he said. "That’s new."

An airport worker found the drone Tuesday night. Officers disarmed the device by removing its detonator, which had failed to go off. In a separate incident at the same airport, another flying object struck a DHL cargo aircraft as it was being diverted away from the airport after the explosive-laden drone was found.

World.title: Former PM joins list of French presidential candidates reportedly targeted by Russian interference
World.content:
Gabriel Attal gestures as he visits his old family home on Île-aux-Moines, France on July 25, 2026. | Sebastien Salom-Gomis/AFP via Getty Images

Three presidential hopefuls have reported Kremlin disinformation efforts against them over the past two weeks.

PARIS — Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal is the latest in a string of French presidential candidates allegedly targeted by a Russian disinformation campaign.

Attal, the candidate of President Emmanuel Macron's Renaissance party, said on Thursday he had been "a victim" of an electoral "interference" attempt originating from Russia, and that he expected such "destabilization efforts" to increase ahead of France's April 2027 election.

Viginum, the country's agency for fighting online disinformation, confirmed it had detected the operation against Attal and attributed it "with a high level of confidence" to "pro-Russian" disinformation tactics.

World.title: Why are Commission staffers so miserable?
World.content:
Working at the European Commission is one of the most coveted civil service jobs in Brussels. Yet, officials employed there describe high pressure, bureaucracy and burnout.

Our colleague Seb Starcevic has interviewed dozen officials from different commissioners’ cabinets and directorates-general, varying in age, nationality and seniority. On the podcast, Zoya Sheftalovich and Sarah Wheaton parse through what these insiders had to say about their working conditions.

Next, last week’s Ceuta crisis — when a surge of migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish exclave — has revived a basic question: Why does Spain still hold territory in North Africa? With Madrid increasingly isolated from both U.S. and European allies, doubts are also growing over who would support Spain if Morocco moved against Ceuta or its other North African city, Melilla.

Plus: Novo Nordisk, the Danish pharma company of Ozempic fame, is launching a pill version of its weight-loss drug Wegovy in Europe … and transatlantic tensions are already brewing.

World.title: The hidden cost of global flight disruptions
World.content:
A new survey quantifies the financial and emotional toll of flight disruptions, pointing to a widening gap between passenger rights on paper and passenger experience in practice.

Nearly eight in 10 travelers experienced a flight disruption in the past year, and for most the damage went well beyond the inconvenience itself. A new survey from AirHelp, a company dedicated to supporting travelers throughout their journey, puts a number on what disruption actually costs passengers: an average of €514 out of pocket, plus a real toll on their time, plans and well-being.

These figures reflect an industry operating under sustained pressure, with disruption continuing to shape the everyday experience of millions of travelers.

Air travel has largely recovered from its pandemic-era lows, but disruption remains a persistent feature of modern flying, driven by everything from air traffic control constraints to weather, staffing and aging infrastructure. Globally, 79 percent of respondents had a flight canceled, delayed by more than two hours or otherwise disrupted in the past 12 months. Of those disruptions, 50 percent were delays over two hours, 15 percent were cancellations, and 14 percent involved delayed, lost or damaged luggage. These figures reflect an industry operating under sustained pressure, with disruption continuing to shape the everyday experience of millions of travelers.
