World.title: 1,000 complaints made to EU Commission’s anti-harassment team
World.content:
The Commission — which has a workforce of some 30,000 — hired a chief confidential counsellor, Lene Naesager, to deal with staff harassment issues, in May 2024. She has a team of 40 counsellors across the Commission and its executive agencies.

Since September 2024, the chief counsellor, who reports to Budget Commissioner Piotr Serafin, has received 960 reports from “colleagues feeling harassed, alleged harassers, witnesses, managers and HR correspondents,” according to a Commission spokesperson.

However, the chief counsellor “has no mandate to investigate and is not entitled legally to qualify the conduct as harassment as defined in the Staff Regulations,” the spokesperson explained.

To make a formal complaint, staff instead have to go to the Investigation and Disciplinary Office (IDOC) or to the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF). The Commission receives around 20 to 25 formal complaints per year, the spokesperson said.

The Commission said 14,000 staff have attended presentations on anti-harassment policy while 2,400 managers have attended mandatory training sessions in the last two years. This increased awareness about how to seek support in dealing with harassment has “generated a relatively high number” of reports to the chief confidential counsellor, the spokesperson said.

A Commission spokesperson said the institution was “committed to being a modern, respectful and attractive place to work,” pointing to a review launched by President Ursula von der Leyen into the Commission’s operations. An internal survey found 74 percent of staff rated the Commission an attractive employer, up six percentage points from 2023.

But a senior official said that same review will not include recommendations on anti-harassment policy, as the issue falls outside its “scope.”

World.title: 'Extreme right-wing' ideology drives surge in referrals to UK anti-terror scheme
World.content:
A record number of people have been referred to an anti-terrorism programme in England and Wales, the UK Home Office has announced.

 

Official data released on Thursday showed that from 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025, a total of 10,293 referrals were made to the government's Prevent programme, up 39% compared to the year prior and marking the highest number of referrals over a 12-month period since records started in April 2015.

The Prevent Scheme

Prevent is an early intervention scheme designed to stop people turning to terrorism.

According to the Home Office, a Prevent referral is made to police "when there are concerns that a person may be susceptible to radicalisation or could be at risk of becoming involved in or supporting terrorism."

Prevent referrals do not lead to a criminal record and are instead about "safeguarding" those at risk of radicalisation and helping protect the public, the ministry says.

The new data shows that the highest number of referrals for the year ending September 2025 were due to concerns over "extreme right-wing" views, making up around 20% of all referrals. That figure was up around 42% compared with the previous 12 months.

Referrals for "Islamist extremism," by contrast, accounted for 8% of total referrals, although the report noted that Islamist terrorism remained "the primary terrorist threat in the UK" and that referral trends were kept "under close review."

It comes as the UK's hard-right has been riding a wave of increasing popularity in the last two years, spearheaded by Reform UK's Nigel Farage and Restore Britain's Rupert Lowe, who have championed anti-immigration policies. There has also been growing support for far-right activists such as Tommy Robinson - real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon - who has attended protests and spoken at anti-immigration rallies across the country.

Surge in referrals

The latest figures also highlighted an increase in referrals relating to "fascination with extreme violence or mass casualty attacks" in the first half of 2025, with 286 such referrals recorded from April to June.

That number dropped to 183 between July and September, although the report noted that the fall could be due to "reduced referral activity from education settings during summer holidays."

Early 2025 was a particularly busy time for Prevent referrals, with a large increase recorded from January to March.

A 2025 report by British barrister Lord David Anderson - who previously served as the Independent Prevent Commissioner - suggested that that surge likely came on the back of publicity surrounding the Southport attack in late July 2024, during which Axel Rudakubana killed three young girls and injured multiple others in a knife attack. Rudakubana was referred to Prevent three times before he carried out the attack.

If someone is deemed as at risk of radicalisation or of becoming involved in terrorism, their case is passed on to Channel, a voluntary multi-agency safeguarding service that aims to provide them with support.

Channel offers help such as mentoring, education, theological guidance, and careers assistance to those who accept. Alternative support methods are found for referrals who do not want to take part. Police can send cases to a Police-Led Partnership if an escalation of risk is identified.

The rise in referrals is putting increasing strain on Channel. The Home Office said it was continuing to work to ensure the programme can run as smoothly as possible, providing advice on best practice and "ensuring case management processes and tools are as robust and efficient as possible."

World.title: Ceuta mayor tells MEPs migrant 'invasion' left city traumatised, demands immediate deportations
World.content:
Ceuta Mayor Juan Jesús Vivas has described the breach of the Spanish enclave's border with Morocco as an "invasion" and demanded the immediate return of migrants still there after last week's border incident.

 

Vivas made the remarks in his testimony before the European Parliament's Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs on Thursday. The hearing was convened after roughly 80,000 migrants entered Ceuta by sea in what has been described as one of the largest migration crises in the EU's history.

The Spanish government declined its invitation to attend the session; the European Commission was represented by Magnus Brunner, the commissioner responsible for migration.

"According to the Royal Spanish Academy's dictionary, the second definition of 'invasion' refers to the anomalous or irregular occupation of a specific place. This is precisely what happened on 30 and 31 July, when some 80,000 people – equivalent to the entire population of Ceuta – stormed into our city," Vivas told MEPs.

The mayor said the episode had called into question the integrity of Ceuta, Spain and the European Union as a whole. Although most of the migrants have since returned to Morocco, he said the crisis had left the city traumatised.

"We faced a humanitarian emergency of enormous proportions, compounded by disturbances to public order and a serious risk to public safety," he said.

Vivas added that between 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remain in local reception centres, which are overwhelmed.

"This in no way allows us to say that our city has returned to normal for its citizens," he said, adding that the exact number of migrants still in Ceuta had not been disclosed owing to a lack of resources.

He renewed his calls for stronger border controls and the immediate return of migrants who entered the city irregularly.

"We demand the immediate expulsion of the Moroccans who have entered our city irregularly and who remain here," Vivas said, while noting that unaccompanied minors could be returned to their country of origin only with their consent.

Responding to a question from an MEP, Vivas said he had no information on whether any jihadists previously expelled from Europe had entered Ceuta during the crisis.

"We don't know from local authorities whether there are any jihadists among those who entered," he added.

Vivas said Ceuta had warned Spanish authorities before last Thursday's surge about rising numbers of irregular arrivals from Morocco.

"We told the ministries about the situation we were experiencing, and we pointed out that there had been an alarming increase in arrival flows," he said.

He also said the city had been unable to establish contact with Moroccan authorities, who had refused to engage.

"What has become apparent," he said, "is that our border is porous and vulnerable."

World.title: From the Crucifixion to pop art: how humanity has painted solar eclipses
World.content:
On 12 August the Moon will once again pass in front of the Sun over much of Spain, and for a few minutes midday will turn into twilight. A total solar eclipse will be visible that day, and astronomical associations are already organising preparations for the event. By no means will this be the first time an eclipse has left humanity open-mouthed.

 

Nor will it be the first time someone has tried to capture it with a paintbrush. For centuries, painters, illuminators and engravers have tried to fix on canvas, fresco or copper plate something that in reality lasts only a few minutes.

When the sky darkened and the world trembled

Before astronomy existed as we understand it today, an eclipse was, quite simply, terrifying. The 'Nebra Sky Disc', a Bronze Age bronze artefact found near Halle in Germany, already shows the Sun, the Moon and the Pleiades together on a single object, although it does not depict an eclipse proper: it is rather the most distant precedent of that obsession with giving a visual form to what happens in the sky.

'Nebra Sky Disc' in the State Museum of History in Halle Shonagon

Herodotus himself left a written record of how a solar eclipse interrupted a battle between the Medes and the Lydians in Asia Minor, an episode both sides interpreted as a sign.

The Middle Ages found in the eclipse a perfect narrative device for one very specific episode: the death of Christ. The Italian painter Taddeo Gaddi depicted, in a triptych dating from around 1330 that is now held by the New-York Historical Society, a Moon approaching the Sun above the cross, and a century later an anonymous Valencian artist did the same in a panel (the painting is called 'Crucifixion') now hanging in the Thyssen-Bornemisza, although with an ochre-coloured sun that suggests its author had probably never seen a total eclipse and did not really know how to paint one.

The sun can be seen in an ochre tone. Anonymous. 'Crucifixion'. Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza

The phenomenon also appeared alongside other wonders: the Augsburg Book of Miracles, an illuminated manuscript from the mid-16th century, illustrates the total eclipse of 1483 accompanied by the locust plague that devastated Italy that same year.

The Baroque, between faith and emerging science

With the Baroque, the depiction of eclipses gained technical ambition without losing its symbolic charge. José de Ribera painted in his 'Christ Crucified' of 1643, today in the Museum of Fine Arts of Vitoria, an almost translucent lunar disc that allows the outline of the Sun behind it to be glimpsed, while Rubens went a step further in his triptych for Antwerp Cathedral: in 'The Elevation of the Cross' (1610-1611) he rendered the beginning of a solar eclipse with striking realism, although he had to draw the full contour of the Moon so that viewers could recognise both celestial bodies.

Not all eclipse paintings from the period sprang from religious faith. Antoine Caron titled his canvas from around 1570-1580, now in the Getty in Los Angeles, 'Dionysius the Areopagite converting the pagan philosophers', although it is better known as Astronomers observing a solar eclipse: a celestial globe, an armillary sphere and a figure doing geometric calculations reveal that what really interested the painter was the astronomical phenomenon.

'Dionysius the Areopagite converts the pagan philosophers' - Antoine Caron Getty Center

By the 18th century, Donato Creti had painted a series of oils on astronomical observations commissioned by Count Marsili, who presented them to Pope Clement XI in order to persuade him to fund an observatory in Bologna. And it worked, as the observatory was built shortly afterwards.

Romanticism and the taste for the sublime

The 19th century, with its fascination for the grand and the inexplicable, produced some of the most picturesque scenes in the genre. Ippolito Caffi portrayed the eclipse of 8 July 1842 over Venice ('Solar eclipse over Fondamenta Nove') from an aerial perspective, and Russian painter Ivan Aivazovsky, better known for his seascapes, turned into a kind of nocturne the total eclipse he observed in 1851 from Feodosia ('Solar eclipse in Feodosia').

'Solar eclipse over Fondamenta Nove' - Ippolito Caffi Wikimedia Commons - holapaco77

The phenomenon also lent itself to political satire: a French almanac from 1706 showed Louis XIV sitting on his throne before the Sun, in allusion to his nickname of 'Sun King', and included in one corner the eclipse of 12 May that year, which coincided with a French military defeat during the siege of Barcelona.

When the paintbrush served science

Towards the end of the 19th century, before photography could properly capture the solar corona, some artists became instruments of precision. The Frenchman Étienne Léopold Trouvelot, better known today for having accidentally introduced the gypsy moth into the United States, found his true vocation in astronomical drawing and travelled with his son to Creston, in the Territory of Wyoming, to observe the total eclipse of 29 July 1878 ('Total eclipse of the Sun').

That scene was eventually turned into a chromolithograph as part of a portfolio of 15 plates published in 1882. A few decades later, the American Howard Russell Butler took that documentary vocation even further.

Trouvelot - 'Total eclipse of the Sun' Wikimedia Commons

A former physics student turned portrait painter, developed a shorthand method of noting shapes and colours that allowed him to work with barely two minutes of totality. Using those notes and some supporting photographic plates, he painted the 1918 eclipse in Oregon during an expedition by the US Naval Observatory, and repeated the feat with the eclipses of 1923 in California, 1925 in Connecticut and 1932 in Maine.

The resulting triptych was exhibited for years at the Hayden Planetarium of the American Museum of Natural History in New York, and half-scale copies exist in Princeton, at the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia and at the Buffalo Museum of Science.

From expressionism to pop art

The eclipse went on to inspire, now in a purely artistic key, throughout the 20th century. Paul Klee devoted a watercolour to it ('Solar eclipse (Sonnenfinsternis)'), and Roy Lichtenstein, towards the end of his career, translated the speed with which totality arrives and passes by layering circles and curves in a manner very typical of pop art in his 1975 work 'Eclipse of the Sun'.

Since then, the phenomenon has never ceased to appear on the contemporary art market, whether as an almost scientific study or as a purely colouristic pretext for playing with the contrast between light and shadow.

On 12 August, when the Moon once again passes in front of the Sun over Spain, thousands of people will take out their phones to photograph the phenomenon. During much of history, the only way to preserve it was precisely that, a paintbrush, a handful of minutes and the memory of whoever dared to look up.

World.title: Great British ‘foodie staycation’ summer: 25.2m get a taste for holidays at home in 2026
World.content:
British travellers are deciding against a foreign holiday this summer, with millions choosing a staycation instead, new research has revealed.

 

According to data from consumer bank Chase, this year is all about the Great British “staycation summer”, as 22.5 million UK adults are set to holiday on home soil during the warmer months – a 40% increase from 2025.

General travel search interest shows a similar pattern, with nationwide searches for “UK holiday ideas” up 50% year-on-year and “UK holiday rental” up 56%.

Aside from airport stress, travel disruption and rising airfares, one of the major trends driving the British staycation boom is food tourism.

The research found that nearly three-quarters of Britons (71%) say that dining is a key part of their “foodie staycation”, with many including the UK’s culinary scene in their itinerary.

‘Foodie tourism’ on the rise

Food experiences are playing a bigger role than ever before in holiday planning for British travellers.

The data found that three in five Brits (58%) identify themselves as “foodies” and two fifths (42%) now place greater importance on good dining experiences.

“Staycationing is no longer a consolation prize or ‘second best’,” said Binay Agarwala, Managing Director for Rewards and Lending at Chase. “Rather, the UK is actively seeking out at-home holidays in order to try out the world-class dining scene this country has on offer.”

How much are staycationers willing to pay?

The importance of food experiences is also reflected in the price that Brits will pay for a good meal when on holiday.

More than three-quarters (76%) say they are willing to fork out on dinners when staycationing – rising to nine in 10 for self-proclaimed “foodies” (89%).

On average, Brits consider a “splurge” dinner to cost around £54.35 (€63.44) per head. However, younger diners aged between 25 and 34 are prepared to pay considerably more at £66.67 (€77.82).

Price is not the only thing that British travellers are investing in – but also time.

The data revealed that the average staycationer spends 36 minutes seeking out the best foodie hotspots – more than the time they spend researching transport or travel (33 minutes) and the weather (26 minutes). Among self-confessed foodies, this increases to 45 minutes – 25% more time.

World.title: Why do so many hit songs sound alike? Meet the 'Gen Alpha melody'
World.content:
You’ve heard it. It’s so ubiquitous it would have been impossible not to. It’s a melody built around four notes, and it reappears in hit after hit, sticking in your ears like honey.

 

Danish musicologist Carl Martin has dubbed it the “Gen Alpha melody”, so named because many of the songs featuring it were released during the 2010s.

'APT.' by Rosé and Bruno Mars. 'One of Your Girls' by Troye Sivan. 'Ode to the Mets' by The Strokes. Artists spanning genres as diverse as rock, pop and EDM – as well as musicians from Spain, India, Norway and beyond – have used it.

Martin noticed the pattern while listening to pop songs from around the world. He recognised the same recurring melodic framework, so he began compiling examples for a YouTube video.

Eventually, he identified around 500 tracks before narrowing the list to 72 songs that shared what he believes is the same melodic pattern. Played back-to-back, the similarities become uncanny. Suddenly, you start to hear it everywhere.

“I’ve never seen a specific melody come as close to being this widely used in popular music,” Martin says in his 14-minute explainer video.

Why does the ‘Gen Alpha melody’ keep resurfacing?

Martin says the melody is built around four “pillar” notes spread across two short musical phrases – the musical equivalent of sentences.

“All other tones revolve around these because they’re landing on strong beats or the melodic phrase ends on them,” he explains.

While songwriters can fill in the gaps between them differently, they all revolve around these same pillars.

Martin believes it works so well because it follows a “question and answer” pattern: it begins with an unresolved idea before ending on a “nice and consonant” resolution.

“It’s a great-sounding melody by itself and it has this bittersweet quality,” Martin says.

That also helps explain why it appears so often in songs about heartbreak and melancholy, two of pop music’s most timeless themes.

And it’s so flexible that the same melody can appear in songs that otherwise sound nothing alike, from Yungblud’s pop rock hits to EDM bangers by Zedd and Tiesto.

Why isn’t anyone getting sued?

The similarities may be striking, but Martin argues they don’t necessarily amount to the most widespread example of copyright infringement in history.

He describes the phenomenon as “interpolation” – in other words, borrowing an existing melody rather than sampling a recording – and says it’s not always a conscious decision. Instead, he believes many songwriters have absorbed the melody simply by hearing it repeated throughout popular music before reproducing it without realising it.

Despite its name, the melody predates Gen Alpha by decades. Among the earliest examples is The Beatles’ 1965 hit 'It’s Only Love'. But the roots likely go even deeper.

Since Martin published his video, some have traced similar patterns back to Beethoven, meaning the Gen Alpha melody may have been hiding in plain sight for centuries.

World.title: Meta launches Muse Code tool amid AI hacking revelations
World.content:
Meta launched its first coding agent, Muse Code, on Wednesday, as the company continues to invest heavily in AI services and models in order to better compete with rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.

 

Muse Code will be accessible to developers via a pay-as-you-go option that will be priced similarly to the Muse Spark 1.1 release, which currently charges $4.25 per million tokens of output and $1.25 per million tokens in input.

This will make it much easier for developers to build apps within a single user interface, even while simultaneously dealing with several AI-powered digital agents.

At the same time, the company also revealed that one of its AI models had hacked another company during a cybersecurity test.

This happened due to a mistake by its independent testing partner Irregular, which allowed the model internet access beyond what was originally planned, letting it change the unnamed company’s internal systems.

This incident comes amid an increasing wave of cases in which AI models from industry giants like OpenAI and Anthropic have breached other companies’ systems during testing.

OpenAI has already admitted to an AI agent hacking Hugging Face, another artificial intelligence startup.

Similarly, Anthropic revealed last week that some of its Claude models had breached three companies. It did not name the organisations in question.

Meta has said that it is investigating the incident.

The rise of AI model hacking

Concern is growing over the power of artificial intelligence models and the companies behind them, after several AI systems broke out of secure testing environments in recent months and gained unauthorised access to outside organisations' systems.

OpenAI and Anthropic have won some credit for voluntarily publishing incident reports about the breaches. Doubts remain, however, over how the failures were allowed to happen in the first place.

Anthropic is also working with METR, an independent AI evaluator, to investigate further.

During safety testing, Anthropic's Claude models were set a task: retrieve a piece of secret information hidden on another machine within a closed test network, hacking in if necessary. A miscommunication with the evaluation partner running the exercise meant the network was, in fact, connected to the live internet.

When Claude's search led it to real systems, the three models involved responded differently. One continued attacking a system even after recognising it was real, another appeared to convince itself it was still inside the test, and the third stopped once it concluded the target was not part of the exercise.

Anthropic has urged other AI companies to check whether their own models have hacked outside organisations without their knowledge.

Neither Anthropic nor the affected organisations were aware of the breaches while they were happening. The company only discovered the incidents after reviewing more than 141,000 evaluation sessions, a review prompted by OpenAI's earlier disclosure that one of its own models had broken into the AI platform Hugging Face during a similar test.

World.title: 'Distressing' imagery: From 'Ali G' to 'The Mummy' - Which movie posters have been banned since 2000?
World.content:
Marketing can be a tricky business.

 

Some movie posters get it right and spark trends. Others spark controversy and don’t make the cut.

The latest to fall in the second category is the poster for Lee Cronin’s The Mummy, which will no longer be allowed to appear on the London Underground.

The UK’s Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) revealed they received multiple complaints about the poster campaign, which features a close-up of a mummified child. The organisation ruled that the figure’s “sunken and lifeless” features gave "a realistic impression of a dead child".

They ruled that the posters must not appear again in public in the same form.

Here is the offending image:

Lee Cronin’s The Mummy Blumhouse Productions - Warner Bros. Pictures

Appropriately banned for some; missing the point of the supernatural horror film for others, as the young girl is successfully exhumed.

Still, it's not the first movie poster to be censored... From horror films to comedies via documentaries, here is a chronological look back at some of the most controversial - and in some cases misjudged - movie posters to be banned since 2000.

Warning: Many of the movie posters were censored by some organisations. Proceed at your own risk.

Spider-Man (2002)

Spider-Man Sony Pictures - Ebay screenshot

Prior to its 2002 release, Sony Pictures unveiled a teaser trailer and posters for Sam Raimi's Spider-Man which featured New York City’s Twin Towers. Following the September 11 terrorist attack, the studio asked for the promotional material to be destroyed and replaced by other buildings in NYC.

Ali G Indahouse (2002)

Ali G Indahouse Universal Pictures

Before Sacha Baron Cohen was Borat, the British comedian was Staines-based rapper Ali G... The poster for his 2002 film received many complaints, with many deeming the ad to be sexist. The UK's ASA ruled the image (and Cohen’s hand placement) was offensive and pornographic.

The Rules Of Attraction (2002)

The Rules Of Attraction Lions Gate Films

In a stroke of genius, the marketing team for the satirical black comedy based on Bret Easton Ellis’ 1987 novel decided to take some stuffed animals and display them in... suggestive poses. Sophomoric for some; hilarious for others. The MPAA (Motion Picture Association of America) banned it in the US, while Canada, the UK and other European territories appreciated the joke and kept the poster just as it was.

Creep (2004)

Creep Pathé

A bloodied hand trying to escape from a metro carriage... Is it any wonder the Transport For London didn't want the poster shown on the Underground?

Saw II (2005)

Saw II Lions Gate Films - X screenshot

The poster for the second instalment of the gory Saw franchise was rejected by the US' MPAA because of the severed fingers. An updated version made it less clear that the fingers had been sliced off. As is usually the case, the news of a banned film poster contributed to the release buzz at the time.

This Film Is Not Yet Rated (2006)

This Film Is Not Yet Rated IFC Films

Somewhat ironically, the poster for Kirby Dick's documentary about cinema censorship was vetoed by several newspapers in the US.

The Road To Guantanamo (2006)

The Road to Guantanamo Revolution Films - Channel 4

For the MPAA, the poster for Michael Winterbottom and Mat Whitecross’ documentary about three British men (the "Tipton Three") held at Guantanamo Bay unlawfully needed to go. In their eyes, the ‘burlap bag’ over the detainee’s head suggested he had been tortured. Some viewed the ban as hypocrisy, considering the base has long been a focal point for debates over civil liberties.

Teeth (2007)

Teeth Roadside Attractions - Screenshot X

Mitchell Lichtenstein's comedy horror became infamous for its central conceit: vagina dentata. Ask your parents. For the marketing, they went for an X-ray of the lead character Dawn's body, an image revealing her dangerous spare set of teeth. Ingenious in the sense the image tells you all you need to know; but authorities in the US and UK decided that it was too disturbing and promptly banned the poster.

Five Senses Of Eros (2009)

Five Senses of Eros Daisy & Cinergy Entertainment

This South Korean anthology film revolving around themes of love, passion and lust created quite the stir and its poster made history in its home country for being the first-ever movie poster to be banned. It was the first time that promotional material featured naked buttocks.

Thirst (2009)

Thirst Focus Features - X screenshot

The poster for Park Chan-wook's horror film based on Emile Zola’s novel "Thérèse Raquin" was banned by South Korea’s Media Rating Board. Not for the strangling of the priest character, but because the naked legs were deemed too sexually suggestive. A subsequent version of the poster removed the offending lallies.

Coco Avant Chanel (Coco Before Chanel) (2009)

Coco Before Chanel Warner Bros. Pictures

Fashion icon Gabrielle 'Coco' Chanel (Audrey Tautou) can be seen smoking a Gauloise on the poster of Anne Fontaine's biographical drama. This led Paris transport authorities to declare that the poster could not be shown in metro stations, as France bans all "direct and indirect" tobacco advertising.

The Last Exorcism (2010)

The Last Exorcism Lionsgate

The ASA in the UK banned the poster for Daniel Stamm's Eli Roth-produced The Last Exorcism, stating that the image of a young woman wearing a blood-splattered gown suggested she had been violently sexually assaulted.

The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo (2011)

The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo Sony Pictures Releasing

David Fincher's very underrated US remake of the Swedish original, based on the books by Stieg Larsson, featured nudity which was too much for some conservative critics. Then, some fans of the novels took against Mikael (Daniel Craig) was using his arm to protect Lisbeth (Rooney Mara) - something they felt misrepresented their character dynamic.

Sket (2011)

Sket Revolver Entertainment - X screenshot

The poster for Nirpal Bhogal's first feature was banned in the UK for featuring a gang beating up David Cameron and the line: "So Mr Cameron, do you still want to hug a hoodie?" The line mocked the British political catchphrase from 2006, which referred to an "empathetic" approach to young offenders. Transport For London pulled the poster, as they feared it would incite violence.

Shame (2011)

Shame X screenshot

There's a certain creativity at play in the Hungarian movie poster for British filmmaker Steve McQueen’s sex addiction film, albeit an idea which may undercut the serious themes at the core of the drama. It was ruled as being too graphic, and most territories went for a more tactful shot of blue bedsheets instead.

Les Infidèles (The Players) (2012)

The Players Mars Distribution - X screenshot

France again for this Jean Dujardin comedy which shocked many through its suggestive poster campaign. The image, which many feared would bring "sex education on the street", ended up being replaced by Dujardin and his co-star Gilles Lellouche sitting down while two models are partially seen at the forefront of the poster.

Sin City: A Dame To Kill For (2014)

Sin City: A Dame To Kill For The Weinstein Company

As you may have noticed, the US can’t handle nudity, and authorities deemed that the image of Eva Green fell in the “excessive nudity” category. More precisely, it was banned for the “curve of under breast and dark nipple / areola circle visible through sheer gown”. Strangely, the loaded gun she’s brandishing was not mentioned or censored.

Mignonnes (Cuties) (2020)

NB: Euronews Culture has decided not to include the image since this it has been deemed by many as sexualising underage girls.

Netflix removed their promotional material for this French drama by Maïmouna Doucouré as it sparked disapproval and even a petition. Netflix said it was "deeply sorry for the inappropriate artwork", which missed the mark completely, as the film tackles how social media pushes young girls to mimic sexualised imagery.

World.title: The Mata Hari affair: Courtesan, spy, legend
World.content:
Regarded the most famous female spy of all time, dancer Mata Hari had men falling at her feet — but was executed for treason. Did she really betray state secrets?

Mata Hari was already a legend in her own lifetime. When she stepped into the Parisian limelight in 1905, she swept high society off its feet.

"She danced with veils and jewel-encrusted bustiers and almost nothing else," the Parisian press reported. "Never had anyone dared to appear unveiled before the gods with such trembling ecstasy. And what wonderful movements she made — both daring and demure at the same time."

Mata Hari had convinced audiences and the press that she was an exotic temple dancer — but the dark-haired performer was actually Dutch.

One of the hallmarks of the Belle Époque era was a heightened fascination with cultures the Parisians deemed to be exotic. Driven by financial desperation, she exploited this demand by pretending to be Indian. To make her act more credible, she fabricated a backstory claiming to be the daughter of a highly esteemed Brahmin.

Mata Hari's sensual dance was her own creation Image: Scherl/SZ Photo/picture alliance

"My mother, first bayadere [dancer] of the Ranganathaswamy Temple, died at the age of fourteen, on the day I was born. After the temple priests cremated her body, they adopted me and named me Mata Hari, which means 'Eye of the Day [a Malay word, Hari means sun]."

She claimed to have learned the sacred temple dances from a young age. During her performances, one veil after another would fall away. Later, she said, "I never danced well. The only reason people came to see me was that I was the first to dare to present myself naked to the public."

From Dutch hatmaker's daughter to Mata Hari

High society couldn't get enough of Mata Hari, unaware that her real name was Margaretha Geertruida Zelle and that she came from the small Dutch town of Leeuwarden.

Born on August 7, 1876, Mata Hari was the daughter of a hatmaker who had become wealthy through stock market speculation. He often spoiled his daughter with lavish gifts. For her sixth birthday, he gave her a carriage drawn by goats.

At the age of 13, Mata Hari's life of luxury ended abruptly. Her father went bankrupt and abandoned the family. Two years later, when her mother passed away, she moved in with relatives. Eventually, she met her husband through a newspaper ad: "An officer from the Dutch East Indies [now Indonesia], currently on home leave, seeks the company of a nice young woman with potential for future marriage. Financial circumstances irrelevant."

The MacLeods around 1900 Image: akg-images/picture alliance

Mata Hari and John Rudolf MacLeod, a Dutch nobleman of Scottish descent who was 20 years her senior, quickly became a couple. In 1897, she accompanied her husband to the Dutch East Indies. But her dream of a happy life never materialized. Frequent arguments strained their relationship. Then, their two-year-old son was tragically poisoned to death. When the MacLeods returned to Europe in 1902, their marriage fell apart. MacLeod left Mata Hari, taking their daughter with him and refusing to pay any alimony, leaving her to fend for herself.

She began her career in Paris as a model for painters and tried her luck at the circus. But it was her creation of the exotic stage persona Mata Hari that ultimately made her famous. She performed at prestigious venues across Europe, including Vienna and Monte Carlo, staying in luxurious hotels. She danced at soirées hosted by the Rothschild banking family and entertained Crown Prince Wilhelm, the son of the German Emperor Wilhelm II. Her success gave her access to the highest social circles, where she formed relationships with diplomats and high-ranking military officers who paid generously for her company.

Mata Hari around 1906: All of Paris wanted to see her Image: akg-images/picture alliance

World War I agent driven by financial hardship

Eventually, Mata Hari's popularity began to wane. Younger dancers began imitating her, and thrill-seeking audiences in Paris moved on to the next sensation. When World War I broke out in 1914, Mata Hari could no longer sustain her luxurious lifestyle.

She accepted an offer from the German consul in the Netherlands to help pay off her debts. She was promised even more money for gathering intelligence from influential figures on the opposing side of the war. Her initial fee was 20,000 francs, a substantial sum at the time. And just like that, she became Agent H 21.

Then, when the French intelligence service approached her and offered her even more money, Mata Hari became a double agent. But she miscalculated the situation. The French had enlisted her so they could catch her spying for the Germans. At the same time, due to increasing suspicion of her activities, the British intelligence service also monitored Mata Hari as she traveled through Europe. On February 13, 1917, she was arrested.

Official photograph of the defendant Margaretha Geertruida MacLeod from 1917 Image: akg-images/picture alliance

On October 15, at the age of 41, Mata Hari was executed for high treason in the moat of the Château de Vincennes, near Paris. Eyewitnesses reported that she faced the 12-man firing squad with her head held high and even blew them a kiss. She refused to wear a blindfold and instead addressed her final words to the commander who gave the order to fire: "Thank you, monsieur!"

Mata Hari's status as a so-called master spy remains questionable. According to documents from the British intelligence service — which remained classified for several decades — any information she may have shared likely did not impact the course of World War I.

It seems that Mata Hari was used as a convenient scapegoat at a time when public enthusiasm for the war had significantly waned. And the French military court needed someone to blame. She herself denied having spied till the very end. Regardless of whether or not she was a master spy, she was undoubtedly a master of self-promotion until her last breath.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Can UN chief's initiative kickstart resolution for Cyprus?
World.content:
UN chief Antonio Guterres considers a resolution to the Cyprus issue to be vital for regional stability and has initiated a new diplomatic effort. What are the prospects for its success?

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres last week became the first UN chief to visit Cyprus in 16 years.

While there, he met the leaders of the island's two communities: Nikos Christodoulides, president of the Republic of Cyprus, and Tufan Erhurman, Turkish Cypriot leader and president of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is only recognized by Turkey.

His aim in doing so was to determine whether the conditions exist for restarting negotiations on the Cyprus issue.

Guterres (center) travelled to Cyprus to meet the leaders of the two Cypriot communities, Nikos Christodoulides (center right) and Tufan Erhurman (center left) Image: TRNC Presidency/Handout/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Progress on talks has remained stalled since the collapse of negotiations in Crans-Montana, Switzerland, in 2017, when the United Nations made its most comprehensive effort to broker a reunification agreement for the island.

Why now?

So, why has Antonio Guterres decided to launch a new initiative now?

According to diplomatic sources, the answer lies less in developments surrounding the Cyprus issue itself and more in the rapidly changing geopolitical landscape of the wider region.

War in the Middle East, deteriorating relations between Israel and Turkey, and growing strategic competition in the Eastern Mediterranean have heightened UN concerns that the unresolved Cyprus conflict could undermine the stability of the entire region.

Guterres said as much after the joint meeting on July 29. "I do believe that a solution in Cyprus is absolutely crucial, not only to preserve the interests and the peace of the Cyprus people, but also as a factor of stability in what is becoming a dangerously unstable region," he said.

Speaking to DW, Andreas Mavroyiannis, former permanent representative of the Republic of Cyprus to the United Nations and former chief negotiator of the Greek Cypriot side, shared the same concern.

"The strengthening of relations between the Republic of Cyprus and Israel, combined with the deterioration of Israel–Turkey relations, increases the risk of the Cyprus issue being instrumentalized," he told DW.

According to Mavroyiannis, the UN secretary-general fears that Cyprus could, instead of serving as a pillar of stability in the Middle East, become increasingly entangled in regional rivalries and emerge as one of the area's most vulnerable flashpoints.

The European dimension

The UN is not alone in viewing the Cyprus issue through the prism of regional security. The EU has also shown increasing interest in playing a more active political role in efforts to revive the peace process.

A significant step came on July 7, when the European Commission appointed Executive Vice-President Raffaele Fitto as the EU's Special Representative for the Cyprus issue.

His mandate is to support the UN-led process and strengthen the bloc's involvement in efforts to restart negotiations.

A more active role for the EU has long been one of President Nikos Christodoulides' key policy objectives.

During Cyprus' recent presidency of the Council of the European Union, he reminded fellow European leaders that he was "the president of the only EU member state that remains under illegal military occupation."

President Nikos Christodoulides has long been keen for the EU to play a more active role in the search for a resolution to the Cyprus issue Image: Laia Ros/REUTERS

The Cypriot government believes that the EU agenda could provide Ankara with incentives to contribute constructively to progress on the Cyprus issue.

Among the issues viewed as potential leverage are the modernization of the EU–Turkey Customs Union, visa liberalization for Turkish citizens, Turkey's participation in the EU's SAFE defense financing instrument and the prospect of gradually reviving its long-frozen EU accession process.

The next step

While Guterres' decision to announce a new informal expanded 5+1 meeting involving the two Cypriot communities, the three guarantor powers (Greece, Turkey and the UK) plus the UN was widely seen as a positive signal, he deliberately stopped short of setting a date.

Instead, he made it clear that the meeting would only be convened once sufficient progress had been made on confidence-building measures, methodology and the substance of the process.

So, it was no coincidence that he stressed upon arriving in Cyprus that "it depends obviously on the Cypriots themselves," underlining that responsibility for moving the process forward rests primarily with the two communities.

His remarks are directly linked to the lack of tangible progress on confidence-building measures.

The UN Secretary-General says that a 5+1 meeting will only take place once sufficient progress had been made on confidence-building measures, methodology and the substance of the process Image: Petros Karadjias/REUTERS

Despite months of discussions, the two sides failed to reach agreement even on the opening of new crossing points — a step which, according to the UN Secretary-General, could have "a tangible impact on the daily lives of Cypriots," while helping to restore a minimum level of trust ahead of the next phase of negotiations.

Ankara's position remains crucial

The key question, however, extends beyond the two communities themselves and concerns Turkey's willingness to engage.

The real test for the UN is whether Ankara is prepared to return to negotiations conducted within the framework of the UN Security Council resolutions and the agreed basis of a bicommunal, bizonal federation, moving away from the two-state solution it has advocated since the collapse of the Crans-Montana talks in 2017.

So far, Turkey has made no public statement indicating such a shift. The only possible indication comes indirectly from Antonio Guterres' remark that he has "the consent of both sides and the guarantor powers to move towards another 5+1 meeting, provided there is adequate preparation."

The wording suggests that, at least procedurally, Ankara is willing to participate in another informal conference under UN auspices. Whether this also signals a substantive change in Turkey's long-standing position remains, for now, an open question.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: Why Iran is sending mixed signals on talks
World.content:
Trump says talks with Iran are underway. Tehran says it is discussing the Strait of Hormuz with Oman, not Washington. Analysts say the gap reflects competing political pressures.

US President Donald Trump on Monday said that negotiations with Iran were ongoing over the Strait of Hormuz, adding that the Islamic Republic was facing a "last chance before decapitation."

Trump told reporters at the White House that he agreed to continue to pursue talks with Iran at the request of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and other countries.

His remarks appeared to contradict public statements from Tehran, which has so far denied that negotiations with Washington were taking place.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei nevertheless confirmed that Tehran was holding talks with Oman over the strategic waterway.

The two sides may therefore be describing the same diplomatic channel in different terms, each using language aimed at its own domestic audience.

Washington describes the Omani mediation as negotiations with Iran. Tehran portrays it as a technical discussion with Oman about shipping through the strait.

Hormuz remains the main obstacle

The Strait of Hormuz has become the main sticking point.

Commercial traffic through key waterway remains severely restricted, while ships continue to face attacks near the strait.

According to data from maritime analytics company Kpler cited by Reuters news agency, only six commercial vessels crossed the route on Monday, down from seven the previous day.

The uncertainty surrounding the key waterway has also affected global markets.

Hopes of diplomatic progress recently pushed oil prices lower and helped stock markets rise. But those movements reflected how sensitive markets remain to any news about the strait, rather than evidence that the crisis had been resolved.

Iran wants some measure of control over vessels entering the Persian Gulf to be recognized. The United States wants the strait fully reopened to unrestricted international shipping.

Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, told DW that the disagreement is no longer simply about whether the two sides are talking.

"The question is what to call those talks and what each side hopes to gain from them," he said.

Trump describes the indirect channel as negotiations because he needs to show that military and economic pressure has brought Tehran back to the table, Dorbeiki said.

He suggested that Iran avoids the same terminology because acknowledging negotiations with Washington could be seen by its domestic opponents as surrender.

The two sides remain far apart.

"Iran wants control over vessels entering the strait, while the United States wants completely free passage," Dorbeiki said. "These positions cannot easily be reconciled."

Divisions inside Iran

The contradictory messages also reflect divisions between rival political factions inside Iran.

Dorbeiki identifies two broad camps.

"The first, which could be described as the 'development and reconstruction through agreement' camp, believes that without sanctions relief and the reopening of Hormuz, Iran's economy cannot recover or even sustain itself," he told DW.

According to Dorbeiki, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and some Revolutionary Guard figures with economic interests may be closer to that view.

The opposing camp, which includes the Paydari Front, a small, ultra-conservative party, "sees an agreement with the United States as an ideological defeat" and favors continued resistance.

Leadership vacuum adds to uncertainty

The lack of a clear leader in Iran has added to the uncertainty.

Strait of Hormuz: Iran's most powerful weapon? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the country's then supreme leader Ali Khamenei was killed in an airstrike on February 28 the first hours of the US-Israeli war against Iran, authority has become more fragmented.

His son Mojtaba Khamenei was named new supreme leader, but his role remains unclear and he has not been seen in public since the war began amid speculation he was severely injured in the strike.

Dorbeiki says this has allowed rival groups to claim they speak for the leadership.

"Indirect talks through Oman are likely to continue," he told DW. "Pezeshkian will remain under pressure, but he is unlikely to be removed for now because the domestic and international political costs would be high."

Dorbeiki noted that keeping Pezeshkian in office leaves open the option of blaming him if the negotiations fail.

Three competing camps inside Iran

Hassan Asadi Zeidabadi, an Iranian political analyst based in Tehran, believes the main decision-makers in Tehran have already accepted the need for negotiations.

However, he says there are three main camps within the Iranian establishment.

The first consists of government officials dealing with the economic effects of the war and blockade, making them more inclined toward negotiations.

"The second group is made up mainly of military figures who want to improve their position in the conflict before negotiating and remain skeptical of US intentions," Zeidabadi told DW.

"The third group is made up of ideological hardliners who believe that reaching an agreement with Washington after the war and the killing of Iran's supreme leader would mark the end of the Islamic Republic's traditional identity, which is rooted in opposition to the West."

"They fear the day after an agreement," Asadi Zeidabadi added. "For them, a deal with the United States would mean the end of the ideological era they represent and, ultimately, their own removal."

Why the US wants to bring Iran back to the negotiating table To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zeidabadi said these hardliners retain influence in parliament, the security establishment and the state's propaganda apparatus, and fear the changes a deal could bring.

The future of the talks may depend less on Muscat or Washington than on which factions gain the upper hand in Tehran.

If supporters of an agreement convince the leadership that continued isolation threatens reconstruction, the economy and ultimately the system's survival, diplomacy could move forward.

If hardliners succeed in presenting any compromise as surrender, even the indirect talks could collapse.

Based on the positions outlined by both analysts, further reports of progress are likely to be accompanied by contradictory public statements.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: AfD threatens to cut funding for 'modern-thinking' culture
World.content:
The far-right party could win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's state election in September. Their cultural program denigrates Bauhaus, Holocaust remembrance culture and diversity in theater.

In upcoming state elections to be held on September 6, polls suggest the Alternative for Germany (AfD) could win an absolute majority in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Based on the far-right's cultural policy program, museums, theaters and cultural institutions in the region say that artistic freedom is one of the far-right party's targets.

The AfD has announced that artists and institutions would be required to sign a declaration pledging "not to hold in contempt Germany and its culture" if they want to obtain state funding. Many of these organizations and individuals heavily rely on these subsidies.

The AfD's interpretation of disrespect to German culture also ambiguously includes what the party calls "anti-German art."

Hans-Thomas Tillschneider is the cultural policy spokesperson for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt Image: Heiko Rebsch/dpa/picture alliance

"We declared in our government program that we no longer intend to spend public funds on promoting anti-German art," said Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, cultural policy spokesperson for the AfD parliamentary group in the state legislature, in a speech held in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament in late June.

Asked by other members of parliament to specify what that meant exactly, Tillschneider said, "Anti-German art is German art that doesn't want to be German." He mentioned as an example an opera production he had seen some years ago; the classical German composer's work was revisited through a "feminist deconstructivist" lens that didn't please him and corresponds to what he sees as "anti-German art."

"This anti-German aversion is still considered de rigueur in large parts of the theater world," he said. "We will no longer support this attitude — let me state that quite clearly."

Bauhaus, a direct target — like in the 1930s

Bauhaus, Germany's iconic architecture, art and design school founded in 1919, was forced to close under the Nazis, who considered their avant-garde ideas and their open-minded attitude to be "un-German." Bauhaus nevertheless went on to become one of design's most important movements of the 20th century; its influence is still felt worldwide.

Today, the AfD once again sees Bauhaus as too modernist and globalist for the "patriotic cultural policy" the party envisions.

100 years of this iconic German design school To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The AfD's criticism of Bauhaus picks up on criticism from 100 years ago; their wording is similar," Barbara Steiner, director of the Bauhaus Foundation, told DW.

The AfD Saxony-Anhalt's program describes Bauhaus as "a controversial school of architecture" and criticizes the current state government for putting too much emphasis on this landmark attraction in their current image campaign, titled "moderndenken" (thinking modern).

The AfD aims to adopt instead a campaign called "deutschdenken" (thinking German), which would downplay the role of Bauhaus and instead "highlight the state's significant contributions to the development of the German nation — from Henry I and Otto I to Luther, Bismarck and Nietzsche."

Historically loaded language

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) strongly rejects comparisons to the Nazi party and Adolf Hitler, often dismissing them as trivializations of Nazi crimes.

Yet in its cultural policy program, the far-right party regularly adopts the language used in Hitler's propaganda, downplays Nazi-era atrocities, challenges Germany's culture of remembrance and uses historically loaded language.

The proposed "deutschdenken" slogan is one example of this: "'Deutsch denken' refers to a speech Adolf Hitler made in 1938" — the "Reichenberger Rede," noted Steiner.

Barbara Steiner, director of the Bauhaus Foundation in Dessau Image: Jörg Linke/DW

Culture needs state support to thrive

The Bauhaus is not the only cultural organization that feels threatened in Saxony-Anhalt. "As cultural practitioners, cultural initiators and artists, we can say that we are now genuinely afraid, because what's being triggered there is, in fact, the idea that art and culture must be 'German,'" Annegret Laabs, director of the Kunstmuseum Magdeburg told DW.

Laabs is a spokesperson for the initiative Kultur ist Vielfalt und Heimat, which roughly translates as "Culture is diversity and home." The initiative brings together a wide range of cultural institutions and artists from the region; they are warning in a joint statement that the AfD's plans could have far-reaching consequences for artistic freedom, historical memory, and public cultural life.

Annegret Laabs, director of the Kunstmuseum Magdeburg Image: Jörg Linke/DW

"We all know that what we do — from theaters to museums to libraries — is paid for with taxpayer money. It wouldn't exist otherwise," said Laabs.

Restricting funding based on an arbitrary definition of what constitutes "German" art basically equates to culture's demise, explains Laabs: "If we look at the bigger picture, we see that culture and art have been free for centuries and have known no boundaries — not even national ones. Wherever there are national boundaries, there is no longer any art or culture worthy of that name."

'Resist the beginnings'

Along with threats to funding, the AfD's program also describes Germany's existing culture of Holocaust remembrance as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" that has "blocked the possibilities for forming a stable national identity." It sees this as an "identity disorder" that needs to be "healed," by focusing on the "positive aspects of German history."

Sabine Schramm, director of the Puppentheater Magdeburg Image: Jörg Linke/DW

Sabine Schramm, director of Magdeburg's puppet theater, finds "it regrettable that we humans are not willing to draw conclusions from a complex history — conclusions that matter both to us as individuals and to us as a society."

She notes that throughout her 30-year career in theater, she has dealt with Germany's culture of remembrance, grappling with the horrors of Nazism on stage.

"It has always been important to me — especially in productions for young people — to tell stories that address precisely this issue: National Socialism, how it begins, and how the various elements interlock," she points out.

"I can still see myself standing on stage talking about 'resisting the beginnings' — that phrase, 'resisting the beginnings,' has become such a cliché," she says, referring to an idea Germans are deeply familiar with; after the horrors of the Nazi era, the generations that followed were urged to speak out against threats to democracy — before it's too late.

"But where, exactly, are the beginnings?" Schramm asks. "Is this the beginning, or are we still before the beginning? Are we right in the middle of it? What must I do to resist the beginnings?"

New report backs ban of German far-right party To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
