Fear of punishment may encourage people to censor themselves. This effect is particularly visible on platforms such as TikTok, where younger users may begin avoiding sensitive topics and refrain from expressing critical or unconventional views. As a result, the space for public debate narrows and the diversity of opinions declines. The principles of necessity and proportionality: Even if protecting public morality is accepted as a legitimate aim, any restrictions must be necessary and proportionate to that objective. Administrative detention ranging from eight to 30 days may appear relatively short. However, its systematic and frequent use can turn punishment into a tool of control. Given the availability of alternative measures, such as warnings, platform moderation policies and media literacy programmes, the necessity of depriving people of their liberty raises important legal questions.

TikTok arrests in Azerbaijan

World.title: From “rapid response” to possible law: who are Georgia’s national values being protected from?
World.content:
The Georgian government has not ruled out introducing legislation against what it describes as the erosion of national identity. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the proposed rules could cover insults directed at saints, monarchs and prominent public figures. No draft law has been introduced yet. However, experts argue that the groundwork is already being laid. Members of the ruling team have already begun discussing penalties and possible regulation of the media.

As the ruling Georgian Dream party debates possible punishment for insulting national values, it is worth examining what such measures could cover and what Russia’s experience suggests.

From assaults to a campaign to “protect national values”

The debate over possible legislation followed an attack on comedian Onise Okriashvili over a joke he made on YouTube. Late on 22 July, a man assaulted him near his home in Tbilisi. The attacker, Niko Khurtsilava, said he acted because Okriashvili had insulted Georgian national culture.

Even before the assault, pro-government television channels had launched a media campaign against Okriashvili. They broadcast a clipped excerpt from his YouTube show in which he referred to renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze using obscene language.

The writer’s grandson, Nodar Macharashvili, publicly backed the attacker. A few days after the incident, MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, who also described himself as Khurtsilava’s friend, announced the creation of a new movement that would provide “rapid response” to insults directed at sacred values, ancestors, religion and history.

“If protecting our culture and national identity requires it, we will not shy away from any threat. We are ready to take responsibility for every action we take and, if necessary, even go to prison,” Kartvelishvili said.

He did not specify what he meant by “rapid response”. He also declined to answer journalists’ questions about the use of physical violence and vigilantism.

On 28 July, the group applied to the Public Registry to register its newly established organisation under the name National Generation.

A week after the attack on Okriashvili, on 30 July, another initiative group emerged to “protect national values”. It brought together actor Giorgi Shanidze, director Giorgi Sikharulidze and Kote Mzhavia, director of the Batumi Theatre.

Unlike the first movement, this group called for legal mechanisms rather than “rapid response”. Its members said the law should protect the church, sacred sites, historical heroes and national values.

“Freedom of expression is a fundamental value. However, that right cannot become a tool for insulting the sacred symbols and core values that form the country’s historical, cultural and spiritual foundation,” Giorgi Shanidze said.

The statement refers to “externally funded destructive groups” whose activities, it says, are creating confrontation between the Georgian nation and small minority groups.

“To prevent the situation from escalating further and reaching the point where even the wise Georgian people could lose patience, responsible steps must be taken and the existing problems must be resolved through legal and peaceful means,” the statement says.

The group plans to hold consultations with lawyers, historians, artists and athletes before drafting a legislative proposal.

However, neither the bill nor its concept has been published, so it remains unclear which actions could become punishable. The proposed form of liability and possible penalties also remain unknown.

What could a law on national values include?

On 3 August, Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that he did not rule out adopting such legislation. However, he said the authorities had not yet discussed any specific proposals.

“There is indeed a need to respond to the coordinated attack against our identity,” Kobakhidze said.

He also identified possible subjects of future regulation, including saints, kings and prominent public figures.

According to Kobakhidze, insults directed at Georgian saints and kings are part of “a chain of coordinated, commissioned actions.”

“These are not simply untalented people. These are people carrying out a specific assignment. The purpose of that assignment is simple: they are trying to weaken our national identity. That is why they are doing all this,” he said.

Kobakhidze did not specify who had allegedly commissioned the campaign. He also provided no evidence to support the claim.

“We must take every possible measure to counter such processes. If that requires adopting a law, we can discuss that as well.”

Kobakhidze’s remarks do not necessarily mean such a law will be adopted. However, they indicate that the initiative has already received political backing from the prime minister.

Meanwhile, MPs aligned with the ruling party have outlined possible restrictions in greater detail.

Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili linked the issue to public swearing, abusive language and hooliganism.

“When people use obscene language against a specific individual or institution at a rally, is that freedom of expression or simply abusive language and hooliganism? We cannot just leave it like this.”

Kadagishvili said he did not know what the legislation might ultimately contain. At the same time, he suggested that the media could also fall within its scope.

The MP claimed that certain television channels — referring to opposition broadcasters — had aired 3,500 “anti-church” reports over the past year and a half. He did not explain how he arrived at that figure or what criteria he used to classify the reports as “anti-church”.

Kadagishvili also suggested that “offensive” media content could become subject to legal regulation.

Guram Macharashvili, a member of the People’s Power party, openly called for penalties for public insults. He said the law should protect faith, the church, the patriarch and national traditions.

“When you publicly insult values such as faith, the church, the patriarch or our traditions, that should, of course, be punishable.”

Macharashvili argued that Georgia had offered excessive protection to dissenting views.

“Dissent has always enjoyed a certain degree of protection in Georgia. But recently, I would say it has been protected in an ultra-liberal, excessive way, and that needs to change.”

What counts as an “insult” — and who decides?

Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression. It also prohibits persecution for expressing an opinion.

The constitution also guarantees media freedom and prohibits censorship.

The state may restrict freedom of expression only by law and only when necessary in a democratic society. Such restrictions may serve aims including public safety and the protection of other people’s rights. The constitution does not list “insulting national values” as a separate ground for limiting freedom of expression.

At the same time, freedom of expression is not absolute. The law may restrict incitement to violence, threats, harassment or defamation. However, such restrictions must be clearly defined and predictable.

By contrast, “insulting national values” is a far more ambiguous concept. It remains unclear whether the proposed law would protect the reputation of specific individuals or instead safeguard abstract values or historical figures.

It is also unclear who would decide which saints, kings and public figures deserve legal protection. Would the law apply only to historical figures? Where would the line be drawn between legitimate historical criticism and an “insult”?

For example, pro-government television channels also launched a campaign against literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili after he criticised the policies of Georgian King Erekle II. Berdzenishvili neither joked about the king nor used obscene language. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream MPs and pro-government media sharply attacked him.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed restrictions would apply to satire, works of art or academic research. Another unanswered question is whether critical media coverage of members of the clergy could be treated as an “insult to sacred values”.

Protecting patriotism or deepening political divisions?

Opposition politicians see the initiative as an attempt to mobilise political support.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the For Georgia party argues that the government is trying to claim a monopoly on patriotism.

“They have a very calculated strategy — to gain exclusive ownership of patriotic issues. Everything serves that goal. They want everyone else to appear as opponents of Georgia’s identity, traditions and church, while presenting themselves as the sole defenders of those values.”

Giorgi Shalamberidze of the First Georgia party believes the proposed law could serve another political purpose.

“It could be a political manoeuvre. It may help mobilise a particular segment of voters, or it could mark the beginning of a much broader tightening of legislation in the long term.”

Shalamberidze acknowledged that freedom of expression can be restricted in certain circumstances. However, he pointed to Georgia’s current political environment.

“If this becomes law and is used as a tool, the question is how it will affect political actors, political parties and their freedom of expression, and to what extent it will become a mechanism for restricting their rights.”

Historians’ concerns

It remains unclear where the proposed law would draw the line between insulting a historical figure and offering a critical assessment. That uncertainty raises concerns for historians, researchers and authors.

Assessing historical figures often requires revisiting disputed facts, competing interpretations and long-established narratives.

If the state decides which interpretations are acceptable, the law could become a tool for restricting academic research and scholarly debate.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed rules would apply to academic publications, public lectures, textbooks or documentary films.

Another unanswered question is who would decide where legitimate historical criticism ends and an “insult” begins.

Historian Irakli Khvadagiani argues that placing faith and artistic expression into legal categories contradicts their very nature.

“Faith and creativity do not recognise prohibitions, nor do they accept categories imposed unilaterally. The idea of banning them through legislation is absurd. Humanity went through this centuries ago. It is simply the obsession of a dictator trying to bend society to his will.”

Risk of creating artificial divisions?

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes the proposed legislation could fuel ethnic and religious tensions. In his view, the vague concept of “protecting national identity” risks creating new fault lines within society.

“There are not enough supporters of this ideology in Georgia for Georgian Dream to sustain permanent tensions between Christians and Muslims, between Georgians and non-Georgians, or between Georgian speakers and those who do not speak the language.”

Zakareishvili sees elements of far-right ideology in the government’s approach. He argues that it runs counter to the principles of equality and justice.

“This is a classic example of pure far-right ideology. Humanity has gone through this countless times, and it has repeatedly led to catastrophe and world wars, bringing nothing but destruction.”

The conflict analyst also links the initiative to the electoral cycle. Georgia’s next parliamentary elections are not due until October 2028. However, Zakareishvili believes the ruling party has already begun preparing its campaign.

“Georgian Dream is getting ready for the elections. Before the vote, it needs to create exactly these kinds of flashpoints.”

Cases of violence carried out in the name of “protecting traditions” Invoking the need to protect national and religious values is not a new phenomenon in Georgian politics. In 2023, a man attacked Zurab Japaridze, leader of the Girchi – More Freedom party, in the city of Gori. The attacker said he acted because Japaridze had insulted the church and was “corrupting children”.

Later that year, protesters disrupted a lecture by Levan Berdzenishvili in Kvareli. They accused him of insulting King Erekle II and Christian values. In Tbilisi, demonstrators also threw eggs at Berdzenishvili.

On 5 July 2021, opponents of Tbilisi Pride attacked journalists and activists. They justified the violence by saying they were defending the family, the church and traditional values. More than 50 journalists were injured.

In November 2019, far-right and anti-LGBT groups tried to disrupt the premiere of the film And Then We Danced. The Georgian Orthodox Church described the film as “an insult to Georgia’s traditional values”. Protesters attempted to storm cinemas. One of them threw a stone at civil activist Anna Subeliani, causing a serious head injury. Police arrested 12 people that evening.

In January 2024, activist Nata Peradze splashed paint on an icon in Tbilisi’s Holy Trinity Cathedral depicting Saint Matrona of Moscow alongside Joseph Stalin. Far-right groups later gathered outside Peradze’s home, demanding that she be punished.

On 17 May 2013, thousands of people, including members of the clergy, attacked participants in an anti-homophobia rally. At least 17 people were injured. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the violence had taken place in circumstances of the state’s effective acquiescence.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is particularly relevant in this context because the substance and rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia years earlier.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially justified their version as a tool to ensure transparency over foreign funding. They later expanded it into a mechanism used against independent media outlets and civil society organisations.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is relevant here because both the substance and the rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia in recent years.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially presented their version as a transparency measure for foreign funding. They later expanded it into a tool used against independent media and civil society organisations.

It is therefore worth looking at how Russia gradually developed legislation under the banner of protecting “traditional values”, religious feelings and historical memory.

Russia did not build its legal framework for protecting religion, historical memory and “traditional values” overnight. The system evolved step by step.

Offending religious feelings

In 2012, members of the punk group Pussy Riot staged an anti-Vladimir Putin performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. A court convicted them of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred.

A year later, Russia toughened Article 148 of its Criminal Code by criminalising public acts that show clear disrespect for society and are committed with the intention of offending the religious feelings of believers.

One of the best-known cases under the law involved blogger Ruslan Sokolovsky, who filmed himself playing Pokémon Go inside a church and posted the video online. In other videos, he also criticised religion and the Russian Orthodox Church.

In 2017, a court gave Sokolovsky a three-and-a-half-year suspended prison sentence. The case involved several criminal charges, including offending believers’ religious feelings and inciting hatred.

In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Sokolovsky’s conviction had violated his right to freedom of expression. The court found that offensive or vulgar speech does not automatically amount to hate speech.

“Traditional values” as state policy

In November 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on protecting “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values”.

The document lists patriotism, dignity, life and the traditional family among those values. It also includes service to the fatherland, historical memory and continuity between generations.

According to the decree, external forces threaten these values by acting inside Russia through extremist and terrorist organisations.

The decree also identifies the United States and other “unfriendly states” as sources of those threats.

Russian authorities have explicitly linked cultural and values policy to national security.

A similar narrative has emerged in Georgian Dream’s campaign. Both initiative groups have spoken of a coordinated attack on Georgia’s “national identity”. Prime Minister Kobakhidze has used the same wording.

Legal protection of history

Article 354.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code is titled “Rehabilitation of Nazism”. Lawmakers originally introduced it to prohibit the denial of crimes established by the Nuremberg Tribunal.

However, the law goes much further. It also bans the dissemination of what authorities consider to be “knowingly false information” about the Soviet Union’s actions during the Second World War. The article also protects the honour and dignity of war veterans.

In 2021, lawmakers added a new offence covering the “insulting of the memory of the defenders of the Fatherland”. The law also criminalises offensive use of military glory symbols.

As a result, the legislation does more than prohibit denial of historical facts. It also protects the state’s official interpretation of the Soviet Union’s role in history.

According to a 2025 study by the human rights project OVD-Info, Russian courts handed down 25 convictions under Article 354.1 between 2015 and 2019. Many of the cases concerned interpretations of the Soviet Union’s actions and historical comparisons.

Between 2022 and May 2025, OVD-Info recorded 212 prosecutions under the same article.

A court gave Kazan resident Zulfiya Sitdikova a two-year suspended sentence over posters reading “No to war” and “9 Way”. She replaced the “M” in “May” with a “W”, and investigators interpreted this as desecration of Victory Day symbols.

Authorities also opened a criminal case against historian Mikhail Belousov. Investigators accused him of denying facts established by the Nuremberg Tribunal and spreading false information about the Soviet Union.

Prosecutors also opened two cases against historian Tamara Eidelman. They argued that her video lectures showed disrespect for Russia’s military remembrance days.

Russia has therefore created a system in which historians and society no longer have the final say in historical debates. Instead, investigators, expert witnesses and the courts have become the ultimate arbiters.

Where will Georgia draw the line?

Georgia has not yet introduced such a bill, so it is impossible to say whether it will follow the Russian path.

However, statements by members of the ruling party already suggest a broad range of protected subjects, including the church, the patriarch, saints, kings, public figures, traditions and even media content.

Russia’s experience also suggests that broadly defined protected values can gradually expand over time.

Protecting national values in Georgia

World.title: Georgian scam call centres: old fraudsters, new address? An investigation
World.content:
Georgian scam call centres that came under the spotlight during an international investigative project in 2025 have reportedly resumed operations from a new location. According to the investigative outlet Monitor, people linked to AK Group have relocated to an office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street in Tbilisi.

The outlet says its journalists conducted covert surveillance at the address for six months. They say they identified several of the same individuals who had been seen near AK Group’s previous office last year. According to Monitor, the footage also shows some of the same vehicles that regularly appeared at the company’s former location.

Journalists say they repeatedly spotted vehicles used by Akaki Kevkhishvili, who is widely believed to be the real operator of AK Group. The cars carried the registration numbers AK100KK and AK200KK. Investigators seized one of them in 2025 as part of the ongoing criminal investigation.

According to Monitor, AK Group’s registered owner and director, Meri Shotadze, also regularly visited the same address. She used two different vehicles, one of which investigators have also seized, while the other is registered to another person.

The investigation also claims that several agents who previously worked at AK Group’s former office have reappeared at the new location. They include Anzhelika Chkhapelia, who allegedly used the alias Marina Novikova; Misha Bayramov; Valerian Gigauri; Giorgi Gotman; and Ketevan Malashkhia, who allegedly used the alias Ashley Moriarty. According to Monitor, Malashkhia is a cousin of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife. The outlet also identified a Belarusian citizen, Lita, who had previously denied working at the call centre.

The journalists also say they identified security staff at the new office who had previously been seen outside AK Group’s former premises. They named former law enforcement officer Manuchar Gegia and former Zugdidi traffic police chief Levan Gogia.

According to the outlet, the office on Mirian Mepe Street closed after it announced the publication of its latest investigation. Both floors of the building are now being offered for rent.

Monitor says the premises had been leased since 2022 by RTM Imports, a company owned by Irakli Kvlividze, the brother of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife.

The journalists say they informed the Prosecutor’s Office on 1 July 2026 that AK Group’s managers and employees had been regularly operating from the office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street. According to Monitor, prosecutors have not clarified whether they investigated the information or whether the inquiry into the alleged fraud is still ongoing.

Background

In 2025, Monitor and more than 32 international media organisations published an investigation into AK Group’s activities. According to the report, the group employed 85 people and defrauded more than 6,100 people across Europe and Canada between 2022 and 2025. The journalists estimated that the operation generated more than $35 million in revenue over that period.

After the investigation was published, law enforcement authorities opened a criminal inquiry into organised fraud and the laundering of proceeds from crime on an especially large scale. Prosecutors have charged 11 people in the case.

In a separate bribery case, authorities also arrested former Georgian State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. Prosecutors accuse him, in one of the counts, of providing protection to the call centres. A court has also frozen the assets and company shares of the alleged organisers and employees of the call centre network.

Investigation continues

According to Monitor, the Prosecutor’s Office told the outlet that it had requested legal assistance from Germany to help identify potential victims. Prosecutors also said they had sought additional information from journalists involved in the investigation, but claimed they had declined to cooperate.

In a written response, the Prosecutor’s Office said that “the final decision in the case largely depends on information and materials to be obtained from abroad through legal assistance.”

A separate Monitor investigation found that Akaki Kevkhishvili and Meri Shotadze had previously worked at another call centre, 100 Marketing Solutions. Authorities began investigating the company in 2023 and froze its shares as part of the inquiry. However, a court lifted the freeze in 2026.

Are Georgian scam call centres still operating?

World.title: An explosives-laden drone was found at a key German airport. Here's what we know
World.content:
German authorities have opened a counterterrorism investigation after a drone carrying explosives was found at Leipzig/Halle Airport, a cargo and military logistics hub, in what the interior minister has called a hybrid attack.

Local media has since reported that the drone was laden with high-military-grade explosives, and was found next to a cargo aircraft carrying a payload of military ammunition.

Airport workers' discovery of the drone in a restricted area on Tuesday, local time, caused flight diversions and the closure of parts of the airport in the east of the country.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said on Wednesday that the incident opened a new level of danger.

Here's why the airport may have been a target, and why it could be connected to the war raging between Ukraine and Russia.

Suspicion has immediately fallen on the Kremlin over the incident. (Reuters: Sergei Karpukhin)

Why is Leipzig important?

Located in Schkeuditz, between the cities of Leipzig and Halle, the airport opened in 1927. It was largely destroyed by Allied bombing during World War Two and was rebuilt under the Eastern Bloc German Democratic Republic.

Following German reunification in 1990, it was privatised and renovated and became a cargo and logistics hub, including for NATO.

The government classifies it as critical infrastructure, warranting heightened government attention and protection.

The discovery brought Leipzig/Halle Airport to a standstill and saw some flights diverted to other airports. (Reuters: Axel Schmidt)

The airport ranks as Germany's largest cargo hub after Frankfurt and is among Europe's busiest, with annual freight volumes totalling around 1.4 million metric tons.

German logistics firm DHL moved its main hub to Leipzig/Halle in 2008, and, today, 7,000 DHL employees move 2,500 tons of freight through the airport every day with 23,600 flight movements every year.

Facilities, including two 3,600-metre runways and extensive warehouses, have attracted other major transport and logistics companies, including Lufthansa Cargo and Amazon.

What is the Ukraine connection?

In addition to its commercial operations, Leipzig/Halle is an important logistics hub for the German military as well as its NATO partners.

It is the main base for NATO's Strategic Airlift International Solution, known as SALIS, which is helping to deliver equipment to strengthen the defence pact's eastern flank.

The explosive-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian Antonov plane. (Reuters: Axel Schmidt)

SALIS established a company called Antonov Logistics SALIS, which flies military and non-military goods in crisis situations for NATO and European Union countries.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Leipzig/Halle-based Antonov Logistics SALIS is the sole organisation providing maintenance for the Antonov An-124-100, among the world's largest cargo aircraft.

Who is behind the drone incident?

According to media reports, this week's incident involved a drone found close to a group of Ukrainian An-124s.

One of those Ukrainian planes was carrying a payload of military ammunition, news outlets including Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported on Thursday, local time.

Terror probe launched after explosive drone found at German cargo hub After the drone was discovered, a diverted plane hit an unidentified object while climbing away from the airport.

Anti-extremism prosecutors and counterterrorism officers have taken over the investigation, but government authorities have given no indication of who might have been behind the Leipzig/Halle incident.

In the past, German officials have blamed Russia for what they term hybrid attacks — incidents of aggression that fall short of acts of war.

"I assume this was a targeted hybrid attack — an attempted act of terror — orchestrated from Russia," Roderich Kiesewetter, a German politician and parliamentary intelligence committee member, told a German newspaper.

Russia's embassy in Berlin did not respond to a request for comment on the drone incident.

What are the stakes?

Tensions have mounted between Germany and Russia over the war in Ukraine and allegations of Moscow's interference elsewhere in Europe.

European security agencies have been investigating a series of incendiary devices in parcels that caught fire in 2024, raising concerns about sabotage of air cargo operators.

Some of the devices were found at a DHL warehouse in Leipzig.

German airports, meanwhile, are on high alert after a series of unauthorised drone overflights at sites including military facilities, energy terminals, seaports and logistics companies that police have said could have been organised by Russian agents.

Russia has denied any involvement in the 2024 incidents and overflights.

Reuters

World.title: US Senate panel votes to hold Fauci in contempt over COVID hearing
World.content:
A US Senate committee has voted to hold Dr Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress and refer him to the Justice Department for potential prosecution over his refusal to answer questions at a hearing focused on his handling of the COVID pandemic.

Dr Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination more than 100 times when he appeared before the US Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs last week.

Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, the Republican committee chairman, has said that constitutional protection did not apply since Dr Fauci last year received a pardon from former President Joe Biden and thus did not have to worry about the threat of prosecution.

Fauci refuses to answer questions at hearing The former top US infectious disease expert declines to answer questions at a Republican-led Senate hearing, labelling it an "unhinged" campaign to see him imprisoned.

But Dr Fauci, in a statement issued before the hearing, said he had good reason to fear the possibility of criminal charges given what he said was Mr Paul’s determination “to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote, behind bars, unquote.”

“Dr. Fauci faced no risk of federal prosecution," Mr Paul, said at the outset of a hearing.

"All he had to do was tell the truth.”

Mr Paul noted that Thursday's vote has nothing to do with Dr Fauci's policies, opinions or anything he has said in previous congressional appearances.

Instead, the senator said, “We are voting on whether a witness who has received the benefit of a sweeping pardon can be ordered by this committee to answer questions and then defy that order without consequence.”

Rand Paul said the vote was not about Dr Fauci's policies or opinions. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

Dr Fauci's pardon from Mr Biden covered acts from 2014 through the January 2025 day it was issued.

It does not shield Dr Fauci from state-level prosecutions or from investigations into any testimony that he did give that politicians thought was false.

Dr Fauci will now be referred to the US attorney's office in Washington, which would make a decision on whether or not to investigate or potentially attempt to prosecute the doctor for contempt.

Mr Paul, who has previously sent referrals on Dr Fauci on his own, acknowledged on Wednesday, local time that contempt resolutions have often gone through the full Senate but said he did not “want to waste time” moving the matter to a vote of the full Senate, where it would be unlikely to muster the required 60 votes needed to advance.

“We still might come to the floor,” he said. “But at this point, the first thing we will do is we will send it over as a recommendation from our committee, if it passes.”

AP

World.title: North Korea fires ballistic missile towards Japan as region boosts military
World.content:
North Korea fired a short-range ballistic missile over the Sea of Japan, according to Japan and South Korea's militaries, a day after Pyongyang criticised Japan's military build-up in the region.

The launch from North Korea's eastern coastal Wonsan area was detected about 5pm Thursday, local time, prompting South Korea's military to bolster its surveillance and share details with the United States and Japan.

South Korea's presidential office said it held an emergency security meeting, condemning the launch as a provocative act that violated United Nations Security Council resolutions.

Authorities in Seoul and Washington were now analysing the missile's exact specifications.

Japan's Defence Ministry said there had been no impact in or around Japan.

In this photo provided by the North Korean government, leader Kim Jong Un supervises the test-firing of two types of new anti-air missiles in 2025. (AP: Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service )

But the country's coast guard had urged ships to use caution and notify authorities if any fallen objects were found.

The ballistic missile launch was North Korea's first since late June, when it tested a tactical ballistic missile, an upgraded 240-mm multiple-launch rocket system and a 155-mm self-propelled howitzer, North Korean state media KCNA said.

Thursday's possible firing comes as the US and South Korean militaries prepare to hold their annual training exercises, aimed at containing the nuclear-armed North, later this month.

US and South Korean officials say the training is defensive in nature, but North Korea believes the manoeuvres are a practice invasion and often responds with its own missile tests and warlike rhetoric.

North Korea, which since 2019 has repeatedly declared itself an "irreversible" nuclear state, featured among growing regional threats in a recent Japanese government assessment.

Japan raised its military expenditure significantly last year. (ABC News: Natalie Whiting)

Japan boosts military with 'sense of urgency'

Tokyo's Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said this week that Japan's military needed to be boosted with a "sense of urgency and crisis".

In a statement carried by North Korean state media on Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong — the sister of leader Kim Jong Un — said Pyongyang's "leadership will set up additional military options which are obviously due to Japan's transformation".

MPs to assess war readiness For the first time since World War II, a formal plan will be proposed, reflecting increasing concerns about conflict breaking out in this region.

Seoul too has strengthened surveillance and maintained readiness for possible additional launches.

Under the South Korea-US combined defence posture "our military is maintaining the capability and readiness to respond overwhelmingly to any provocation", Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said on Thursday.

Tokyo raised its military expenditure by 9.7 per cent to about $88.3 billion in 2025 — equivalent to 1.4 per cent of GDP, its highest share since 1958.

China, a key ally of North Korea, has also recently expressed alarm at what it sees as "new militarism" by Japan.

AFP/AP

World.title: Israel accused of targeting journalists in deadly series of strikes
World.content:
Human rights organisations have accused Israel of committing a war crime in southern Lebanon, alleging the Israel Defense Forces deliberately targeted two Lebanese journalists earlier this year.

Amal Khalil, a 42-year-old journalist working for the Al-Akhbar newspaper, was killed in the attack in the village of Al-Tiri on April 22. Her colleague Zeinab Faraj, a 21-year-old freelance photographer and camera operator, was seriously wounded.

Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch investigated the incident, piecing together firsthand accounts from Faraj, emergency crews who tried to save the pair and examining photos and videos of the attack.

There were three strikes by the IDF on Al-Tiri that day. The military said it had been targeting Hezbollah fighters.

The first strike hit a vehicle in front of the car Khalil and Faraj were in, forcing the journalists to take shelter.

An hour later, a second strike hit their vehicle and the pair were wounded in the explosion. The third strike followed an hour after that.

During that time, Israeli surveillance drones were hovering overhead.

"The drones got extremely close, coming through the broken roof. Less than a meter away," Faraj told investigators.

"I was covering my face, thinking of a video I had seen where a drone killed someone like that. I thought it would explode in my face.

"The drones didn't carry visible explosives, but they were hovering and provoking fear constantly."

At the time, Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam accused Israel of a war crime.

The chain of events led the two human rights organisations to demand an investigation.

"After the first strike had eliminated the military-stated target, and with two drones flying low overhead, the Israeli military knew or should have known that two civilian women were sheltering in that building," Amnesty International's Heba Morayef said.

"Despite this, they proceeded with what we have reasonable grounds to believe amounted to a direct attack on civilians, demonstrating a shocking disregard for international humanitarian law."

Human Rights Watch said the investigation shattered the IDF's insistence that it did not target journalists.

"The facts and evidence show that it has repeatedly done so," the organisation's Ramzi Kaiss said.

"Amal Khalil and Zainab Faraj are the latest victims in a long series of such attacks.

"The evidence is clear that the Israeli military knew or should have known that Faraj and Khalil were civilians, but attacked them anyway, and then prevented paramedics from rescuing them for hours."

Investigations outline timeline of the incident

The investigations laid out a timeline of events leading up to the first, second and third strikes.

They found Khalil and Faraj had driven towards Al-Tiri, close to the town of Bint Jbeil, on April 22.

The purpose of their journey was to verify reports Israeli soldiers had withdrawn from the area, as part of their reporting on the war in Lebanon.

The pair were following another vehicle driven by Ali Nabil Bazzi, the local mayor, and his friend Mohammed Hourani.

The IDF has claimed the two men were Hezbollah operatives.

Moments after arriving in Al-Tiri, before 2:30pm, the vehicle the two men were in was attacked.

Calls we made to the Lebanese Civil Defence and the Lebanese Red Cross a little more than 10 minutes later.

One of the Civil Defence officials said the crews were held at a Lebanese military checkpoint and told by officers they were waiting for approval from the IDF to enter the site.

This was a process implemented as part of the November 2024 ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah, involving officials from the UN peacekeeping force stationed along the border to monitor the situation.

Still stuck at the checkpoint, Civil Defense called the journalists and told them to rush to leave the area immediately as there was no guarantee Israel would not attack again.

Screenshots of a video call between Faraj and her sister show the car travelling in front of Khalil and Faraj burning after the Israeli strike. (Supplied: Human Rights Watch)

The pair had been seeking shelter near their car and surveillance drones were circling.

"There was a crack in the roof, and we could see the quadcopter right above peering in," Faraj told Human Rights Watch.

"For one hour, we waited under the tiled roof and the entire time there were two quadcopters above us.

"The quadcopter would go up and come down. It kept doing this."

At about 3:40pm, the second strike hit the journalists' car. Khalil and Faraj were injured in the attack but managed to get word back to the Civil Defense that they could not get out.

"Glass and debris flew toward us. My ear felt like it burst," Faraj told Amnesty International.

"She [Amal Khalil] was bleeding heavily from the nose and head and had shrapnel wounds in her arm and thigh; she couldn't move her leg."

The women managed to seek shelter inside a nearby building while waiting for help. Civil Defense crews remained waiting at the checkpoint.

Red Cross abandoned scene due to threat

The third Israeli strike, according to the investigations, came at about 4:25pm.

It hit the building the women were hiding inside, causing it to collapse and trapping them under the rubble.

The Lebanese Red Cross was given permission to enter the area after 5pm, without Civil Defense support, and the crews managed to rescue Faraj.

She had suffered a fractured skull, injuries to her right eye and leg, and a crushed hand. Khalil remained trapped under the rubble.

The Red Cross crews were forced to leave at about 6pm after threats of further attacks.

It was not until about 7:20pm that authorisation was received for crews to return to the site — and only after a flurry of phone calls, including from the offices of the Lebanese president and prime minister.

This time, Red Cross crews arrived with an ambulance and a small bulldozer to try to pick through the rubble of the building.

Islamic Risala Scout Association paramedics waiting for approval to access al-Tiri at a Lebanese Army checkpoint 2.6 kilometres north of the strike site. (Supplied: Human Rights Watch)

That work began at 9pm and Khalil's body was recovered. Her time of death, as recorded on her death certificate, was 7pm. The cause was recorded as "cardiac arrest due to a head trauma and severe bleeding".

Amnesty International said the Lebanese government should join the International Criminal Court and demand an investigation for war crimes.

"The impunity enjoyed by Israeli forces for the killing of journalists and other civilians in Lebanon over the past three years has enabled the Israeli military to continue with its unlawful air strikes, including direct attacks on civilians," Ms Morayef said.

"Amal Khalil's killing must be independently and impartially investigated. It is well past time that the international community impose a comprehensive arms embargo on Israel."

Israel claims two Hezbollah military operatives killed

In response to the investigation by the human rights groups, the IDF told the ABC that Khalil was killed "during a sequence of events in which two military operatives in Hezbollah's military wing, Ali Nabil Bazi and Mohammad Al-Khourani, were eliminated".

"The incident has been referred to the General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism to conduct a comprehensive factual assessment," it said in a statement.

"Upon its completion, the findings will be submitted to the Military Advocate General for review, who will determine whether any additional measures are required.

"The IDF regrets any harm caused to journalists. The IDF does not target journalists and respects freedom of the press and the important role journalists play."

World.title: Legend's first try in 1426 days inspires Cowboys turnaround
World.content:
North Queensland hit back from last week's debacle to re-enter the NRL's top eight with a 30-8 win over Gold Coast, as playmaker Jaxon Purdue turned from villain to hero.

When the Cowboys lost 82-12 to Sydney Roosters in their previous outing in Townsville there were huge doubts they could bounce back from the most points conceded in a premiership match in 91 years.

At Robina, in front of 11,740 fans, the Cowboys got the response coach Todd Payten wanted after he labelled last week the club's "darkest day".

Scott Drinkwater, Jason Taumalolo, Heilum Luki and Purdue — four of their biggest stars — came up with key plays at the right time on Thursday to ensure the rout by the Roosters would not derail their season.

This was a test of character, which the Cowboys passed. It wasn't pretty, but it was enough to secure their 12th win of the year and move temporarily to seventh on the ladder. One more win may be enough to play finals.

"I'm really proud of their efforts and that we held our nerve," said Cowboys coach Todd Payten.

"I have no doubt about who we are and what we can be.

"I stressed this on Monday, one game doesn't define who we are.

"I'd take a win any way it comes, but we played with a fair bit of control and I didn't think the game was in doubt after 18-4. We stuck at it.

"We had to do it the hard way, defending our line in the first half and with the sin bin in the second half."

The turning point came in the second half when the Cowboys led 18-8. Purdue had been sin-binned for a professional foul and two minutes after returning he raced 70m from dummy-half to score an individual try for the ages.

Veteran prop Taumalolo set the scene in the fifth minute when he broke a 69-game try drought with a barnstorming charge after a scintillating 40/20 by fullback Drinkwater, his third of the season.

The Cowboys legend's previous try was week one of the finals series in 2022.

Purdue put his halves partner Jake Clifford through a gaping hole for a 12-0 lead after 13 minutes.

But the visitors didn't put their foot on the throat and the Titans found a way back into it.

Winger Phil Sami's 84th try for the club put him one behind Titans all-time record holder Anthony Don, courtesy of a slick Jaylan De Groot pass.

Shocking errors and defence by the Titans all but handed Cowboys second-rower Luki a try on the cusp of halftime.

Sami equalled "The Don" after halftime with his second try of the night after Purdue's infringement.

The Titans could not make the most of the advantage. After Purdue's magic, Luki scored his second try of the night to secure a crucial win.

AAP

Re-live the action in our live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our ScoreCentre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.

World.title: Citizenship granted to Iranian soccer players who sought asylum
World.content:
Two Iranian women's soccer team players who sought asylum in Australia after competing in the Asian Cup have been granted citizenship.

Iran competed in Australia in March as war broke out in the Middle East after a US-Israel attack on the Islamic Republic.

Concerns were raised about the national team's safety after the players refused to sing the Iranian national anthem ahead of their game against South Korea and were criticised on Iranian state television.

Seven team members, including a handler, were granted humanitarian visas to remain in Australia, but five withdrew their claims and returned to Iran.

Concerns were raised over the potential for the players to face retribution from the Iranian government when returning home. (AAP: Russell Freeman)

'Deeply grateful'

The two remaining players, Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh, were granted citizenship on Wednesday.

Ms Pasandideh and Ms Ramezanisadeh were sworn in as citizens by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke at a ceremony in Brisbane.

The women were sworn in by Minister for Home Affairs Tony Burke. (Supplied)

They were accompanied by members of the local Iranian community, with friends and supporters celebrating the occasion.

Ms Pasandideh said it was "one of the happiest days of my life".

"After everything we've been through and all the challenges we faced, this moment means more than words can express," she said.

"Thank you, Australia, for giving me this opportunity. I'm honoured to be part of this nation."

The two women said the ceremony and their citizenship "meant a great deal to us". (Supplied)

Ms Ramezanisadeh said she was "deeply proud to become an Australian citizen".

"Australia has given me the opportunity to build my life and my future, and I feel, more than ever, that I belong here," she said.

" At the same time, my roots and my memories of Iran will always remain a part of who I am. "

More Iranians living 'in limbo'

Associate legal director at the Human Rights Law Centre (HRLC) Laura John urged the government to extend the same pathway to citizenship to Iranians formerly in offshore detention who have been living in Australia for years.

She said the HRLC understood that about 700 refugees have lived in the Australian community for more than a decade on "short-term, insecure bridging visas".

How community united to help Iran's footballers The remaining members of Iran's women's football team might have left Australia, but the journey is far from over, as members of the Iranian-Australian community share what really went into the fight to protect their countrywomen.

"Almost most half are from Iran and cannot return there," Ms John said.

"Many have close family members, including children and spouses, who are Australian citizens or permanent residents."

She said HRLC clients Fatemeh Lahmidi and Mahsa Mazaheri have been in Australia for more than 13 years and have not yet been granted citizenship.

Ms Lahmidi, who is a mother, aged care worker and refugee from Iran, said she was happy for the soccer players but felt "heartbroken" she was unable to obtain citizenship.

"My family has been waiting for so many years, and it's hard to understand why we are still living with so much uncertainty while others receive citizenship so quickly," she said.

"Australia is the only home my children really know.

" We have done our best to build our lives here, and all we want is the chance to stop living in limbo and finally have the safety and security every family hopes for. "

Small business owner Ms Mazaheri said her daughters and husband were Australian citizens and that the country had been her home for more than 10 years.

"It is painful to see the difference in how some people are treated while many others, like us, remain in uncertainty for so many years," she said.

World.title: Police settle lawsuit with Gippsland man left with brain damage
World.content:
A young father who suffered permanent brain damage after a Victorian police officer fell on him during a bungled arrest has quietly settled a lawsuit with the force, in a deal believed to be worth millions.

Brodie Holt last month reached a confidential settlement with Victoria Police in the Supreme Court over the incident outside a pub in his home town of Traralgon, which left him with injuries so severe that he was forced to move back home with his parents.

Mr Holt, now 27, still has no memory of what happened and only remembered waking up in The Alfred hospital after being roused from an induced coma. His family was told he had post-traumatic amnesia.

He watched security footage of the alleged incident on Wednesday for the first time, four years after the incident.

Brodie Holt still has no memory of his 2022 arrest. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"It was pretty brutal," he told the ABC after watching the video.

" They just treated me like I was some piece of meat. "

"[They were] just throwing me around, pushing me into walls and shit and then I supposedly fell over, which is not what happened at all."

His mother, Kellie Holt, who launched the lawsuit as his guardian, said the incident forever changed the way she saw police.

Brodie Holt has been heavily reliant on his parents since the incident. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

She had to quit her job at the local supermarket to care for her son, who is completely reliant on her.

"No-one is taking accountability for it, they're just throwing money at it to go away," she said.

Her husband, Joe Holt, said it had shattered his trust in police.

"Now I wouldn't trust them at all. I would never contact them even if someone was trying to break into my house," he said.

Kellie Holt says her family would never trust the police again. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Arrest happened on Mother's Day

A Victoria Police spokesman said allegations against an officer were "found to be unsubstantiated".

"Victoria Police resolved a subsequent civil claim based on independent legal advice," the spokesman said.

Court documents reveal that the special damages claimed by the young father — including medical treatment, loss of earnings and ongoing care — come in at $13.7 million.

On Mother's Day in 2022, Mr Holt was out drinking with friends at the Hotel Traralgon when he was arrested by three police officers in the early hours of the morning.

The details of what happened before, during and after the incident are still hotly contested by both sides in court documents seen by the ABC.

Brodie Holt's lawyers say he broke no laws when arrested at the Hotel Traralgon in 2022. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Lawyers for Mr Holt said he had broken no laws when he was arrested and escorted outside where he was handcuffed.

They told the Supreme Court he was shoved into a brick doorway on the way out and that after he spat on the ground he was threatened, grabbed by the throat, thrown against a brick wall and then tackled to the ground where his head struck the concrete.

Victoria Police said it arrested Mr Holt because he was drunk and a potential danger to himself and others.

They conceded he "struck" a brick doorway on the way out of the pub, but said he spat at police, resisted them after being handcuffed and had to be restrained so he would not headbutt them.

Brodie Holt was put into an induced coma at The Alfred hospital after his arrest. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Victoria Police told the Supreme Court the officer who tackled Mr Holt to the ground "lost his footing and his balance", which caused the young father's head to strike the concrete.

"This was not intended by any police member," it said.

Incident was 'entirely avoidable' says lawyer

Mr Holt was taken to Latrobe Regional Hospital before being flown to Melbourne.

His lawyer, Jeremy King from Robinson Gill, said what happened to Mr Holt was "entirely avoidable".

"At its worst, all you could really say was that Brodie might be guilty of mouthing off to police and as a result of that he suffered a lifetime brain injury," Mr King said.

"He requires care, he won't be able to work and he's very reliant on his parents and family for a lot of support.

His parents say it feels like they're raising their son all over again. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"I think what's important to understand in this case is that this happened in a regional area and that if you live in a regional area, it's almost impossible to complain about police because you're complaining about someone who is effectively in your local community.

" You're effectively trying to complain about your neighbour and it's a huge disincentive for people to make complaints. "

'Forgetful' Brodie now struggles to be a parent

Since his injuries, Mr Holt has moved back into the family home with his parents and remains entirely reliant on them.

"It's like I have to look out for him all over again," Joe Holt said.

His injuries have affected Brodie's parental relationship with his five-year-old daughter. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The couple said it was like living with a forgetful teenager again and that his injuries had affected the relationship he had with his own five-year-old daughter.

"He was always the doting dad running after her, doing everything for her, looking after her," said his father.

"It's just kids growing up, you just put up with it, whereas nowadays he just gets irritated by it all," he said.

" I wanted a normal life with my son, take him out to the footy … that type of shit. "

"And now I can't … he's a different person."

World.title: Bangladesh's ousted 'Iron Lady' plans to return to politics. Can she do it?
World.content:
Politics has defined almost every chapter of Sheikh Hasina's life.

Widely known as Bangladesh's "Iron Lady" during her 15 years in power, the former prime minister and daughter of the country's founding leader lived a life shaped by the nation's most powerful political dynasty.



She was last seen in her home country fleeing on a military helicopter while thousands of protesters stormed her official residence, the culmination of weeks of mass demonstrations against her leadership.



Now, two years later, a rare appearance from the 78-year-old suggests she is unwilling to accept that her political career is over.

Despite being sentenced to death by Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal, she used her first public address since fleeing the country in 2024 to publicly declare she would return home in December.

Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina vows to return to Bangladesh The 78-year-old fled to India in August 2024 by helicopter at the height of the student-led uprising that toppled her government.

In a tightly packed room at New Delhi's Foreign Correspondents' Club, journalists strained to hear the former prime minister via a dodgy audio link on a large screen.

But rather than confront the crimes she has been convicted of, and sentenced to death over, in Bangladesh, the press conference instead resembled a carefully choreographed relaunch of her now-banned Awami League.

Rather than reflecting on the allegations against her, Hasina spoke of returning to Bangladesh and reclaiming her political future.

Will Sheikh Hasina really return?

Sheikh Hasina's family were assassinated in the 70s, forcing her into exile. (AP: Pavel Rahman)

The prospect of returning to Bangladesh is hardly an attractive one.

Beyond the death sentence, Hasina faces multiple criminal cases, including allegations of murder, attempted murder and abduction. Bangladesh's BNP government has repeatedly said she would be arrested immediately upon arrival.

But whether she ultimately boards a flight to Dhaka may be beside the point.

Simply declaring that she will return allows Hasina to project defiance, reassure loyal supporters she has not abandoned them, and place herself back at the centre of Bangladesh's political conversation.

Her return would also create a dilemma for Bangladesh's government.

Tarique Rahman became Bangladesh's prime minister earlier this year. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Although the BNP has repeatedly demanded Hasina's extradition, bringing her back into Bangladesh also risks reigniting the political tensions that have only recently begun to settle after years of upheaval.

Sreeradha Datta, an international affairs professor at Om Prakash Jindal Global University, said that despite the Awami League being banned from politics, Hasina's public statement would likely "uplift the lagging spirit" of loyalists.

"There is very little leadership; most of the senior Awami leaders have fled. I think this is Hasina's way to motivate them," she said.

Professor Datta said the BNP government likely feared Hasina's return would spark a mass mobilisation of Awami League supporters.

"There's the possibility of violence," she said.

Bangladesh court issues death sentence against ex-PM who fled country A Bangladesh court has sentenced ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina to death after finding her guilty of crimes against humanity.

Hasina's political influence is not lost on the BNP.

In the lead-up to the event, Bangladesh's government warned local media against publicising her speech and criticised New Delhi for allowing it to proceed.

Professor Datta also believes the death sentence itself could eventually become negotiable.

"I think they would rethink it. She was the prime minister, and I think the government will say, 'We're a different Bangladesh; we're not vindictive like we used to be' to convey a sense that they are much more evolved."

A calculated move by India

In the days leading up to the event, Bangladesh criticised India for allowing the address to proceed, calling it another setback in already strained bilateral relations.

New Delhi responded by describing it as a private event beyond the government's control.

In practice, however, it is difficult to imagine a politician as controversial and strategically significant as Sheikh Hasina staging a high-profile public appearance in India's capital without approval.

"If the Indian government didn't want this to happen, it would not have happened," Professor Datta said.

The protest movement was met with a violent police crackdown. (Reuters: Mohammad Ponir Hossain)

India's continued decision to shelter Hasina remains deeply contentious. For the families of the estimated 1,400 people killed during the 2024 protests, her exile in New Delhi represents denied justice.

But politically, exile may suit both governments better than extradition.

Bangladesh's BNP government can continue portraying India as the protector of a convicted former leader while avoiding the domestic instability her return could trigger.

India, meanwhile, retains a politician who has been loyal to India's interests for decades and may still command loyalty among sections of Bangladesh's political elite.

World.title: AFL LIVE: ‘We’ve got rid of blokes who were letting us down’: Star’s brutal comment after North’s stunning win
World.content:
The Western Bulldogs blew a golden chance to secure a wildcard berth as North Melbourne snapped a seven-year losing streak against them to claim their biggest scalp of the season.

As important as the win was for Alastair Clarkson’s Kangaroos in a rare prime-time appearance, the biggest beneficiaries of the shock result were not even at Marvel Stadium on Thursday night.

Luke Davies-Uniacke was a man on a mission for North Melbourne. AFL Photos

Wildcard hunters Carlton, St Kilda and GWS stand to gain the most from North’s 23-point win, which has left the Dogs needing to beat either the Blues or Melbourne at the Demons’ MCG fortress to guarantee a spot in the top 10.

World.title: Grand finalists really do face a baptism of fire
World.content:
George Zivkovic of Northmead reckons “talk of the NRL having to move the 2028 NRL Grand Final because of Pope Leo’s visit to Sydney on the October long weekend ignores the possibility of including the pontiff in the bunker for a truly impartial perspective.”

Before we submerge this debate, here’s Col Burns of Lugarno: “Our national underwater hockey team (C8) deserves a catchy, alliterative name that irreverently embodies both reaching the top of one’s game and having a reputation for aquatic invincibility. I’ve left the porch light on for the Harold Holt Hockeyroos.”

It was happy days for Hong Kong resident Richard Cunningham when he realised our quiz compilers get some material from their own backyard: “My first order of business of each day is the Herald Superquiz (I save C8 for lunchtime diversion). While I’m still chasing the elusive perfect 30 score, I have to thank you for providing me with the knowledge to score five of my points on Wednesday’s quiz. Had the questions not seemingly been directly scraped from recent C8 items, I would’ve otherwise been clueless about meatball recipes and underwater team names.”

Crossing certain borders will always cause a scene. Graham Russell of Clovelly recalls that “during our two-person road trip around Europe in April 1971, my colleague and I drove from Spain to Morocco via Ceuta. I was accepted with a smile, but my colleague was rejected because his hair was too long. He had to drive from Ceuta back to a village twenty kilometres away for a haircut. It was a dreadful haircut, but Ceuta accepted him.”

Mary Carde of Parrearra (Qld) finds that some inventions leave her cold: “I’ve been wondering, has there been a more spectacularly pointless invention to date than the single bottle electric wine chiller that was trendy in the early 2000s, and which was about as useful as a solar-powered torch in a cave?”

World.title: ‘The pressure is on Australia’: Eddie Jones fires a shot at the Wallabies. Sort of
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘The pressure is on Australia’: Eddie Jones fires a shot at the Wallabies. Sort of Iain Payten August 6, 2026 — 9:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

He came, he zoomed, he logged off. So went a brief, and only mildly spicy, pre-game press conference from Eddie Jones on Thursday night, as his Japan side prepares to meet the Wallabies on Saturday in Osaka. Eddie Jones at Japan training. Getty Images The anticipation of some verbal fireworks from Jones was only natural. Here is a man who has, over the course of his long career, made an art of dropping a well-placed barb or pressurising critique of a green rival. Sometimes, as it unfolded near the end days of his ill-fated 2023 Wallabies return, those barbs were even aimed straight back at the scribes asking the questions, along with instructions to apply some self-inflicted upper cuts.



Jones departed the Wallabies soon after and landed back in Japan. Almost three years on, Australia are in Osaka to meet his Brave Blossoms. It is not the first meeting - Jones’ side lost to the Wallabies in Tokyo last year - but with residual tension still in the air, a new Wallabies coach and Japan an ever-improving side, the clash on Saturday still carries just as much meaning. And so it came to pass that Jones was sitting at a desk in the Japan team hotel on Thursday night, doing a press conference after naming his side to meet the Wallabies. For reasons not explained, the conference was not in person, but rather conducted on Zoom. A handful of Australian journalists sat dotted amid a group of around 40 Japanese entrants. Japan coach Eddie Jones looks on during a session. Getty Images The fireworks would have to be virtual. “It’s another test match for us to grow and learn and compete against the team in the top eight in the world,” Jones said. “You know, our record against Australia, there’s been seven official Test matches, we don’t have a win yet, so it’s a fantastic opportunity for Japan to create new history.



“And we saw last year that we were getting closer to Australia, and believe that gap, if there’s a gap now, is going to be minimised again on the weekend.” So far, so diplomatic. Jones was asked about the make-up of his team, which surprisingly didn’t contain former Reds big man Harry Hockings in the starting side. Wallabies coach Les Kiss had, just hours earlier, said they’d identified Hockings and captain Warner Dearns as the major threats for Japan. Jones had moved another Aussie, Jack Cornelsen, into the second row to pick Kanji Shimokawa, a mobile backrower tasked with shutting down Fraser McReight. “This is the best 23 and we’ve got the highest confidence that they can do the job for Japan on the weekend at Osaka,” he said. Eddie Jones resigned as Wallabies coach after failing to make it out of the World Cup group stage in 2023. Getty



“The team’s prepared really well. I think we probably had one of our best preparation periods, and we feel like we’re ready to go after Australia. You know, there’s a lot of pressure on Australia.” Here we go. “They got a very experienced team,” Jones continued. “It’s a game that they’d be expected to win. So we want to make sure we’re putting pressure on them right from the start.” Before Kiss, Jones was the last Australian coach to take over mid-season, when he replaced Rod Macqueen in 2001. Did he sense that handover could provide the cracks required for Japan to get that win over Australia? “Les and Joe have had a pretty close relationship going back to when Les was in Ireland, so their thinking would be the same,” Jones said. ”



Eddie Jones talks to Les Kiss in 2019 when the pair were coaching in England. nna\sworthington “There’ll be little nuances they change, but I think it’ll be a reasonably easy transition given also that Les coached the Reds and a number of the players he selected have come from the Reds team. “I see that being a fairly seamless transition. Look, we’re more interested in ourselves than Australia. You know, we believe it’s a team that can beat Australia. And Australia’s got a very experienced team. “If you look at a number of those players, they were young players back in the 2023 World Cup, now they have 50 or 60 caps next to their name. “So they’re coming into their prime stage of their careers. So we’re going to have to be at our best, and we’re prepared to be at our best, so we’re really looking forward to getting the chance to make history.”



Just seven players in the Wallabies 23-man squad were at the 2023 Rugby World Cup, and the trio who now have more than 50 caps - Tate McDermott, Rob Valetini and Taniela Tupou - were 24, 25 and 27 in 2023. Related Article Australian rugby The 310 seconds of All Blacks defence that should give Wallabies fans hope But never mind that. Back to the fireworks. Jones was asked if the heatwave conditions in Japan at the moment could be to his side’s advantage over the Wallabies. “Well, I’ve never gone to France at Stade de France and they put on the heaters for you, have you?” he asked.



No Eddie. “That’s Test match rugby, you know? You go home and away, and you play in the conditions.” And then - 18 minutes into a 30-minute press conference - thanks were offered and the screen went blank. Jones had gone, the Zoom was over and those fireworks had failed to truly pop or crackle. Oh well. There is always game day.
